News.title: Four rushed to hospital after smoke fills plane forcing passengers to use oxygen masks as pilot makes emergency landing
News.content:
MID-AIR CHAOS Four rushed to hospital after smoke fills plane forcing passengers to use oxygen masks as pilot makes emergency landing







Next

SEVERAL passengers have been rushed to hospital after a plane was forced to make an emergency landing in Portugal.

Fourteen people were treated for smoke inhalation, with four passengers rushed to hospital to receive medical treatment after smoke was detected in the cabin.



The flight was en route to Boston, US, when it was forced to make an emergency landing in Porto on Saturday afternoon.

On board the Airbus A330, 12 of those affected had to be given oxygen mid-air, according to the Portuguese press.



As the aircraft was about to cross the Atlantic Ocean, it made a sudden u-turn and flew south-easterly.

The crew then declared an emergency using squawk code 7700 and diverted to landing at Porto’s Sá Carneiro Airport.



A level two alert was sounded around 5.30pm to warn emergency teams of the aircraft’s arrival.

Firefighters, police, and ambulances were mobilised on the tarmac to prepare for the plane’s unscheduled landing.



Additionally, air traffic in the area was momentarily suspended to allow for a safe touchdown.

In total, four passengers were rushed to hospital, with two men admitted to Sao Joao Hospital’s A&E suffering from smoke inhalation.

A spokesman said both had “mild” respiratory symptoms and were in a stable condition.

The remaining 282 uninjured passengers were evacuated and placed on an alternative flight scheduled for this afternoon.

The plane had taken off from Barcelona’s El Prat airport around 3.40pm local time and landed around 3 hours later.



Disruptions to the airport’s operations are understood to have been brief.

Popular flight tracking sites, such as FlightRadar24, monitored the whole ordeal for aviation fanatics to follow.

News.title: Elderly man, 84, rams car into wife & kills her during botched parking attempt before causing £80K damage in crash spree
News.content:
OAP HORROR Elderly man, 84, rams car into wife & kills her during botched parking attempt before causing £80K damage in crash spree







Next

AN ELDERLY man rammed into his wife and killed her during a failed parking attempt in Germany, police said.

The 84-year-old man was reversing his car in Niedernhausen when he smashed into a parked vehicle.



He then accelerated forwards at high speed and hit his wife who was standing in front of the car, police said.

Cops are continuing to investigate the tragic death.



After fatally striking his wife, the man reportedly continued to race down the road at a terrifying speed.

He collided with several garden fences, two parked cars and a camper van.



His car later came to a halt after making it just 500ft, police said.

Initial estimates put the damage at more than £86,000.

The wife tragically died at the scene while her husband was taken to hospital with serious injuries.

It remains unknown why the man sped from the scene of his dying wife.



A police probe into the incident continues.

It comes after another terrifying incident that saw a driver launch his car into the air during a high-speed chase with cops in America.

The jaw dropping scene unfolded as the man fled the scene of a traffic stop.

In shocking dashcam footage, police were seen pursuing the man in a white car as the chaos unfolded.

The driver suddenly swerved his vehicle to the right as it sped down the I-41 at Military Road in Wisconsin.



Careening the car across two lanes, the vehicle then ploughed straight off the road.

It crossed the grass bank between two intersections, then sped up the small road-side ditch.

In a hair-raising second, the vehicle became airborne as it flew over another car.

The vehicle then crashed down on the other side of the road and ground to a halt.

Abandoning the crashed car, the driver attempted to flee across an empty field on foot but was quickly accosted and arrested by police.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

According to Wisconsin State Patrol, there was an active felony warrant out for the vehicle in the county.

During a routine traffic stop, the driver took off after a Fond du Lac County sheriff’s deputy and another trooper arrived.

News.title: First Strictly live show had its messy moments – but it reminded us of some important truths about the show
News.content:
Next

FIRST we had the silences from Josh Widdecombe missing his cues, then the maelstrom of Johannes Radebe trying to speak amid the cheers of the Clauditorium.

Finally a third sound – Strictly producers frantically ringing round agents to see if Mick Fleetwood and Sam Fox were still available.



A bit harsh, I know.

After all The Brits is a big beast to harness and Mick and Sam didn’t have Emma Willis there to save them, either.



She was, once again, absolute perfection amid the messier moments of Saturday night’s first live show.

But overall, it really wasn’t that bad at all.



Strictly is always greater than the sum of it’s not insubstantial parts and perhaps we’re all over scrutinising the presenters?

Let’s not forget Tess Daly was nicknamed the Tess-bot by some unkind viewers and Claudia Winkleman was initially greeted with some scepticism when she first started.

But in the end they bedded in nicely as a duo.

In fact Saturday night’s episode was a reminder of some important truths about Strictly.



Nothing, and no one, is bigger than the show.

Also, the fame of the competing stars really doesn’t matter as much as the performances, and the judges – particularly the consistently hilarious Craig Revel Horwood – are actually more important than the hosts.

Which is just as well.

If all else fails we can, obviously, rely on Katya Jones doing something with one of the male celebrities that will keep us distracted until Christmas.



Sometimes it’s dancing.

News.title: Three people rushed to hospital after being cut free from two mangled cars following serious crash
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

CRASH PANIC Three people rushed to hospital after being cut free from two mangled cars following serious crash







Next

THREE people have been rushed to hospital after being cut free from two mangled cars following a horror crash.

Emergency services rushed to Blackrod Bypass in Bolton, Greater Manchester at at around 4.20pm on Sunday.

Fire crews quickly arrived on the scene as they pulled out three people trapped in the wreckage.

They were treated at the scene by emergency medics before being raced to hospital for further treatment.





The circumstances around the shocking crash currently remain unclear.

Cops have closed the A6 in both directions as crews continue to clear the area of debris with no indication of when the road will reopen.

The fire services were at the scene for around 90 minutes before leaving.

A spokesperson for Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service (GMFRS) said: “At around 4:20pm this afternoon (Sunday, 27th September), firefighters were called to reports of a crash on Blackrod Bypass in Blackrod, Bolton.

“Two fire engines from Horwich and Hindley fire stations, along with the Enhanced Rescue from Leigh fire station, quickly arrived at the scene which involved a collision between two cars.

“Firefighters extricated three casualties who were trapped inside the vehicles.

“All casualties were treated by colleagues from the North West Ambulance Service and conveyed to hospital.

“Greater Manchester Police closed the road in both directions while crews worked to clear the roadway and make the area safe.



“Crews were in attendance for approximately 90 minutes.”

The Sun has contacted Greater Manchester Police and North West Ambulance Service for comment.

News.title: Starving Ukrainians left for dead in besieged city by Putin & forced to eat only weeds as ‘Russians shoot down supplies’
News.content:
VLAD'S BARBARITY Starving Ukrainians left for dead in besieged city by Putin & forced to eat only weeds as ‘Russians shoot down supplies’







Next

STARVING Ukrainian civilians have been left for dead with Vladimir Putin’s brutal forces accused of shooting down and stealing aid drops.

The Russian-occupied city of Oleshky was once brimming with life before it was captured by Putin’s ruthless troops with terrified residents now forced to survive on just weeds.



Home to 24,000 people in 2022, Oleshky now serves as a desperate hideout for an estimated 6,000 people – including 200 malnourished children.

Tetiana Hasanenko, Head of Oleshky City Military Administration, said food was last officially delivered on May 26.



With the constant fear of prowling Russian drones, bodies of the dead are left to be eaten by dogs in the streets.

The population is living under a “full blockade” by Russian forces, according to Ukraine‘s Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.

Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the city.

He warned of a coming “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”.



Over the weekend, the Ukrainian military used large drones to carry out the first airdrop of emergency food, water and medical supplies for months.

The military governor’s office said four tonnes of food were dispatched to 100 locations.

But it was unclear how much made it to ground before it was intercepted by patrolling Russian troops.



It came after Moscow reportedly rejected a ceasefire to evacuate civilians again.

Ukraine’s successful drone campaign targeting Russian supply lines has resulted in Putin’s desperate troops stealing what little food Ukrainians have left.

In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they survived on one meal of soup made from courgette and weeds a day.

“We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer.

“Come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying.”



The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years ago.

Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced “a critical situation” and “problems with supplies of food and medicine”.

But the regime said it was working to resolve the issues and instead blamed Kyiv.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ukrainian officials believe Russia is preventing evacuation of the remaining civilians to try and ward off a Ukrainian counterattack.

Hasanenko said: “The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields.”

News.title: Labour’s disastrous stampede down Benefits Street will never end – so does spendaholic Burnham have courage to stop it?
News.content:
Next

ON this day 50 years ago, Labour Chancellor Denis Healey was nursing a VIP gin and tonic at Heathrow ahead of a flight to an International Monetary Fund summit.

The global economy was under threat from a Middle East oil crisis and the IMF was on standby as a last-resort cashpoint to save poor countries from going broke.



As Healey waited for his plane, a shock collapse in the Pound turned Britain into one of those countries.

The Chancellor was forced to go cap-in-hand for a multi- billion dollar IMF loan to bail out his own Treasury crisis.



With a threatened currency, soaring inflation and sky-high oil prices — an echo of events today — a humiliated UK became The Story.

“Britain is bust,” trumpeted The Economist.



“Goodbye, Great Britain,” chorused the Wall Street Journal.

Half a century later, we face a mirror image of the crippling debt crisis that brought this once-great nation to its knees.

And we have another Chancellor Healey — ex-Defence supremo John Healey — whose task is to save us from going bust.

The September 28, 1976, fiasco coincided then as it does today with the annual Labour conference, then in Blackpool.



PM Jim Callaghan told sullen trade union bosses: “We used to think you could spend your way out of a recession.

“I tell you in all candour, that option no longer exists.”

Instead of seeing sense, the comrades stepped up their “wildcat” strikes, paralysing the NHS and state-run car, coal, steel and railway industries.

It was the beginning of the infamous Winter of Discontent.

Today the warning signs are flashing again from friends and critics of this spendaholic Labour regime.



Does Labour PM Andy Burnham have the courage this week to tell welfare-hooked socialist MPs that their bloated £330BILLION benefits bill is “no longer an option”?

Will he listen to Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden, who moans that every Cabinet big-spender asks: “Who can we tax to pay for benefits”?

Does the PM understand UK taxpayers cannot for ever carry the £3TRILLION burden of national debt?



Or pay the £110billion- a-year interest due to the bond market he blames?

Burnham cannot pretend he doesn’t know.

Nor can he resort to blaming the Tories — even Liz Truss.

His pal, Labour economic guru Lord Jim O’Neill, warns Britain’s debt-interest costs are “increasingly crazy”.

Labour fan and ex-Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane says: “The Achilles heel of this Government has been its unwillingness or inability to cut public spending.”



In 1979, as hospital admissions were vetted by striking health workers and rubbish piled up in the streets, Jim Callaghan asked: “Crisis? What crisis?”

It was his defining moment as PM.

Today the IMF itself fears a replay unless Labour slashes its monstrous debt and cuts handouts.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva says: “It’s impossible to stress strongly enough how critical it is to take the steps necessary.”

These warnings will fall on deaf ears in Liverpool this week.



Labour MPs have already toppled one prime minister over the two-child benefit cap.

They will not vote to slow the stampede down Benefits Street.

Chancellor Healey Mk2 might try in his October 28 budget to seem prudent.



As they say, you can put ­lipstick on a pig. But it’s still a pig.

Burnham himself shows no sign of grasping the lesson.

He thinks the Seventies were Britain’s Golden Age.

Yet the 1976 meltdown led to almost two decades of Tory rule, neutered trade union militants and Britain’s revival from “Sick Man of Europe” to world-beating economy.

The union militants have not gone away.



They have simply moved to the public sector — Whitehall, local government, the judiciary and the police.

They run our shroud-waving charities and multi-billion pound quangos.

Under the pro-Gaza flag, they now control the Home Office, Border Force and immigration tribunals.



Spiteful socialists despise everything that once made Britain great . . . free speech, a free Press and the rule of law.

They loathe the capitalist system which uses those freedoms to create prosperity instead of forcing us to rely on state handouts.

It is strange but true that Labour MPs love mass immigration and open borders.

So-called asylum seekers are mostly frauds but the issue divides society usefully.

It fuels public anger over the huge cost of migrant health care, and the unfairness of housing and education, at the expense of the citizens who foot the bill.



Ministers will do nothing this week to stop it.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

At some point, voters will decide enough is enough.

And that will be the end of Andy Burnham’s butterfly reign as Prime Minister.

News.title: Man, 44, charged with murder after beloved mum, 44, found dead in flat above city pub
News.content:
MURDER CHARGE Man, 44, charged with murder after beloved mum, 44, found dead in flat above city pub







Next

A MAN has been charged with murder after a beloved mum was found dead in a flat above a city pub.

Leanne Park, 44, was pronounced dead inside a flat over The Greyhound on Parkgate in Darlington, Durham at around 9.15pm on September 23.



Andrew Bell, of Darlington, has now been charged with murder and remanded in police custody, Durham Police said.

The 44-year-old will appear at Newton Aycliffe Magistrates’ Court on Monday.



A 27-year-old man arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender has been released on bail, the force added.

Leanne’s family paid a heartbreaking tribute to her as “the best mam, nana, daughter, and friend we could wish for” on Saturday.

They said: “She was loved by everyone and would do anything for anyone.

“She was the life and soul of the party and loved to dance.



“We love her so much and miss her more than words can describe. We are completely devastated. Her death has ripped the heart out of our family.

“We are grateful for all the kind messages and the support since her death.

“We ask that everyone remembers her for the kind-hearted woman she was.”

Emergency services had been called to the pub at around 9.15pm on Wednesday, September 23.

Tragically, despite the best efforts of medics, Leanne was pronounced dead at the scene.



Durham Police said a cordon will remain in place for some time.

The force said specialist crime scene investigators continue to work at the scene.

Leanne’s death has sparked an outpouring of tributes, including with bouquets of flowers which have been left outside the pub.

One tribute read: “Always in our hearts, taken too soon. Heaven has gained a beautiful angel”.

Another said: “RIP our beautiful Auntie. You are so loved and going to be a huge miss, love you always”.



Her colleagues at the Ventress Hall care home in Darlington previously said she would “do anything for anybody”.

In a Facebook post the home, said: “I can’t actually believe I am writing this, but it is with a heavy heart that I say we have lost our friend and work colleague, Leanne.

“Leanne was always so kind and would do anything for anybody, especially our residents.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The world is beyond cruel and you have been taken too soon. We love you much Leanne. Love all your Ventress Work Family. You will never be forgotten. Our condolences to all Leanne’s family.”

A spokesperson from Durham Police said: “Anyone with any information is asked to call Durham Constabulary on 101, quoting incident number 521 of September 23.”

News.title: Body pulled from water in search for missing teen who vanished over 10 days ago sparking urgent seaside search
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TRAGIC GEORGE Body pulled from water in search for missing teen who vanished over 10 days ago sparking urgent seaside search







Next

A BODY has been found in the agonising search for an 18-year-old who vanished in a seaside town over ten days ago.

George, from Portishead in Somerset, was last seen in the coastal town at around 8.20pm on Thursday, September 17.



A large search was launched in the days that followed, involving cops, coastguard teams, the RNLI and other emergency services.

But police have now confirmed a body has been recovered from a coastal location near Newport on Sunday morning.



Avon and Somerset Police said the clothing worn by the man matched what George had been wearing when he was last seen.

A formal identification process will now be carried out.

Cops have informed George’s family of the latest development.

The force says it is continuing to support them with a specially trained officer.

The force added that the death is not being treated as suspicious.

It will now be a matter for the coroner.



George’s disappearance had prompted repeated appeals for information as emergency crews search the coastline.

Neighbourhood chief inspector Andy Barry previously praised the “strength and resilience” of George’s family during the search.

He said: “I would like to recognise the strength and resilience of George’s family during this time and we continue to keep them updated through a specialist liaison officer.”

The force added that George’s family had been touched by the support they have received.

News.title: Five arrested as counter-terror police investigate major incident near RAF Fairford
News.content:
Five men have been arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act and explosive offences after three "suspicious vehicles" were reported travelling towards an RAF base, police have said.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire were evacuated following the report at about 00:45 BST on Sunday.

An Army explosive ordnance disposal team has been examining vehicles near the base, which is used by the United States Air Force (USAF), as counter-terror police lead the investigation.

Residents evacuated from the nearby village of Whelford have been told they will not be able to return home overnight, but officials say they believe the incident is contained.

Aerial pictures showed a remote-controlled robot approaching stationary white vans in a wooded area, though its use has not been confirmed by police.

A 400m cordon has been placed around the area, where a hazardous area response team was deployed as part of a major emergency service response.

News.title: Protesters disperse after blocking controversial Orange Order parade
News.content:
Hundreds of protesters blocked a road in Portadown on Sunday after a contentious Orange Order parade was given late-night clearance to march down it for the first time in almost 30 years.

Following a series of legal challenges, a ruling by the Parades Commission permitting the Drumcree parade down the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road was upheld in an "unprecedented" sitting of the High Court in Belfast.

Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill joined the protesters, while members of the Orange Order and Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) politicians gathered about a mile away, waiting for the road to clear.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said O'Neill was breaking the law by protesting.

He said the first minister had "broken her pledge of office".

News.title: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
News.content:
"This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack."

The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away.

Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed.

It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz.

Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war.

We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close.

News.title: Watch: BBC reports from the front-line of an escalating war in Yemen
News.content:
In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone, the BBC has travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where the Houthi control ends and no man's land begins.

Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war.

From the front-line a drone is heard above, which a soldier accompanying the crew in south-western Yemen said is usually followed by an attack.

Within about 10 minutes, after the crew had driven away, the loud thuds of strikes followed, senior international investigations correspondent Nawal Al-Maghafi reports.

News.title: My hometown shows that high streets have to change or die
News.content:
The empty building that used to be the home of Marks & Spencer in Aberdeen is one of the first things you see when you arrive off the train and come into the city centre. The sign has gone, though the shape of the lettering can still be made out; the windows are blacked out and the doors boarded up.

This is my hometown. As a teenager, I spent hours on Union Street, its main thoroughfare, nicknamed the Granite Mile after the local silver-grey stone. It was the place to try on all the latest fashions from the likes of Clockhouse and Chelsea Girl.

The street used to be packed with shoppers from across the north-east of Scotland.

Now, it's pockmarked with empty shops.

"I come to Union Street to take a bus somewhere else... there's nothing to shop for nowâ¦ it's horrendous," complains Marie Sim, a lifelong Aberdeen resident.

It's a similar story across the country: High Streets, once bursting with shops, hit first by the rise of out-of-town retail centres and then by online commerce.

But Aberdeen is in the thick of an ambitious turnaround plan. The port city has essentially declared war on its empty shop problem, taking an unusually hands-on approach to filling vacant units and bringing long-neglected upper floors of buildings into use.

News.title: Republic of Ireland 'raised awareness worldwide' in Israel game
News.content:
The Republic of Ireland players were jeered by the small number of Israel fans in attendance when they emerged for their pre-game warm-up.

While the FAI confirmed no tickets would be sold to Republic of Ireland supporters, a handful of fans were spotted inside the stadium.

Hallgrimsson confirmed Bazunu would be included in the squad for Thursday's game against Austria in Dublin, but not for the second match against Israel.

"I think he is very happy that we have won the game," said Hallgrimsson.

"Nobody was questioning his decision. It was only the timing that was difficult for us to kind of react to it, but none of us were asking him not to take his stand and now he's flying back with us on the plane."

When asked if player's opinions regarding the fixture were taken into account when selecting his team for Sunday's game, Hallgrimsson said: "Absolutely not.

"This team selection was about who we thought could make the best performance for Ireland."

During a dramatic day on Saturday, doubts emerged over whether the game would take place after the Republic of Ireland's pre-match news conference was postponed because of the squad meeting.

When the news conference commenced at 14:30 BST on Saturday - more than five hours later than planned - Courell said a players' vote on whether to play the game passed by a "significant majority".

Courell added that the Republic of Ireland would not engage in pre-match formalities such as handshakes.

In 2024, the Ireland women's basketball team chose not to shake hands with Israel players or stand on court for the anthems before a EuroBasket qualifier in Riga, but the teams did exchange handshakes when they met again last year.

The Republic of Ireland have faced calls to boycott the matches since the Nations League draw in February.

Last November, the FAI approved a motion calling for Uefa to suspend Israel from Uefa competitions.

In May, the team's friendly against Qatar was interrupted after fans threw tennis balls featuring the Palestinian flag on to the pitch.

In June, the FAI confirmed their home fixture would be played behind closed doors in Backa Topola instead of Dublin's Aviva Stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil".

At an extraordinary general meeting in July, delegates backed an FAI motion to proceed with the games amid concerns that boycotting the fixtures would cause "significant and lasting harm" for the association.

Calls for the Republic of Ireland to boycott the games have intensified in recent weeks. Earlier this week, more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by Irish Sport for Palestine group urging the team not to play.

Courell also said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the Republic of Ireland and Israel to be kept apart in future competition draws.

Tensions between the teams were raised this week when the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity" after the coach said, "we're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide".

Speaking on Saturday, Hallgrimsson said it was "a wrong word for me to use", while Israel FA head of communications Shlomi Barzel said he would not apologise for his association's response but said he would "take back the word stupidity".

The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

Israel has repeatedly denied that it has committed genocide, as well as war crimes and crimes against humanity. It says its military operations in Gaza have been conducted in self-defence and in accordance with international law.

News.title: Healey to promise 'new age of industrialisation' for UK in conference speech
News.content:
John Healey will promise "a new age of industrialisation" for the UK, when he delivers his first Labour conference speech as chancellor on Monday.

Healey will tell delegates "our coal mines are not coming back", but that Labour will remake Britain's industrial past "for the modern age" by backing advanced manufacturing.

He will also announce plans to boost Britain's shipbuilding industry, with new orders for Royal Navy floating docks and a maritime research vessel.

With just a month to go until his first Budget, the chancellor is under pressure to cut spending or raise taxes to tackle the ballooning cost of government borrowing.

But he is not expected to reveal any details about his Budget plans in his speech at Labour's annual conference in Liverpool.

Instead, he will attempt to set out a positive vision for the future of British industry, based around what he will call a "new confidence in Britain".

The former defence secretary will announce that three new floating docks at HM Royal Naval Base Clyde, at Faslane, will be built in the UK, rather than put out to international tender.

Plans for the new docks were first set out in 2023 and are expected to upgrade Faslane's facilities for the next generation of British submarines.

The docks form part of a wider Â£15bn upgrade programme for the Royal Navy's shipyards and are expected to come into service in the early 2030s.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh said in a speech on Sunday that the government would also commission a new marine research vessel as part of plans for a "new era of reindustrialisation".

The chancellor is expected to announce Â£115m in funding for the ship, which is also set to come into service in the early 2030s.

Ahead of his speech, Healey said: "By backing British shipyards, we are not only boosting national security but also securing resilience in the industries that will drive growth today while building the capabilities the country needs for the future."

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the plans were "reheated announcements" with "no clarity on where the money is coming from".

He added: "Labour are running scared of making the tough choices needed to pay for Britain's defence.

"All they can offer is reannounced docks and more hot air from Healey. Only the Conservatives will cut the welfare bill to fund defence."

Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, national secretary of the GMB union, which has campaigned for the move, said it would be a "massive boost" for the UK's shipbuilding sector.

"For too long juicy contracts have been sent to overseas - often subsidised - yards.

"This policy could reinvigorate UK yards and the communities that depend on them," he added.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who is due to deliver his big conference speech on Tuesday - has previously spoken about his ambition to "reindustrialise" Britain, including in talks last week with US President Donald Trump.

But in a survey to be published on Monday, the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) will highlight falling economic activity across key sectors such as retail and services in the three months to September, with manufacturing declining more moderately.

CBI deputy chief economist Alpesh Paleja said rising energy and employment costs combined with weak demand were continuing to put pressure on profit margins.

He added: "Uncertainty ahead of next month's Budget is also holding back activity in some sectors.

"Against the backdrop of renewed fiscal pressures, the Budget must draw a clear red line under any more rises in the cost of hiring, investing and doing business."

The chancellor is also under pressure from some of Labour's trade union backers to do more to tackle the cost of living.

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, has called on Healey to "do something for workers and the working class" in his Budget.

She urged him to unfreeze income tax thresholds "to put money back into people's pockets" and take further action on energy bills.

In his conference speech, Healey will also announce plans to bring back a training scheme run by trade unions, to help workers in England gain new skills and adapt as technology, including AI, changes the workplace.

The Union Learning Fund will get Â£15m in taxpayers' money, taken from existing government budgets.

Employees do not need to be union members to benefit, with support options ranging from essential English, maths and digital skills, to training for jobs in growing industries, such as advanced manufacturing.

News.title: More questions than answers after major incident near RAF Fairford
News.content:
But some eyes, too, have turned to Moscow.

Danish intelligence warned last week Russia could in the coming months launch a limited military attack on a Nato country.

Germany has already formally accused Russia of using a drone carrying explosives in an attempted attack on Leipzig in August.

Over the summer, the Russian embassy in London warned the UK against allowing Ukraine to use British drones deep inside Russian territory: "The deeper [the UK's] involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv's terrorist machinery, the higher price it will pay."

That, too, was seen as a direct threat.

There are also possibilities of some kind of Islamist attack, or even an incident of direct action by a group opposed to both the US-Israeli war on Iran or the use of UK bases to launch strikes.

One central question is whether the authorities were prepared for such an attack.

The US handles security within the base; the UK is responsible all threats outside the perimeter. What did the authorities know?

President Trump said the suspects had been under investigation "for a long time".

But there are also suggestions the incident was foiled only because a passing driver reported strange vans to the police.

At the time of the explicit Iranian threat against the UK, a spokesman for the Ministry of Defence said: "Our armed forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it's on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself."

So for now, there remain more questions that facts.

Was a hostile foreign state involved, or were proxies acting on its behalf? What was intended and what was the potential risk to local people?

One thing is clear: the threat from conflicts involving the UK will not always stay overseas.

News.title: Burnham proposes NHS-style social care system for England
News.content:
Andy Burnham wants to offer access to free social care services to everyone in England, and will put his plans before voters at the next general election.

The prime minister told the BBC that it would be a system in which "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". He did not rule out tax rises, acknowledging it may be "difficult or unpopular" with some.

Burnham said he wants to set out his "vision" on Tuesday and Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey, who is conducting a review, will advise on the "best way of doing it".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the PM was suggesting Labour wanted "more tax rises" to pay for the reforms, adding the Conservatives would not support this.

Burnham has made reforming social care one of his flagship policies and has spoken of the experience of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's and died earlier this month.

While he has been clear on his ambition to make changes to the system, he has yet to explain how any changes would be funded.

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than Â£23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the prime minister said: "I am talking about a system that works on NHS principles because that is the only way you can make it work.

"There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same and it's not something we're going to rush."

Personal care offered in Scotland is available to all adults who are assessed as needing help with tasks including eating and bathing.

News.title: Ten NHS staff removed over Noah Woods data breach
News.content:
Ten NHS staff have been removed from duty or suspended after a data breach involving the digital medical records of three-year-old Noah Woods.

Launching an "urgent" investigation, Dr Martin Mansfield, deputy chief medical officer at East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust, said that any unauthorised access of patient data was "completely unacceptable".

The trust has apologised "unreservedly" to Noah's family and said disciplinary action would be taken if needed.

A major search for Noah was carried out in the village of Brantham, Suffolk, after the child went missing on 15 September. His body was found the next day in a nearby pond by police divers.

A spokesperson for the trust said 10 employees had been "removed from active duty or suspended whilst investigations are concluded".

It comes after Sir Jim Mackey, the chief executive of NHS England, wrote to every trust on Friday, ordering stronger measures to tackle data breaches.

"We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust, and enough is enough," said Sir Jim.

"Anyone who thinks they can satisfy their curiosity by looking at a patient's record should know this: they will be found out, they may lose their career and could end up with a criminal record."

News.title: More than 50 arrested at Palestine Action support rally
News.content:
Merseyside Police said more than 50 people had so far been detained at the Defend Our Juries event and that officers were in the process of making arrests on suspicion of wearing/carrying an article supporting a proscribed organisation.

A force spokesperson said it respected everyone's rights to protest lawfully while also aiming to keep the peace and ensure public safety.

The force said it made "detailed and co-ordinated plans ahead of such events to ensure it can apply this consistently, fairly and proportionately".

The spokesperson said not everyone present at the protest had been committing a criminal offence.

The arrests were criticised by Amnesty International, which called them a "shameful attack on freedom of speech".

One of those detained was human rights barrister Margaret Owen, 94.

A spokesperson for Defend Our Juries said: "We had hoped the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, would do the sensible thing and bin the ban on Palestine Action given the weight of public pressure to do so and the escalating amount of resources required in enforcing it.

"Continuing the charade of the proscription of Palestine Action is illogical, unsustainable and immoral."

News.title: Thousands affected and roads closed after burst pipe
News.content:
Thousands of homes in parts of West Sussex have water supply issues and a number of roads have flooded after what police are describing as a "significant" leak.

Roads around the Southgate Roundabout in Crawley have been closed on Sunday morning due to the burst water pipe, Sussex Police said.

Southern Water said about 9,000 customers were impacted, but as of 19:45 BST, most customers had seen their supplies restored.

A company spokesperson said: "Our teams are on site and working as quickly and safely as possible to repair the burst and restore supplies."

The company said customers were experiencing a loss of water supply or low pressure in the following areas - Woolborough Road, Holmcroft, Southgate, Tilgate and Furnace Green.

It first reported at 12:00 that supplies had returned to some homes.

Southern Water said its teams were still carrying out repairs but the damaged section of pipe had been removed and its replacement installed.

"We apologise for this disruption and would like to thank customers for their patience while we complete the repair," it added.

John Boulton, who is 82, and his partner were without water earlier.

He said: "It's pretty disgusting, really - we pay so much for the water supply."

Boulton said he had just paid Â£22 for bottled water in a shop.

News.title: Murder probe as cyclist dies following moped crash
News.content:
A murder inquiry has begun after an e-bike cyclist died following a collision with a moped in west London.

Emergency services were called to North Pole Road, North Kensington, at about 01:20 BST on Friday where the seriously injured 24-year-old man was found. He was pronounced dead at the scene shortly after.

Police said the investigation was at an early stage but it was believed the moped had been pursuing the e-bike cyclist prior to the crash.

Dt Ch Insp Neil John said detectives were "pursuing a number of lines of inquiry, including efforts to identify and trace the rider of the moped".

"Our thoughts are with the victim's family at what is a very difficult time," he added.

"We have launched a full investigation and are working hard to get answers and establish exactly what happened.

"As part of this, we're urging anyone who was in the area at the time and may have seen the e-bike or the moped to get in touch with us as soon as possible. If you have any information that could help, please come forward."

News.title: Traitors star burgled after sharing holiday photos
News.content:
Traitors star Paul Gorton did not think twice about sharing photographs on social media while enjoying a family holiday with his wife and two young children.

But when he returned home he discovered that his house in Cheshire had been burgled just days earlier.

"The eerie bit is at 21:10 BST I posted that me and Kate were by the side of the pool, we've got full bellies, the kids are in bed, we're actually having our little bit of the holiday," he said.

"About 20 minutes later, little did we know, our house has been broken into."

Paul's bike as well as several sentimental items including an irreplaceable ring from Kate's grandmother were stolen in the burglary on 28 August.

The perpetrators managed to break in through the bi-fold doors at the back of the house by using a technique known as lock snapping before cutting the broadband connection.

News.title: Man charged with murdering woman in Darlington
News.content:
A man has been charged with murdering a woman who was found dead by police.

Andrew Bell, 44, of Darlington, is accused of killing Leanne Park, 44, in the town on Wednesday.

Durham Police said she was pronounced dead at an address in Parkgate at about 21:15 BST. Her family said she was the "best mam, nana, daughter and friend we could wish for".

Bell is due to appear at Newton Aycliffe Magistrates' Court on Monday.

A 27-year-old man arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender has been released on bail, the force said.

A spokesperson said crime scene investigators would continue to work at the scene and a police cordon was "expected to remain in place for some time".

Anyone with information about the murder is urged to contact detectives.

News.title: Inside the sleepy Cotswold village woken up by a suspected terrorist plot
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For the villagers of Whelford, an early autumn Sunday morning would usually bring very little activity.

With no shops or pub, the community has just a 19th century church, hosting one service a month, and a mixture of homes mostly located on a main road linking the more well-known village of Kempsford and town of Fairford.

But in recent months, tensions had been mounting.

For situated on the village’s doorstep is the RAF Fairford base, where the government has granted the US permission to use for defensive strikes against Iranian missile sites. The move has resulted in increased police presence, as well as hundreds of protestors taking to its streets.

And early on Sunday morning, a usual peaceful morning turned into a desperate scramble for dozens of families who were woken to officers banging at their doors, demanding they evacuate their homes immediately.

With no explanation, or even time to brush their teeth, villagers left behind their pets and headed to the nearby Cirencester Leisure Centre, which is being used as an emergency shelter.

It began when a villager, driving home from a party, called 999 after spotted vans blocking the road and then men in balaclavas heading into nearby trees. Within 15 minutes officers had arrived at the scene, she said.

open image in gallery A vehicle drives past a Whelford sign as police block roads near the RAF Fairford ( Reuters )

“A plucky amateur shouldn’t be spotting an unusual bit of activity at 1am when the air base is on high alert,” she said. “I think it’s absolutely astonishing.”

Quickly, a major incident was declared and a large emergency services presence, which included a Hazardous Area Response Team within a 400-metre cordon, was put in place.

Five men were arrested on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offences. Counter Terrorism Policing detectives took over the response and are said to be investigating whether the alleged plot is linked to Iran, according to The Times.

Aerial footage showed a bomb disposal robot inspecting three white vans, two of which had open rear doors, and were surrounded by large black barrels scattered on the ground.

Julian Tudsbery and his wife were among 85 households ordered to evacuate on Sunday morning.

The Whelford resident, who has lived there for 30 years, was still in his dressing gown when he heard a loud bang on his door around 7am.

“There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there’s been a major incident, said he couldn’t elaborate,” he said.

open image in gallery Armed police set up a cordon in Whelford following the major incident ( PA )

Mr Tudsbery, who had to leave behind his cat, Misty, said a resident had reported three “suspicious vans” in the village in the early hours of Sunday.

Jo, who has lived in Whelford for 18 years, was also evacuated at around 7am and made to leave her dog, Coco, amid the rush.

“We were asleep and [police] were just banging on our door”, she said. “They said it was a critical incident and we’ve got to leave straight away, and they basically wouldn’t leave the doorstep until we left.

“We just had to throw our clothes on and come. We didn’t know anything.”

“(The police) literally waited (at the door). I didn’t even brush my teeth or nothing,” she added. “We didn’t know what, but we knew it must be serious.”

Villagers have described “heightened tensions” and an increased military presence in Whelford in recent months.

open image in gallery Protestors display a banner with the slogan 'US go home' during an anti-war demonstration outside the main gate of RAF Fairford airbase in July ( Reuters )

One woman, who has lived on the perimeter of RAF Fairford for around 50 years and asked not to be identified, said “great big concrete walls” and vehicles had recently appeared at some of the base’s gates.

“In the prior few weeks they have put heavy, very heavy, vehicles across all gates,” she said. “Obviously they’re taking security seriously.”

Jason, who was evacuated to the nearby leisure centre with his family, told reporters he heard a helicopter near the village at around 1.30am.

“Then we were woken up about 6am with a couple of police at the door,” the 50-year-old consultant, who did not want to give his surname, said.

His family left behind their 11-week-old puppy and two cats without knowing what had happened.

open image in gallery An evacuated resident walks at Cirencester Leisure Centre ( Reuters )

“There’s obviously been heightened tensions in the area, because obviously the base is used by USAF.

“The police response was very rapid. They just need to clear the area now. Just hoping to go home.”

Gloucestershire County Councillor Paul Hodgkinson described the incident as “destabilising” for residents, many of whom will not be able to return to their homes on Sunday night.

“We’re not used to something where there’s a potential terrorist incident,” he said. “It’s not something we’ve encountered in Gloucestershire before in recent times, and so it is worrying.

“I mean, clearly it’s destabilising. Although that’s the whole point of terrorism, isn’t it? Is to destabilise. And clearly, we don’t know yet exactly what the circumstances are.”

News.title: RAF Fairford: Terror police ‘investigate Iran link’ to suspected bomb plot near airbase
News.content:

Five men detained near an RAF base used by the US have been arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.

A major incident was declared and 85 homes evacuated near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire after several men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences on Sunday morning.

Counterterrorism police and detectives leading the response are said to be investigating whether the alleged plot is linked to Iran, according to The Times.

Detectives are reported to be keeping an open mind, but one line of inquiry is likely to be whether the incident is connected to Tehran because the base hosts the United States Air Force (USAF) and has been used to launch operations against the Islamic republic.

US president Donald Trump claimed the alleged plot was “looking to do big damage” as he praised the joint operation with UK law enforcement.

“We had them under investigation,” he told reporters in the US. “They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great.”

Four USAF bombers landed at RAF Fairford this spring after then-prime minister Sir Keir Starmer granted permission for “defensive” US action against Iranian missile sites from UK bases.

open image in gallery An image understood to show five men arrested near RAF Fairford. BBC Verify said the picture appeared authentic after geolocating it ( BBC )

In July, the British government insisted it “stands ready 24/7 to defend itself” after Iran said UK airbases used by the US were considered “legitimate targets”.

Aerial footage from the scene in the village of Welford, near the base, showed a British army bomb disposal squad using specialist robotic equipment to examine three white vans.

A force spokesperson said: “At around 12.45am today, police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles, which appeared to be travelling towards the air base.

“Armed officers responded and five men were arrested in the Whelford area on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act. They were further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act.”

Investigators will be working to analyse any devices seized from those arrested to establish details of any plot and any potential motivation.

open image in gallery Counterterrorism police are leading the investigation ( PA )

Fairford has been raised to the highest threat level, Delta, while US airbase Lakenheath in Suffolk is on Charlie alert, the second-highest threat level that can be issued by the US Department of Defense.

The police operation near the village of Whelford in Gloucestershire was not intelligence-led, meaning investigators had not known about any potential plot in advance.

Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said a resident had reported three “suspicious vans” in the village in the early hours of Sunday morning.

“Evidently, they phoned the airbase police, who didn’t answer the phone,” he said. “It just rang out, so she dialled 999.”

He said he was evacuated at around 7am, adding: “(The police) were then banging on the door, so I went downstairs in my dressing gown.

“There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there’s been a major incident, said he couldn’t elaborate.”

A 400m cordon has been put in place around the vehicles while villagers were evacuated to a nearby leisure centre.

A large emergency services presence was seen in the area, including a Hazardous Area Response Team, the fire service and local police.

open image in gallery A US Air Force B-1 Lancer bomber is pictured on the tarmac at RAF Fairford ( AFP/Getty )

Gloucestershire Police said: “A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident.

“It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act. The army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles.

“The local residents are being evacuated to a nearby leisure centre. A cordon is currently in place, but we’d like to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained.

“We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place.”

A spokesperson for the US Air Force said its personnel based at RAF Fairford “remain vigilant”.

“For operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures,” the spokesperson added.

“The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families.

“We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families.”

open image in gallery Fire crews at the scene of the incident in Gloucestershire ( Reuters )

Security measures at the site in southwest England have significantly increased, with roadblocks and armed police preventing access and emergency vehicles parked nearby, Reuters reported on Sunday.

The airbase also hosts the annual Royal International Air Tattoo (RIAT), though this year’s event in May was cancelled because of the military operations.

Prime minister Andy Burnham, currently attending the annual Labour Party conference in Liverpool, is receiving updates on the situation.

A government spokesperson added: “We are grateful to the emergency services, who have acted quickly to detain several suspects and put measures in place to keep the community safe.

“It would be inappropriate to comment further whilst investigations are ongoing.”

Defence secretary Wes Streeting confirmed the incident is “being dealt with” and thanked the emergency teams who acted “so swiftly”.

“It is exactly why our emergency response teams and armed forces are on standby 24/7,” he added.

A woman living on the base’s perimeter described an apparent increase in military security in recent weeks.

open image in gallery RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk has also been put on high alert ( Reuters )

The woman, who asked not to be identified, told the Press Association: “In the prior few weeks they have put heavy, very heavy, vehicles across all gates.”

She described them as “very big tractors and things like that” parked behind crash-gates into the base, adding: “So obviously they’re taking security seriously”.

“Great big concrete walls” have also been placed behind some gates, including on Dunfield Loop and Whelford Road, the resident, who has lived there for about 50 years, told the press association.

The arrests come amid heightened concerns around the threat from hostile states to the UK, with Russia and Iran among those that have used proxies to commit crimes on their behalf on British soil.

Andy Burnham said that “broken” social care will eventually break the NHS as he outlined his plans to reform the system.

At the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, the prime minister will pledge that his government will bring about radical change for Britain, and he told the BBC he would “grasp the nettle” of social care reform in England.

The former Greater Manchester mayor said he would put his plan for a national care service along the lines of the NHS, funded by the taxpayer and free at the point of use, to the public at the next general election.

Mr Burnham, whose father died earlier this month, told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg: “For me, obviously, coming in to this journey as prime minister as my dad was ending his, has been hard.

“But it pushes me on, and I’m going to grasp the nettle on social care.”

He described social care in England as being as “unfair as American healthcare, where the most vulnerable in society can lose everything.”

As the conference began in earnest on Sunday, Merseyside Police arrested two demonstrators outside it during a protest in support of Palestine Action.

Collectable Cluedo coins are being launched by The Royal Mint – which is also offering the chance for one “supersleuth” to win a gold 50p.

The coins are available to buy from the Mint from Monday and have been produced in collaboration with games and toy company Hasbro.

To mark the milestone, The Royal Mint is inviting amateur detectives to solve “the case of the missing coin”, an online competition with the chance of winning a gold Cluedo coin.

Collectable Cluedo coins are being launched by The Royal Mint – which is also offering the chance for one “supersleuth” to win a gold 50p.

A new clue will drop each week on The Royal Mint’s website and social channels, challenging fans to uncover “the who, the where and the what” – the suspect, the location and the coin type.

Those cracking the three clues will be entered into a prize draw for the chance to win a Cluedo Gold 50p coin, which the Mint said is worth more than £2,000.

The competition is free of charge to enter and the winner will be revealed after the case closes on October 19, The Royal Mint said.

Strictly Come Dancing champion Ellie Leach, who played Miss Scarlett in the stage show Cluedo 2, inspected the coins, alongside Marcia Lewis, daughter of the detective-themed boardgame’s creator.

open image in gallery Strictly Come Dancing champion Ellie Leach, who has played Miss Scarlett, inspected the coins, alongside Marcia Lewis, daughter of Cluedo creator (David Parry/PA Media Assignments)

The coin’s design brings Miss Scarlett to life alongside five other suspects – Colonel Mustard, Professor Plum, Mrs Peacock, Reverend Green and Mrs White – with some coin editions featuring colours associated with the board game.

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

The design also contains “hidden” features including intricate microtext naming the game’s characters, locations and weapons, encouraging collectors to reach for a magnifying glass to take a closer look.

Tim Mulhall, head of fandom at The Royal Mint, said: “Every coin we create tells a story, and the Cluedo 50p is no exception.

“Cluedo has captivated millions of players for decades, and we’ve channelled that spirit of mystery and intrigue into every detail of the design.

open image in gallery (David Parry/PA Media Assignments)

“We hope members of the public enjoy cracking the case of ‘the missing coin’ as much as we’ve enjoyed bringing the coin to life.

“There’s a real thrill to coin collecting, and we hope solving this case connects that same passion for collecting with the mystery and excitement of a game like Cluedo.”

Cluedo has captured families’ imaginations for generations, since it was invented by Anthony Pratt.

Ms Lewis, daughter of Mr Pratt, said: “My father invented the game at his home in Birmingham during the long nights under blackout in the Second World War, while my mother, Elva, designed the board.”

open image in gallery (David Parry/PA Media Assignments)

She added: “Visiting The Royal Mint to strike my own coin and to see the range of skills, craftsmanship and minute attention to detail that went into its production was a moment I will always cherish and one I know my parents would have too.

“Cluedo has brought entertainment, escapism and delight to hundreds of millions of people and I’m immensely proud to know my father’s legacy, so cleverly represented in this coin, will now be treasured by collectors and families for many years to come.”

Ms Leach said: “Playing Miss Scarlett on stage was one of my favourite roles, so getting to bring her back to life for The Royal Mint was such a fun challenge.”

Marianne James, senior vice president, global licensing at Hasbro, said: “Cluedo has brought generations together through mystery, strategy and play.”

The Cluedo collectable 50p coin is available to purchase from The Royal Mint’s website from 9am on Monday, with prices starting from £19.95.

From October 6, visitors to the Royal Mint Experience, based in Llantrisant, South Wales, will have an opportunity to strike their own Cluedo 50p coin, featuring a more simplified design with a magnifying glass set against a game board.
