What the warning level means

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) is Britain’s foreign ministry. Its advice has two warning levels above normal caution: against all but essential travel, and against all travel.

Cuba sits on the first of those, for the whole country. It is not a ban, and British tourists may still go.

The practical catch is insurance. Many standard policies do not cover trips against FCDO advice, and the page tells travellers to make sure theirs covers Cuba.

The change note lists what was revised on 25 September. It covers protests, power outages, fuel and water shortages, travel disruption, card payments, insurance, visas, crime, money, taxis and healthcare.

How the advice has hardened this year

The change history shows a steady build-up. The FCDO moved to its current warning on 11 February, and two days later added that airports lacked aviation fuel.

In March it updated airport operations and flight suspensions and added the first notes on protests. In May it updated the fuel section, and in June it added the ban on foreign cards.

July brought new information on crime and power cuts. The 25 September review is the widest revision since the level was raised.

Protests and crime

The FCDO says Cuba’s worsening economy “has led to frequent protests”. “To date most of these have remained peaceful but be aware that protests can escalate,” it adds.

Visitors are told to stay away from large gatherings and follow local authorities. The advice notes that the internet can be blocked at times of political tension.

Opportunistic crime is rising, it says, although levels remain lower than in the UK. It reports muggings in Havana, burglaries and fuel siphoned from parked cars, and advises against walking at night.

It recommends official yellow taxis. Three-wheeled Coco-taxis may be unsafe, it says, and tourists have been injured and killed riding in them.

Power, fuel and flights

The national grid “has collapsed a number of times over the last few months”, the advice says, and further collapses are likely. A nationwide blackout hit on 18 September.

Fuel rationing affects transport, medical care, communications, water and street lighting. Travellers are told to conserve fuel, water, food and phone charge, and to expect significant disruption.

Cuban authorities have announced that all international airports are without aviation fuel, the advice says. Only Terminal 3 at José Martí International Airport in Havana is operating.

It lists all Canadian airlines, Air France, Iberia, World2Fly and LATAM as having suspended Cuba flights. “Options for leaving the country could reduce further if the situation worsens,” it warns.

“The situation has the potential to deteriorate quickly and without warning,” the advice adds. Anyone already in Cuba is asked to consider carefully whether their presence is essential.

The collapse shows in the arrivals data. Only 30,490 foreign visitors came in August, against about 136,000 a year earlier.

Money: bring cash

This is the section most likely to catch visitors out. Cuba’s central bank has announced that international cards such as Visa and Mastercard are no longer accepted.

Foreign cards cannot draw cash from ATMs either. Visitors should bring enough cash for their whole stay and for emergencies, such as medical treatment or a delayed flight.

US dollars and euros are widely accepted, according to the FCDO. It suggests asking hotels and tour providers whether they can be paid in advance by bank transfer.

Money may be changed only at Cadeca, the state exchange houses. Changing it anywhere else, including with people on the street, can bring a fine or a prison sentence.

Foreign currency worth more than US$5,000 must be declared on arrival. The Cuban peso cannot be exchanged outside Cuba.

Getting in, and getting care

British tourists need a tourist card or electronic visa before travelling. They must also complete the D’Viajeros arrival form online within 72 hours before entry and show its QR code.

Passports must be valid for at least six months after arrival. You cannot fly on from Cuba to the United States without a US visa.

Travellers departing from the US face a separate hurdle. US rules do not authorise tourist travel to Cuba, and visitors must fit one of 12 approved categories.

The emergency number is 104, but the FCDO calls the ambulance service limited and generally unreliable. It reports severe shortages of basic medicines and a chikungunya outbreak, alongside other mosquito-borne diseases such as dengue.

What comes next

The FCDO updates its pages as conditions change and has revised the Cuba advice many times since February. The Cuban news site CiberCuba noted that Canada, the Netherlands, Germany and Ireland have issued warnings of their own.

The update does not raise the warning level, and it does not say tourists are being targeted. It means a trip now needs cash, flexible plans and insurance that is valid for Cuba.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can British tourists still travel to Cuba?

Yes. The FCDO advises against all but essential travel, but this is advice, not a ban. Travellers should check that their insurance covers a trip against that advice.

Can I use my bank card in Cuba?

No. According to the FCDO, Cuba’s central bank has announced that Visa and Mastercard are no longer accepted, and foreign cards do not work in ATMs. Bring enough US dollars or euros in cash.

Are flights to Cuba still running?

Some are. The FCDO says only Terminal 3 at Havana’s José Martí airport is operating and several airlines have suspended routes. Check with your airline or tour operator before travelling.

Do I need to declare cash when entering Cuba?

Yes. Foreign currency above US$5,000 must be declared on arrival, and an online arrival form must be filed within 72 hours before entry.

World.title: Guyana Plans a New Migration Policy as Its Oil Boom Runs Short of Workers
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

GUYANA · MIGRATION

Key Facts — The country Guyana, on South America’s Caribbean coast, counted 878,674 people in its 2022 census, roughly the population of San Francisco. Offshore oil has made it one of the world’s fastest-growing economies.

— The background For decades more people left Guyana than arrived. The foreign-born share of residents has since nearly tripled, to 3.07 percent in 2022, and building sites now rely on imported labour.

— Why now The government plans gas-fed industries, including a fertiliser plant, an alumina plant and large data centres. Ali says a new migration policy must supply the workers to build and run them.

— What happened President Irfaan Ali said in an interview, first reported on 23 September, that the government is crafting a “flexible, dynamic, modern migration policy”.

— The numbers Ali expects at least three million people “passing through” the economy by 2030. That means visitors and workers, not residents; Guyana recorded 453,489 visitor arrivals in 2025.

— What it means for you Nothing changes yet for foreigners who want to work in Guyana. No draft has been published, and today’s visa and work-permit rules still apply.

— Still open There is no timetable, and no detail on quotas, permits or rights. An earlier idea of residency without voting rights has not been confirmed.

Guyana, a small South American country turned oil producer, is preparing a new migration policy. President Irfaan Ali says the economy cannot keep growing without more workers from abroad.

Some reports have said Guyana expects an influx of three million people by 2030. That is not what the president said, and for a country of under a million people the difference matters.

What the president said

Ali spoke in an interview with journalist Kiana Wilburg about Guyana’s ties with Qatar. The state-owned Guyana Chronicle reported them on 23 September, and the government’s Department of Public Information published them on 26 September.

“We have to have a flexible, dynamic, modern migration policy,” he said, to meet “our needs and requirements in the future”. He named no date for it.

He pointed to Qatar, which built its economy with imported labour. The Gulf state sits close to large labour markets in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, the Philippines and China. “Here in Guyana, we are far away from large labour markets,” he said.

“But as a matter of necessity, we now have labour that is being imported.” On building sites, he asked: “Can you imagine a construction sector without the foreign workers now?”

Three million is not a population forecast

“I see an economy by 2030 where at least three million people will be passing through this economy,” Ali said. That, he added, “by itself creates its own demand”.

The government’s own summary describes these as people entering Guyana “for business, leisure and work”. It is a measure of traffic through the country, not of people settling there.

Neither Ali nor the government said whether three million is a yearly figure. For scale, Guyana recorded 453,489 visitor arrivals in 2025, a record and 22 percent more than in 2024.

The resident population is far smaller. The 2022 census counted 878,674 people, and the statistics bureau estimated about 956,000 by the end of 2024.

Three million new residents would more than triple the country. No official source projects anything of the kind.

Why Guyana needs workers

Guyana began pumping oil from the offshore Stabroek block, run by ExxonMobil, at the end of 2019. The revenue is now funding roads, housing and power projects, and the IMF counts Guyana among the world’s fastest-growing economies.

Its people were long heading the other way.

The 2022 census recorded a 17.6 percent rise in population over ten years. Officials presented it as the end of decades of decline.

Foreign-born residents rose from 1.10 percent of the population in 2012 to 3.07 percent in 2022. Ali said the next wave of projects will need more of them.

He listed the plan to bring offshore gas ashore, a large urea fertiliser plant, an alumina plant and hyperscale data centres. He also said Guyanese living abroad are central to the plan, with many returning to start businesses.

What the policy may contain

The government has been talking about a migration policy for more than a year. Before the 2025 election, Ali said the Attorney General’s office was studying foreign laws on imported labour.

In November 2025 Vice-President Bharrat Jagdeo said residency without voting rights was being considered. “We want people to come and work because we need that … but they can’t change the nature of our society,” he said.

Jagdeo also linked the policy to a planned electronic ID system that would record details of non-nationals. He said the rights and duties of migrants would be discussed in a constitutional reform process.

What comes next

The next step would be a published draft or a bill in the National Assembly. Neither has appeared, and the government has given no timetable.

This does not mean Guyana is opening its doors to mass immigration, or that three million people are coming to live there. It means the government accepts that foreign labour is now a lasting part of its economy, and wants rules to manage it.

For anyone weighing a move, the practical guide remains current law. The Rio Times guide to moving to Guyana covers visas, work permits, costs and daily life in Georgetown.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Guyana expecting three million new residents?

No. President Ali spoke of at least three million people passing through the economy by 2030, meaning visitors, business travellers and workers. Guyana has fewer than a million residents.

Has Guyana changed its immigration rules?

Not yet. The government says it is crafting a new migration policy, but no draft or bill has been published. Existing visa and work-permit rules still apply.

Why does Guyana need foreign workers?

Oil revenue is funding construction and new industries faster than the small local workforce can supply labour. The president says construction already depends on foreign workers.

What does Guyana’s three million figure mean?

President Irfaan Ali expects at least three million people “passing through” the economy by 2030 — visitors and workers, not residents; Guyana recorded 453,489 visitor arrivals in 2025.

World.title: Peru’s Biggest Oil Producer Drills Again After Output Fell by a Third
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

PERU · OIL

Key Facts — The country Peru, a country of about 34 million people better known for copper and gold, pumps only a small amount of crude oil and imports most of what it burns.

— The background PetroTal, a Canadian-registered company, runs the Bretaña field in the Amazon region of Loreto. It produced almost a third of Peru’s oil in June.

— Why now It drilled no new well after January 2025. Output fell from a record 19,473 barrels a day in 2025 to about 12,300 in September 2026.

— What happened On 21 September PetroTal began drilling well 25H, about a week ahead of plan. It is the first of eight new wells and costs about US$15 million.

— The numbers The company wants to get back to about 20,000 barrels a day. It says 22 drilling locations remain, on 106 million barrels of proven and probable reserves.

— What it means for you For investors, PetroTal itself guided 2026 as a low-output year. Any recovery depends on the eight new wells performing as planned.

— Still open How fast the field can dispose of the water it produces, and when a stalled river-erosion defence at the site is finished.

Peru’s largest oil producer is drilling again. PetroTal started a new well at its Bretaña field in the Amazon on 21 September, its first since January 2025.

The field’s output has fallen by more than a third since last year. Because PetroTal pumps almost a third of Peru’s crude, that slide has dragged down the whole country’s production.

An oil field reached by river

Bretaña sits in Block 95 in Loreto, Peru’s largest and most remote region, in the Amazon basin. It is reached mainly by river, and heavy equipment arrives by barge.

PetroTal is registered in Calgary and listed in Toronto and on London’s AIM market. It began producing at Bretaña in June 2018 and became Peru’s largest crude producer in early 2022.

In June 2026 Bretaña produced about 11,200 barrels a day, 31.1 percent of national output.

Peru as a whole pumped 35,900 barrels a day, 16.6 percent less than a year earlier. The figures come from SNMPE, the mining and energy industry association.

That is a small figure for a country of Peru’s size.

Neighbouring Colombia pumps about twenty times as much. Peru relies on imports for most of its fuel, a gap that keeps widening.

From a record year to a slump

The decline did not start in 2025, as some reports suggest. PetroTal averaged a record 19,473 barrels a day that year, 9 percent more than in 2024.

The trouble was that it wrapped up drilling early in 2025 and then drilled nothing more. Oil fields fall off without new wells, and by the fourth quarter output was down to 15,258 barrels a day.

In January chief executive Manuel Pablo Zúñiga-Pflücker admitted that problems with “rig availability and production reliability” had hurt investor confidence. The company had already suspended its dividend, and it guided to about 12,000 barrels a day for 2026.

It has roughly hit that. Group output averaged 11,709 barrels a day in August and 12,286 so far in September, the company said.

The new well

Well 25H is PetroTal’s 20th horizontal well at Bretaña. It will reach about 4,300 metres along the bore, targeting oil-bearing rock some 2,700 metres down.

Drilling and completion should take about eight weeks.

The rig, called Estrella, entered Peru from Leticia in Colombia on 4 August. It was moved on by barge from the city of Iquitos.

The rig is contracted for eight wells.

Peru’s environmental certification agency, Senace, approved an expansion plan in March after a wait of about three and a half years. It allows up to 23 new production wells and five water injection wells.

“The resumption of development drilling at Bretaña is the culmination of months of hard work,” Zúñiga-Pflücker said. He called it “the first step in restoring our production base to a sustainable plateau” of about 20,000 barrels a day.

The water problem

Bretaña’s wells bring up far more water than oil, and that water has to be pumped back underground. In early March, 15 horizontal wells were producing and five were shut because the field could not handle the water.

Work on two injection wells lifted that capacity to just over 190,000 barrels of water a day in September. That is 9 percent more than in August, and helped raise Bretaña’s own output by about 600 barrels a day.

The company aims for 320,000 barrels a day of water capacity by the end of 2028.

A separate project to shield the site from river erosion stalled when PetroTal dismissed its contractor in March. A new contractor is still being chosen.

What comes next

PetroTal says it will update the market as drilling progresses. Well 25H should be finished around mid-November if the eight-week schedule holds.

One well does not reverse a slump.

Peruvian media report the company is aiming for about 20,000 barrels a day within the next 12 months. That depends on both drilling and water capacity.

It also does not change Peru’s position as a net importer of crude.

The district around the field depends on the output too. PetroTal says its payments into a development fund for the local district of Puinahua topped S/128 million (about US$37.7 million) since 2022.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is PetroTal?

PetroTal is an oil company registered in Calgary, Canada, and listed in Toronto and London. It has been Peru’s largest crude producer since 2022, mainly from the Bretaña field in the Amazon.

Why did PetroTal’s output fall?

It drilled no new wells after January 2025, so natural decline set in. Limited capacity to reinject water produced with the oil also forced some wells to shut.

How much oil does Peru produce?

About 35,900 barrels a day in June 2026, according to the industry association SNMPE. That is a small volume, and Peru imports most of its crude and fuel.

When did PetroTal start drilling again?

On 21 September 2026 PetroTal began drilling well 25H at its Bretaña field in Loreto, about a week ahead of plan — the first of eight new wells, costing about US$15 million.

World.title: Chile’s Defence Minister Says Britain Has Held the Falklands for 200 Years
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

CHILE · ARGENTINA · FALKLANDS

Key Facts — The country Chile, a country of about 20 million people, shares one of the world’s longest land borders with Argentina. Its far-southern Magallanes region looks out towards the Falkland Islands.

— The background Britain has held the Falklands since 1833, and Argentina, which calls them the Malvinas, claims them. Chile has backed Argentina’s claim as state policy for decades, and President José Antonio Kast restated that support this year.

— Why now Punta Arenas, Magallanes’ capital, hosts a Falklands business delegation on 28 and 29 September to prepare a new sea route. Argentina is sanctioning firms linked to Falklands oil.

— What happened During a visit to Magallanes this week, Defence Minister Fernando Barros told the regional broadcaster Radio Polar that Chile supports Argentina’s claim, “but there is a de facto situation: a friendly country has exercised sovereignty for 200 years”.

— Who is who Barros runs defence in Kast’s cabinet; foreign policy belongs to Foreign Minister Francisco Pérez Mackenna. Argentine outlets reported the remarks on 27 September as Chile “conditioning” its support.

— What it means for you Nothing changes for travel or trade today. The minister said Magallanes businesses may trade with the islands within the law, which Argentina objects to.

— Still open Whether Chile’s foreign ministry endorses, softens or corrects the wording, and whether Argentina protests formally.

Chile’s defence minister has said Britain has exercised sovereignty over the Falkland Islands for 200 years. In the same breath, he insisted his country still backs Argentina’s claim to them.

Fernando Barros spoke in the southern region that faces the islands. Argentine media read his words as a crack in one of Argentina’s steadiest diplomatic supports.

What the minister said

Barros spoke to Radio Polar, a broadcaster in Punta Arenas, during a visit to Magallanes on 24 and 25 September. The quotes below come from Ámbito’s transcription of that interview.

“Chile has said that it supports the Argentine claim, its claim of sovereignty over the Malvinas or Falklands,” he said. “But there is a de facto situation: a friendly country has exercised sovereignty for 200 years.”

He added that supporting a claim against “a friendly country” must be done “in accordance with international law”. It must also respect “the will and interest of the people involved”, and use “peaceful means”.

He was also asked about a sea route from Punta Arenas to the islands. Chile and Magallanes have the right to trade within the legal framework, he said, and he saw no problem with it.

Is it a new condition?

Not in so many words. The newspaper Ámbito headlined that Chile “conditions” its support.

Barros did not, however, set a condition or withdraw Chile’s backing.

What stands out is the vocabulary. Argentina calls British rule an occupation that began by force in 1833, so “exercising sovereignty” is language Buenos Aires rejects.

The phrase about the islanders also matters. The 1965 United Nations resolution on the dispute asks both sides to consider the population’s “interests”; Barros spoke of their “will” as well as their interests.

Britain bases its position on the islanders’ right to decide their future. Argentina rejects that argument, so adding that word places Barros closer to London’s reading.

Strictly, the figure is rounded: British control dates from January 1833, which makes it 193 years.

Chile’s official line

Chile’s formal support for Argentina is long-standing. In April, Kast signed a joint statement in Buenos Aires backing Argentina’s rights over the islands and the surrounding waters.

In June, at the summit of Mercosur, the South American trade bloc, he joined a declaration supporting Argentina’s “legitimate rights”, Ámbito notes. He restated that support in Santiago on 3 September.

Foreign policy belongs to Pérez Mackenna, whom the lower house has summoned to answer questions on 28 September.

Why Magallanes cares

The remarks were made in the region that stands to gain from closer ties with the islands. About 25 Falklands business people are due in Punta Arenas for meetings on 28 and 29 September.

A Chilean shipping company aims to open the islands’ second South American sea link, after Montevideo. The first voyage is planned for November.

Punta Arenas mayor Claudio Radonich has backed opening trade with the islands, Radio Polar reported earlier in September.

The Falklands question has already spilled into Chile’s Congress. It sits alongside a quarrel over Argentine descriptions of the Strait of Magellan as shared waters.

History adds weight. During the 1982 war, Chile under Pinochet was officially neutral, but British files show it quietly helped Britain.

Argentines have not forgotten that episode. Any Chilean phrase that sounds like London’s is read against it.

What comes next

No reaction from Argentina’s foreign ministry had been reported by Sunday afternoon. The comments land as Britain hardens its own line on the islands and Argentina widens sanctions on firms working there.

Pérez Mackenna faces formal questioning in the lower house on Monday. It centres on other foreign-policy issues, but deputies can ask whether Barros spoke for the government.

The remarks do not mean Chile has recognised British sovereignty or dropped Argentina’s claim. They do show that at least one of Kast’s ministers voices that support with qualifications Buenos Aires does not accept.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Chile stopped supporting Argentina on the Falklands?

No. Chile’s defence minister said Chile supports Argentina’s claim, and President José Antonio Kast has backed it in formal statements this year. The minister added that Britain has exercised sovereignty in practice for about 200 years.

Who said the UK has ruled the Falklands for 200 years?

Fernando Barros Tocornal, Chile’s defence minister, in an interview with the Punta Arenas broadcaster Radio Polar during a visit to Magallanes in late September. No report attributes the wording to Kast or to the foreign minister.

Why does the wording matter to Argentina?

Argentina regards British rule since 1833 as an occupation and rejects the idea that the islanders can decide sovereignty. Barros spoke of the islanders’ will as well as their interests, wording closer to Britain’s position.

Is there a sea route between Chile and the Falklands?

Not yet a regular one. A Chilean company plans a new cargo route from Punta Arenas, with a first voyage expected in November, and the defence minister said he saw no problem with legal trade.

World.title: Panama Business Chamber Urges Lawmakers to Rethink a Rushed Election Bill
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

PANAMA · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Panama is a dollarised country of about 4.5 million people, best known for its canal. Its laws pass through a single 71-seat National Assembly, and its next general election is due in May 2029.

— The background In 2025 the Electoral Tribunal, Panama’s independent election authority, gathered parties, independents, business and civil society to agree new rules. The result became Bill 699, a 169-article rewrite of the electoral code.

— Why now On the night of 23 September an Assembly committee approved the bill in first debate by 7 votes to 2, after making more than 50 changes.

— What happened On 27 September the Chamber of Commerce, Industries and Agriculture of Panama asked lawmakers to hold the next debate “in the light of day, without haste”, with “transparency, participation and deliberation”.

— The numbers Private donations to a mayoral candidate could reach US$150,000 to US$500,000, depending on the district’s size, and US$300,000 to US$500,000 for a deputy. New parties would need over 68,000 members.

— What it means for you Nothing changes yet: the current electoral code applies until the bill clears two more debates and the president’s signature.

— Still open Whether the full Assembly reverses the committee’s changes, and whether the Electoral Tribunal takes any article to the Supreme Court.

Panama electoral reform has drawn a sharp warning from business. The Chamber of Commerce, Industries and Agriculture of Panama says lawmakers rewrote the rules in a late-night session and must slow down.

“Democracy is not legislated in the dark,” the chamber said in a statement published on Sunday 27 September. Its target is Bill 699, which a National Assembly committee approved in first debate four days earlier with dozens of late changes.

What the business chamber said

The chamber, known by its Spanish initials CCIAP, is one of Panama’s main business associations. Its statement was signed by its president, Aurelio Barría Pino.

It said the committee approved substantive changes during a marathon night session, outside the consensus built in 2025. It described a debate held “between intentional haste, opacity and the darkness of the night”.

The chamber accepted that the Assembly has the right to amend bills. But it said any major departure from a widely consulted text needs proper deliberation and technical support.

The chamber had taken a similar stand in 2021, during an earlier rewrite of the code.

This time it asked lawmakers to hear the Electoral Tribunal, business groups and civil society before the second debate. “Under no circumstances should we accept less,” Barría said on Sunday.

What the committee changed

The biggest change concerns money. Two deputies, Benicio Robinson and Luis Eduardo Camacho, raised the cap on private donations for candidates, scaled by the number of voters.

A mayoral candidate could raise US$150,000 in a district of up to 50,000 voters and US$500,000 where there are more than 200,000. For deputies the ceiling runs from US$300,000 to US$500,000.

Independent candidates face higher hurdles. The committee raised the signatures they need to 3 percent and cut the time allowed to collect them.

The committee also removed separate lists of independent candidates in constituencies that elect more than one deputy, a change Vamos opposed.

New parties would need more than 68,000 members, and the signatures of a party’s founders would no longer count towards that total. The chamber also objects to a change it says allows simultaneous re-election to two elected posts.

Who voted, and how they defend it

The Government, Justice and Constitutional Affairs Committee approved the bill by 7 votes to 2. The two votes against came from Alexandra Brenes and Walkiria Chandler of Vamos, the independent coalition that forms the largest bloc.

The votes in favour came from the PRD, the former ruling party, and from Realizando Metas, President José Raúl Mulino’s party. Three smaller parties joined them.

Brenes said citizens hoping to run as independents lose most. She complained that the changes were voted on without discussion.

Robinson, who chairs the committee and leads the PRD, said the session was public and televised.

“Vamos deputies talk about democracy, but they do not accept losing a vote. Stop lying!” he wrote on social media.

The election authority’s view

Narciso Arellano Moreno, who presides over the Electoral Tribunal, said the committee made more than 50 changes to his institution’s text. Some, he said, altered the spirit of the proposal.

He said the tribunal persuaded deputies to withdraw two changes it considered unconstitutional. One would have stopped it from issuing rules once an election had been called.

The tribunal says it will go to the Supreme Court only if an article in the final law breaches the constitution.

For background on the country and its politics, see Panama Explained: The Canal, the Economy, the Politics and What to Watch.

What comes next

The bill now goes to the full Assembly for its second debate, where articles can still be changed or removed. A third debate and the president’s signature would follow.

Mulino can also object to a bill and send it back to the Assembly.

The committee vote does not make these rules law, and the current electoral code still applies.

Nor is the chamber’s statement binding. It speaks for employers who call trust in institutions one of a country’s most important assets.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Panama’s Bill 699?

Bill 699 is a 169-article reform of Panama’s electoral code, drafted by the Electoral Tribunal after a national consultation in 2025. It sets the rules for the 2029 general election, including party formation, independent candidates and campaign finance.

Why is Panama’s business chamber criticising the reform?

The Chamber of Commerce, Industries and Agriculture of Panama says a committee approved major changes overnight without proper debate. It objects to higher hurdles for independents and new parties and to changes on private campaign money.

Is the electoral reform already law?

No. It has passed only a committee’s first debate. It still needs second and third debates in the full National Assembly and the president’s signature, and the current electoral code applies until then.

What campaign-finance limits would Bill 699 set?

Private donations to a mayoral candidate could reach US$150,000 to US$500,000 depending on the district’s size, and US$300,000 to US$500,000 for a deputy; new parties would need over 68,000 members.

World.title: Honduras Fuel Prices Rise for an 11th Week Despite a Bigger Subsidy
World.content:

Get the brief

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

HONDURAS · ENERGY

Key Facts — The country Honduras is a Central American country of about 10 million people, roughly Portugal’s population. It produces no oil and imports all its fuel, so rises in world prices soon reach its pumps.

— The background The energy ministry sets maximum pump prices every week for the two main cities. Regular petrol sold for L89.53 (about US$3.33) a gallon in January.

— Why now World fuel prices keep climbing. The government raised its temporary support from 50 to 65 percent of the increases on 21 September, and to 70 percent from Monday.

— What happened From Monday 28 September, premium petrol in Tegucigalpa costs L153.17 (about US$5.70) a gallon, up L4.87 (about US$0.18). Radio HRN counts eleven straight weeks of rises.

— The numbers Regular rises to L135.26 (about US$5.03) and diesel to L153.53 (about US$5.71). A 25-pound cooking-gas cylinder stays frozen at L249.62 (about US$9.28).

— What it means for you Filling a 15-gallon tank with regular in the capital now costs about L2,029 (about US$75). Diesel also feeds into bus fares and food prices.

— Still open How long the government keeps paying the support, and whether world prices ease before the next weekly price list.

Honduras fuel prices rise again on Monday 28 September, for what Radio HRN counts as the eleventh week in a row. Premium petrol in the capital, Tegucigalpa, will cost L153.17 (about US$5.70) a gallon.

The government has raised the share of the increase it absorbs on regular petrol and diesel from 65 to 70 percent. That softens the rise but does not stop it.

What changes on Monday

The Secretaría de Energía, the national energy ministry, published the new price list on Saturday night. All figures are per US gallon, the unit Honduras uses at the pump.

In Tegucigalpa, premium rises L4.87 (about US$0.18) to L153.17 (about US$5.70). Regular rises L2.45 (about US$0.09) to L135.26 (about US$5.03), and diesel L2.43 (about US$0.09) to L153.53 (about US$5.71).

Kerosene rises L3.84 (about US$0.14) to L138.39 (about US$5.15). Liquefied gas for vehicles rises L0.83 (about US$0.03) to L51.92 (about US$1.93).

San Pedro Sula, the northern industrial city, pays slightly less. Premium there costs L148.69 (about US$5.53), regular L130.98 (about US$4.87) and diesel L149.20 (about US$5.55).

Dollar figures use the Central Bank of Honduras buying rate of L26.89 per US dollar on 25 September.

How Honduras sets fuel prices

Honduras does not let stations price freely. The energy ministry publishes maximum prices each weekend, and they apply at every station from Monday.

This week a fake table promising rises of up to L10 (about US$0.37) circulated first on social media. The ministry said it was false and that it had not yet published the real list, the newspaper El Heraldo reported.

A bigger subsidy that only softens the rise

The government calls its support “temporary economic aid”. Until mid-September it covered half of each weekly increase on regular petrol and diesel.

It rose to 65 percent with the prices of 21 September and reaches 70 percent this week. This week the state absorbs L5.83 (about US$0.22) of each gallon’s rise on regular in Tegucigalpa, and L5.74 (about US$0.21) on diesel.

Premium petrol and kerosene get no such support. That is one reason they rise most this week.

Household cooking gas is protected separately. The 25-pound cylinder stays at L249.62 (about US$9.28) in Tegucigalpa, with the state covering L33.46 (about US$1.24) of its cost.

Who pays for the support

Finance Secretary Emilio Hernández Hércules said on 22 September that the government plans to keep energy and fuel subsidies in 2027. The amounts have not been broken down, and the draft 2027 budget is still before Congress.

The 2026 budget set aside L680 million (about US$25 million) for fuel support. By June the state had already paid out L860 million (about US$32 million).

By December it expects to have spent L1.2 billion to L1.3 billion (about US$45 million to US$48 million), the newspaper Tiempo reported. That is nearly twice the original budget.

How far prices have come

In January regular petrol sold for L89.53 (about US$3.33) a gallon, according to El Heraldo. At Monday’s price it costs about half as much again.

Fuel is feeding into wider prices: annual inflation reached 6.2 percent in August, above the central bank’s 4 percent target. The bank has since raised its policy rate to 6 percent.

Economists quoted by El Heraldo expect inflation to finish the year above 6 percent. A former head of the Central American Bank for Economic Integration named diesel prices as a threat to the target.

For the wider picture of the country, see Honduras Explained 2026.

What comes next

The next price list is due next weekend, for Monday 5 October. Nothing in this week’s figures suggests the run of increases has ended.

Visitors hiring a car should budget at Monday’s prices or higher.

The rise is about price, not supply: nothing in the ministry’s list points to shortages. Nor does the larger subsidy mean prices are falling, only that they rise more slowly than world markets.

World oil prices remain the main driver; see Oil Tops US$106 as Iran Warns Its War Could Spread to the Indian Ocean.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does petrol cost in Honduras now?

From 28 September 2026, premium petrol costs L153.17 (about US$5.70) a gallon in Tegucigalpa and regular L135.26 (about US$5.03). Diesel costs L153.53 (about US$5.71).

Who sets fuel prices in Honduras?

The Secretaría de Energía, the national energy ministry, publishes maximum prices every weekend for Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula. They apply at stations from the following Monday.

Does Honduras subsidise fuel?

Yes, partly. From 28 September the government covers 70 percent of the weekly increase on regular petrol and diesel, and it keeps the price of a 25-pound cooking-gas cylinder frozen. Premium petrol and kerosene get no support.

What do drivers in Tegucigalpa pay from 28 September?

Premium petrol costs L153.17 (about US$5.70) a gallon, regular rises to L135.26 (about US$5.03) and diesel to L153.53 (about US$5.71); a 25-pound cooking-gas cylinder stays frozen at L249.62 (about US$9.28).

World.title: Brazil’s Bahia Grows More Crops but Earns Less: Farm Output Up 5.7%
World.content:

Yesterday’s subject line: “The US Army is quietly planning for Cuba”

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

BRAZIL · BAHIA · AGRIBUSINESS

Key Facts — The country Brazil is one of the world’s largest food exporters. Bahia, a north-eastern state larger than mainland France with about 15 million people, is best known abroad for Salvador and its beaches.

— The background Its far west is one of Brazil’s big soy and cotton belts. The wider farm economy, from seeds to shipping, makes up about a quarter of Bahia’s output.

— Why now The state statistics office, SEI, published its farm bulletin for April to June on 22 September.

— What happened Farm and livestock output grew 5.7 percent in the second quarter from a year earlier, more than double the state economy’s 2.3 percent.

— The numbers Farm prices fell 13 percent. The farm economy’s value dropped 8.2 percent to R$40.3 billion (about US$7.75 billion) despite higher volumes.

— What it means for you For investors and traders, Bahia is shipping more soy and cotton, with China its biggest buyer, but local farm prices are down 13 percent.

— Still open The figures are preliminary, and SEI warns that a possible El Niño could hurt the next harvest.

Farms in the Brazilian state of Bahia produced 5.7 percent more between April and June than a year earlier. The state statistics office, SEI, credits a record soy crop, more cotton and a record cattle slaughter.

The same bulletin shows the other side. Prices for farm goods fell 13 percent, so the sector earned less money even while it grew more.

What the bulletin says

SEI, the Superintendence of Economic and Social Studies of Bahia, is the state government’s statistics agency. It published the quarterly farm bulletin on 22 September with the state agriculture department.

The 5.7 percent is a real, volume-based figure for farming and livestock alone. Bahia’s whole economy grew 2.3 percent in the quarter, when its output was worth an estimated R$154.7 billion (about US$29.8 billion).

Farming has now outgrown the state economy for six quarters in a row, SEI said. The sector grew 5.8 percent in the first quarter and 9.1 percent in the last quarter of 2025.

Gross farm production, meaning volume times price at the farm gate, reached R$26.5 billion (about US$5.1 billion). Crops accounted for 82 percent of it and livestock for 18 percent.

A record soy crop, and more cotton

Soy is Bahia’s main crop. IBGE, Brazil’s national statistics institute, estimated its 2026 soy harvest at 8.9 million tonnes in June, 3.8 percent more than in 2025.

Aiba, the western Bahia farmers’ association, calls the soy harvest a record. IBGE puts the state’s total grain crop at about 13.3 million tonnes, up 3.2 percent on 2025’s 12.8 million.

Cotton is the second pillar. IBGE expects 1.84 million tonnes of seed cotton, 2.8 percent more than last year.

Bahia is Brazil’s second-largest cotton producer after Mato Grosso.

Coffee and cocoa also rose. IBGE expects 12.5 percent more coffee and 15.4 percent more cocoa this year.

Cattle: a record, but a small one

Slaughterhouses in Bahia killed about 390,000 cattle in the quarter, the most since IBGE records began. That is only 0.9 percent more than a year earlier.

The mix matters. Slaughter of cows rose 7.6 percent while that of males fell.

SEI reads this as farmers selling off breeding stock, a sign the cattle cycle may soon turn.

Chicken slaughter rose 8.6 percent and pig slaughter 4.9 percent. Milk output fell 3.9 percent, squeezed by high costs.

Exports up, prices down

Bahia’s farm exports reached US$1.75 billion in the quarter, 9.3 percent more in value and 14 percent more in volume. Farm goods made up 51.3 percent of everything the state sold abroad.

Soy did the heavy lifting, with shipments up 21.4 percent. Cotton exports rose 41.4 percent in volume, and China took 45.7 percent of the state’s farm exports.

Sales to the Netherlands, a gateway to the European Union, jumped 75.2 percent. SEI links this to the provisional start of the trade agreement between the Mercosur bloc and the European Union, which cut tariffs.

Meat exports grew 15.1 percent in volume, but they are small: about US$13 million, under 1 percent of the total. Cocoa export revenue fell 44.3 percent and coffee 21 percent, as world prices dropped.

That price slide explains the gap. The wider farm economy’s volume rose 4.7 percent, yet its value in current reais fell 8.2 percent.

It came to R$40.3 billion (about US$7.75 billion), or 26.1 percent of the state economy. A year earlier the share was 29.6 percent.

Dollar figures use the central bank reference rate of R$5.1991 per US dollar for 25 September. For comparison, see Mato Grosso’s record farm output, Brazil’s largest farm state, and a guide to Brazil’s agribusiness.

What comes next

SEI lists the risks plainly. Net farm hiring was only 614 jobs in the quarter, against 3,205 a year earlier.

Rural credit has also tightened because of high interest rates and farm debt.

It also flags a possible El Niño in the second half of the year, which could hurt the 2026–27 harvest. All the quarterly figures are preliminary and may be revised.

The growth figure does not mean farmers are earning more. It measures how much Bahia produced, not what it was paid, and on prices the quarter was weak.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Bahia grow?

Mainly soy and cotton in the western plains, plus maize, coffee, cocoa and fruit. It also raises cattle, chickens and pigs, and exports pulp from its forestry sector.

Why did farm output grow while its value fell?

Volumes rose, but prices for farm goods fell 13 percent in the quarter. Local soy prices dipped 2.7 percent, while cotton and coffee fell by about a third.

Who buys Bahia’s farm exports?

China took 45.7 percent in the second quarter, mostly soy, pulp and cotton. The Netherlands, a gateway to the European Union, was second with 10.1 percent.

How big is farming in Bahia’s economy?

The wider farm economy, from seeds to shipping, makes up about a quarter of Bahia’s output; in the second quarter of 2026 its value dropped 8.2 percent to R$40.3 billion (about US$7.75 billion) despite higher volumes.

World.title: Cuba Says US Sanctions Are Holding Back Its Opening to Private Business
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

CUBA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Cuba is a one-party communist state of under 10 million people, 90 miles from Florida. A US trade embargo has been in place for more than 60 years.

— The background For decades almost every business was state-run. Private small firms became legal only in 2021, and in June 2026 parliament approved 176 measures to widen private and market activity.

— Why now Cuba’s diplomats are in New York for the UN General Assembly, where President Trump called the island a failed state. Washington added new sanctions this month.

— What happened On Friday 25 September a senior Cuban diplomat told Bloomberg Television that US sanctions are holding the reforms back, and that easing pressure would make them “truly irreversible”.

— Who is who Carlos Fernández de Cossío, deputy foreign minister, handles relations with the US. Marco Rubio, US secretary of state, says no one will invest under Cuba’s current model.

— What it means for you Nothing changes yet. US law still bars most American trade and investment, and blackouts and fuel shortages continue.

— Still open Whether stalled talks with Washington restart, and whether the 176 measures are carried out in practice.

Cuba’s government is now blaming Washington for the slow pace of its market reforms. US sanctions are holding back its economic reforms, a senior Cuban diplomat said in New York on Friday.

He also made an offer of sorts. If the US eased the pressure, he said, the opening could become permanent, which he argued is what Washington says it wants.

What the diplomat said

Carlos Fernández de Cossío is Cuba’s deputy foreign minister and the official who deals with the United States. He spoke to David Gura of Bloomberg This Weekend while in New York with Cuba’s delegation to the UN.

He said that if the US eased “the amount of pressure”, the changes “can go a long way and become truly irreversible”. That, he added, “is our aim and in theory is what the US wants to happen.”

He argued the reforms cannot work while the US subjects Cubans to what he called oppression and asphyxiation, according to Bloomberg Línea. Even when the power grid works, he said, fuel limits leave most people with electricity for only a few hours a day.

He also turned Trump’s UN speech against him. Trump called Cuba a failed state while claiming more US pressure than ever, which he said admitted the cause.

What is new about it

Days earlier, the same official had admitted that Havana does not know where its reforms will lead. This time he put the burden on Washington.

The pitch is new as well. Instead of defending the measures as a crisis response, he called their permanence “our aim” and said Washington should want it too.

He called talks with Washington practically stalled. He told Bloomberg it was very hard to believe negotiations would bring results while the US keeps adding new measures and sanctions.

Asked whether Venezuela, once Havana’s closest partner, was still an ally, he replied: “Ally is too strong a word.” Venezuela stopped sending fuel to Cuba after US forces captured Nicolás Maduro in January.

An economy under strain

The reforms arrive in a deep economic crisis. A de facto US fuel blockade has worsened blackouts and shortages of basic goods, Bloomberg reported.

Venezuela had supplied about 26,500 barrels of oil a day, roughly a third of Cuba’s energy needs, CiberCuba reported. Those shipments stopped on 9 January.

Tourism, long a main source of hard currency, has also collapsed. Only 30,490 foreign visitors arrived in August, against about 136,000 a year earlier, official statistics show.

The power grid also failed nationwide again on 18 September, one of several complete blackouts this year.

The reforms he means

The National Assembly, Cuba’s parliament, approved a package of 176 measures in June. It is the country’s broadest economic opening in decades.

A decree-law published on 2 September put the rules for private firms into force. Private firms may now employ more than 100 people and work in almost every branch of the economy.

The package also allows private exchange houses and more foreign investment in the non-state sector. The head of the state agency that oversees private firms said some were waiting to hire beyond the old cap.

The US view

Washington sees it differently. Speaking in New York on 23 September, Rubio said the reforms exist only on paper and must be carried out and sustained.

“No one is going to invest in Cuba under their current governance model,” he said. He said the administration would help if Havana seized what he called a golden opportunity for change.

The pressure has continued all month. The Treasury sanctioned a grandson of Raúl Castro and five state firms on 3 September, and more designations followed.

Rubio also stressed that US policy on Cuba is written into law, not set by the president alone. The 1996 Helms-Burton Act ties a full lifting of the embargo to political change in Havana.

Trade that goes around the state

One paradox runs through all this. While sanctions on the state tighten, US shipments aimed largely at Cuba’s private sector are rising.

About 45 ships have made more than 200 trips from US ports to Cuba this year, the independent outlet 14ymedio reported. Through August they carried some 327,000 tonnes. US exports to Cuba reached about US$674 million from January to July, 61.8 percent more than a year earlier.

Fernández de Cossío said Havana welcomes the goods, though they fall short of demand. But he said the US was clearly trying to create dependency.

Cuba, he added, does not want to be dominated by any other country.

What it means for investors and travellers

For investors outside the US, the new rules widen what private Cuban firms may do. Rubio’s warning about legal certainty describes the risk they must weigh.

For American citizens and companies, US law still restricts trade, investment and tourist travel to Cuba. Nothing said on Friday changes that.

What comes next

Trump said on Saturday he expects a deal with Cuba without military force, but gave no terms. Fernández de Cossío called hopes that US midterm elections in November would ease pressure an illusion.

His remarks do not mean sanctions are easing or talks have resumed. Nor do they make the reforms irreversible; that depends on Havana carrying them out, whatever Washington does.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can private businesses operate in Cuba?

Yes. Private small and medium firms have been legal since 2021. Since September 2026 they may employ more than 100 people and work in most sectors, though some activities still need special permission.

Can Americans invest in Cuba’s new private companies?

Mostly not. The US embargo is written into law and still bars most American trade and investment. Some US exports to Cuba’s private sector are allowed, and those shipments have grown in 2026.

Who is Carlos Fernández de Cossío?

He is Cuba’s deputy foreign minister and the official responsible for relations with the United States. He often gives interviews to American media.

When did Cuba legalize private small firms?

Private small firms became legal only in 2021, and in June 2026 parliament approved 176 measures to widen private and market activity.

World.title: Mark Castillo fined $1,605 after pleading guilty to possession of 231 grams of cannabis with intent to supply
World.content:
Mark Castillo fined $1,605 after pleading guilty to possession of 231 grams of cannabis with intent to supply

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 32-year-old Neal’s Pen Road resident has been fined $1,605 after pleading guilty to possession of more than 230 grams of cannabis with intent to supply.

Mark Raymond Castillo, a labourer of Belize City, appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2, where he pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply after police reportedly found 231.3 grams of cannabis at his residence.

The court imposed a fine of $1,600 plus $5 cost of court, which Castillo must pay by January 15, 2027, or serve six months in prison.

In determining the sentence, the Senior Magistrate considered the quantity of cannabis found and concluded that the amount was consistent with possession for financial gain.

The court also considered several mitigating factors, including that Castillo had no previous drug convictions, was a first-time offender for possession with intent to supply and entered an early guilty plea, saving the court the time and expense of a trial. His early plea resulted in a one-third reduction being applied to the sentence.

According to the facts presented in court, members of the Violence Interdiction Enforcement Team visited Castillo’s residence on Sunday, September 20, 2026 after receiving information.

Police asked Castillo whether he had anything illegal to declare, to which he reportedly replied no.

During a search of a bedroom, however, an officer allegedly discovered a black drawstring bag containing plastic bags with green leafy material suspected to be cannabis.

Castillo was cautioned and taken to the Fabers Road Police Station, where the suspected drugs were weighed in his presence and amounted to 231.3 grams.

He subsequently accepted responsibility and pleaded guilty to the charge.

World.title: Wilmer Rivera, accused of cutting ex’s throat, attempted murder trial set for April 2027
World.content:
Wilmer Rivera, accused of cutting ex’s throat, attempted murder trial set for April 2027

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 34-year-old construction worker accused of attempting to murder his ex-girlfriend in 2023 is scheduled to stand trial in the High Court next April.

Wilmer Javier Rivera appeared before Justice Candace Nanton, where his trial on charges of attempted murder and use of deadly means of harm upon his ex-girlfriend was set for April 6-9, 2027.

Rivera was represented by attorney Ronell Gonzalez, who requested additional time to prepare for the second part of the case management conference and indicated that he was still awaiting instructions from his client. Gonzalez also told the court that discussions were ongoing with the Crown.

The prosecution indicated that it is ready to proceed to trial and that its witness is prepared to testify.

Justice Nanton granted the adjournment and scheduled a further case management conference for December 1, 2026.

The charges stem from a May 19, 2023 attack near Linda Vista Street in the Mile 2½ area of the George Price Highway in Belize City.

Reports said the woman was waiting for a taxi when she was allegedly attacked by Rivera, her former boyfriend. Police said at the time that the woman suffered stab wounds and was taken to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital for treatment. Channel 5 reported that she was stabbed in the abdomen and cut across the throat.

Police also confirmed in 2023 that she had previously made a report involving Rivera which had been dealt with by the Domestic Violence Unit.

Rivera, then 31, was arraigned in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on May 23, 2023 on one count of attempted murder and one count of use of deadly means of harm. He was initially remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

The allegations against Rivera remain unproven unless and until he is convicted in court.

World.title: 60-year-old ‘Lizzard’ remanded to prison; Unable to meet $200 bail on crack charge
World.content:
60-year-old ‘Lizzard’ remanded to prison; Unable to meet $200 bail on crack charge

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man in his late 60s was remanded to the Belize Central Prison after he was unable to meet $200 bail on a charge of possession of cocaine.

McElroy Bennett, also known as “Lizzad,” of a Tigris Street address, appeared in Court #5 of the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was read a single charge of possession of an undetermined amount of crack cocaine.

Bennett initially pleaded guilty to the charge.

However, when the Magistrate questioned him about whether he was admitting that the cocaine was in his possession, Bennett explained that police had found the substance on the ground.

Because that explanation amounted to a denial of possession and was inconsistent with a guilty plea, the Magistrate declined to accept the plea and entered a plea of not guilty on Bennett’s behalf.

Bail was offered in the sum of $200 plus one surety of the same amount.

Bennett was unable to meet bail by the end of the court day and was therefore remanded to the Belize Central Prison until he is able to do so.

He is scheduled to return to court on November 30, 2026.

World.title: Stevedore fined $405 for crack pipe possession days after leaving prison
World.content:
Stevedore fined $405 for crack pipe possession days after leaving prison

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 35-year-old Belize City stevedore has picked up another conviction for possession of a crack pipe, only days after being released from prison.

Moises Conorquie, of a George Price Highway address, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court and pleaded guilty to possession of utensils used in connection with smoking a controlled drug.

The charge arose from an incident shortly after midnight on September 19, 2026, at the corner of Johnson Street and Cemetery Road.

According to the facts presented in court, police officers on motorcycle patrol saw Conorquie sitting in Constitution Park and approached him. During the encounter, officers reportedly found a silver metal pipe measuring approximately 3.8 centimetres inside a white cloth rag.

Police alleged that the pipe had been adapted for use in smoking a controlled drug.

Conorquie was escorted to the Precinct 1 Police Station, where he was charged.

He pleaded guilty in court and asked the Magistrate not to send him back to prison, telling the court that he had only been released the previous week.

Conorquie said he was released on Tuesday, September 15, after serving a three-month prison term. He also told the court that he had served another three-month sentence earlier this year, from January to March.

For his latest conviction, Conorquie was fined $400 plus $5 cost of court. He has until October 26, 2026, to pay the fine or face four months in prison in default.

World.title: Waste Control worker who says he has a drinking problem fined $300 after allegedly attacking woman with pint bottles
World.content:
Waste Control worker who says he has a drinking problem fined $300 after allegedly attacking woman with pint bottles

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 32-year-old Waste Control worker who admitted threatening a woman with bottles during an altercation on Euphrates Avenue has been fined $300 after pleading guilty to aggravated assault.

Kirk Douglas Howard appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded guilty to committing aggravated assault upon a woman on Wednesday, September 23, 2026.

According to the facts presented in court, Rowland reported that at around 6:40 p.m. Howard arrived on Euphrates Avenue with another person to pick up his sister.

She alleged that Howard began directing remarks at her before the situation escalated. Howard reportedly picked up a black bottle and threw it in her direction from approximately three feet away. The bottle missed her and shattered against a wall.

Rowland told police that Howard then entered a room and returned carrying two more bottles, one in each hand. Fearing for her safety, she subsequently went to the police station, made a report and requested court action.

Howard accepted the prosecution’s facts and told the court that he knew his actions were wrong. He acknowledged that he had been drinking and admitted having a drinking problem.

In mitigation, Howard told the court that he is the sole breadwinner in his household and has a son whom he works to support and send to school. He claimed the dispute began after the woman arrived with his sister-in-law and did not greet him.

The Magistrate considered that Howard was a first-time offender and that his guilty plea had saved the court the time and expense of a trial, entitling him to a reduction in sentence.

Howard was fined $300 plus $5 cost of court. He has until November 30, 2026, to pay the fine or face one month in prison in default.

World.title: Pre-trial hearing set for Cecil ‘G.I. Joe’ Franklin in rape case
World.content:
Pre-trial hearing set for Cecil ‘G.I. Joe’ Franklin in rape case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A pre-trial case management hearing has been set for Cecil Gilbert Franklin, also known as “G.I. Joe,” who is accused of raping a 58-year-old woman inside her Belize City apartment in October 2024.

Franklin appeared before High Court Justice Candace Nanton this week in connection with the rape charge.

Franklin, who had been unrepresented, has now been appointed attorney Javier Williams. However, Williams told the court that he had not yet had an opportunity to properly consult with Franklin and requested additional time to meet with him and receive instructions on how the defence intends to proceed.

Justice Nanton granted the adjournment and ordered the defence to file its case management forms by October 16, 2026.

Crown Counsel Glenfield Dennison, appearing for the prosecution, was also questioned about additional evidence in the case. The Crown indicated that if further evidence becomes available, a notice of additional evidence will be filed.

Franklin, who remains out on bail, is scheduled to return to the High Court on November 16, 2026, at 1:00 p.m.

Earlier this year, while Franklin was still without legal representation, he reportedly indicated a guilty plea after being indicted for rape. Justice Nanton did not accept the plea at that stage and instead gave him an opportunity to obtain legal representation and advice before proceeding.

The charge stems from an alleged incident on the night of October 21, 2024.

According to the woman’s report to police, she arrived at her apartment at about 8:40 p.m. and, while opening her door, was allegedly grabbed from behind by a man she recognized as Franklin.

She alleged that the attacker placed a knife against the right side of her throat, forced her inside the apartment, pushed her onto a bed and raped her.

A neighbour reportedly heard a commotion coming from the apartment and contacted police. Franklin was detained shortly afterward and later charged with rape.

Contemporaneous reporting from October 2024 stated that Franklin was initially remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being arraigned because the Magistrates’ Court could not grant bail for the indictable offence.

Franklin has not been convicted of the rape allegation, and the case remains before the High Court.

World.title: High Court to decide whether Shedrack White remains in prison or returns home after being found unfit to stand trial
World.content:
High Court to decide whether Shedrack White remains in prison or returns home after being found unfit to stand trial

By Breaking Belize News Staff: High Court Justice Candace Nanton is expected to decide next month whether Shedrack Richard White, who was found mentally unfit to stand trial for murder in 2024, will remain at the Belize Central Prison or be released into the care of his family.

White appeared before Justice Nanton this week, when the matter was adjourned to October 16, 2026, for a decision on where he should be housed and how his continuing psychiatric treatment will be managed.

The court is also awaiting one final psychiatric evaluation before the decision is handed down.

Justice Nanton expressed concern about ensuring that White has reliable access to his medication and appropriate mental-health care regardless of where he is placed.

White’s sister, Priscilla White, appeared in court and was questioned about the arrangements that would be made if her brother were allowed to return home. The court raised concerns contained in a Community Rehabilitation Officer’s report about whether sufficient living space would be available.

His sister told the court that space would not be an issue, explaining that White occupied the lower flat of the family’s home before his incarceration and that the area remains vacant. She said it would only need to be cleaned and prepared for him.

She also assured the court that she would be able to oversee the administration of White’s medication and ensure that he receives it as required.

The latest proceedings come more than two years after Justice Nanton ruled that White was unfit to stand trial because of mental illness.

In February 2024, the High Court ordered that White be detained in a suitable location at the Kolbe Foundation, receive treatment for schizophrenia and undergo psychiatric reviews every six months. The results were to be provided to the court, particularly if doctors ever determined that he had become fit to stand trial.

Evidence presented during the 2024 competency proceedings showed that White had undergone several psychiatric evaluations. Government psychiatrist Dr. Alejandro Matus testified that earlier assessments had identified bipolar disorder and psychosis before White was diagnosed with schizophrenia.

White is accused of murdering William Emmanuel Rubio in Belize City on July 29, 2020. According to contemporaneous reports, Rubio was fatally stabbed during an altercation near the Pound Yard Bridge area, and White was subsequently arrested and charged with murder.

White has not been tried or convicted of Rubio’s murder because of the finding that he was mentally unfit to stand trial.

Justice Nanton is scheduled to return to the matter on October 16.

World.title: Calypso legend Mighty Sparrow dies at 91
World.content:
Calypso legend Mighty Sparrow dies at 91

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Caribbean is mourning the loss of one of its most celebrated musical icons after legendary calypsonian Slinger Francisco, better known as the Mighty Sparrow, died at the age of 91.

According to a statement from his family, Sparrow died peacefully in New York on Sunday following a brief illness. He was surrounded by loved ones during his final moments.

“It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of Trinidad and Tobago’s Calypso icon, Slinger Francisco, known to the world as ‘The Mighty Sparrow’,” the family said.

Sparrow became one of the most influential figures in Caribbean music, building a career that spanned decades and helping to bring calypso to audiences far beyond Trinidad and Tobago.

Known for his unmistakable voice, sharp lyrics, humour and commanding performances, Sparrow used music to explore politics, culture, relationships, social issues and everyday Caribbean life.

His extensive body of work helped define an era of calypso and inspired generations of singers, songwriters and performers throughout the region.

Beyond the stage, his family remembered him as a husband, father, grandfather, great-grandfather, life partner and friend.

The family also said Sparrow embraced Christianity in his final days and was baptised into the Seventh-day Adventist faith.

His death marks the end of an extraordinary chapter in Caribbean music.

For generations, the name Mighty Sparrow became synonymous with calypso, and his influence stretched across Trinidad and Tobago, Belize and the wider Caribbean.

As news of his passing spreads, tributes are expected from artists, fans and cultural leaders remembering a man whose music helped shape Caribbean identity for more than half a century.

Mighty Sparrow was 91.

World.title: Between horror and hope
World.content:
Patients seated in Kingston Public Hospital’s morning clinic waiting area at 11:30 am last Tuesday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

HOSPITAL horror stories are all too familiar for Jamaicans, and though the age-old issues of long wait times, lack of resources, and poor service appear unyielding and have only led to more frustration when accessing the country’s public health-care system, there appears to be at least a glimmer of hope.

While Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton continues to highlight increased government spending in the public health sector, Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes has argued that there are major disparities in access and quality between the wealthy and the poor.

Last week, this Jamaica Observer reporter visited public health facilities in Kingston, St Andrew, and St Catherine — namely University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), Kingston Public Hospital (KPH), Spanish Town Hospital, and Linstead Public Hospital — to find out from patients whether public health care reliably serves them, who are the ones depending on it.

“I would like to see a total revamp of what is going on here, and the health-care system,” said Norman James, a patient at KPH who was sitting under a tent with people awaiting blood tests last Tuesday.

James said he got out of bed at 5:30 am to ensure he was on time for his 9:00 am appointment.

When the Sunday Observer arrived at the hospital at approximately 11:30 am, he had already been seen by a doctor and was waiting to leave the compound. But James said his experiences at KPH were often markedly different.

The 70-year-old recalled one admission to the hospital, which saw him waiting days before being properly accommodated on a ward.

“I’ve come to this hospital a couple times to be admitted, and let me tell you, that’s a whole other story. I came in here the Friday night, and Saturday passed and it was Sunday before I could get a bed,” he said.

His concerns also extended beyond waiting times. Pointing to the wheelchair in which he was sitting, James said its wheels lacked rubber, leaving only the metal rim to support him.

“Where are the funds going? They don’t have enough beds, they don’t have enough chairs, fans, and their wheelchairs don’t have rubber on them. They can do better,” he argued.

Across from him, a woman who asked not to be named, said she had been waiting since 7:00 am for medical attention and that her doctor had still not arrived.

She also complained about limited seating and the intense heat in the waiting area, while another woman said the lack of basic amenities needed for patient comfort often made hospital visits unpleasant.

This was also true for Kelly-Ann Dwyer, a patient at Spanish Town Hospital who was recently transferred from KPH, due to what she said was a three-year waiting list for a surgery on her leg that has been broken since February.

She told the Sunday Observer that, while she was more comfortable at the St Catherine hospital, it was not because of the facilities, but rather the dedication and compassion shown by the medical staff.

According to her, Spanish Town Hospital is still lacking in many critical areas.

“I find that there aren’t certain types of specialists here; there are no cardiologists, no neurosurgeons. I also find that the Drug Serv [pharmacy] doesn’t have much medication — no high blood pressure tablets, no sugar [diabetes] tablets. They just basically have the minimal stuff — cold medicine, itch cream, and stuff like that. There isn’t much to work with, and if you’re going to do surgery, more than likely you must buy some of the things. There aren’t many things for the doctors to work with,” she added.

But while Dwyer was fond of the service she received from medical practitioners, another client of the hospital was having “one of the worst experiences ever” at the facility.

The woman, who asked not to be named, was visibly upset as she told the Sunday Observer that she brought a family member experiencing a mild stroke to the hospital and he was left to sit in a wheelchair overnight.

“Tell you the truth, if I get sick, God forbid, I don’t want to come here. They should do better,” she said.

Speaking on the wider health-care system, she also highlighted high medication costs, though she noted that she does not have health insurance and is not the holder of a National Health Fund (NHF) card.

“Sometimes you have to just buy what you can afford, and in-between that, to make it serve you a little longer, you ease off of it and take your herbal medicine; boil your bush and drink it,” she said.

Her comments come against the backdrop of concerns raised by Tufton about the standard of care being delivered in the public health system.

The minister said last month that more than 1,000 complaints recorded through the Ministry of Health and Wellness’s Client Care Connect system pointed to problems involving communication, professional conduct, and patients’ overall experience.

He said the ministry would intensify efforts to expose system failures and hold negligent health workers accountable, while emphasising the need for patients to be treated with compassion, empathy, dignity, respect, and fairness.

Tufton also announced the rebuilding and modernisation of 101 health centres across five western parishes. Furthermore, he has spoken of major hospital redevelopments, including at Spanish Town Hospital and Cornwall Regional Hospital.

At Linstead Hospital, however, several patients were more than pleased with the facility and its staff.

They sang praises about the “always clean” compound, compassionate doctors and nurses, and the life-saving procedures they’ve received at the hospital.

“I’ve been admitted here more than six times. Last year I was admitted because of a blood clot in my chest. Two weeks after, I got a stroke and was stuck one place, and I’m telling you, they really took care of me. I couldn’t walk or talk, I couldn’t do anything. You see even the ladies who took care of me? Oh God man, they treat me so good,” said one woman.

Others agreed, noting that they’ve had similar experiences. While they expressed hope that the hospital’s capacity to handle specialised procedures would improve, it was their belief that the standard of care at the Type C facility is exemplary.

At UHWI, Errol Campbell sat among patients who had filled the hospital’s halls for their morning clinic visit, many having arrived before 8:30 am.

Campbell, who has been a patient at the hospital for more than three years and has undergone three surgeries there, had nothing but praise for the facility and its staff.

“It’s a bit expensive, but the care and the service I received with my surgeries were worth it. All my surgeries were life-threatening. One was cancer, and they stopped it in its track before it spread to my blood. The other was a brain surgery. So, I’m just really pleased with the service I’ve gotten here,” he said.

Campbell said clinic wait times vary, but he was not particularly bothered by delays, explaining that he expected a longer process on busier days.

“The health-care sector outside of the hospital is slack. To me, the treatment here is the best you’ll get. I don’t have any troubles sourcing the medication either; yes, it’s expensive, but I can access it. So I really and truly don’t have any problems,” he said.

Inside the hospital’s registration room, however, 86-year-old Herman Perkins offered another assessment.

“The University Hospital is not for the poor, it’s for the rich,” he said, pulling from his bag a list on which he had recorded the costs of medication and services from his previous visit. Perkins said he had paid $34,000 out of pocket.

“The Government not helping the poor. I’m telling you, it’s all just talk… So, the whole situation is bad,” he said.

The differing experiences described by patients paint a picture of the broader debate about the state of Jamaica’s public health-care system.

Last Sunday, Dr Dawes was scathing in his comments on the public health system.

“Under this Government, one Jamaica means having money [so] you get to live. In the other Jamaica, nobody listens to you unless you go on TikTok Live. Same flesh and blood, same country, same taxes — two different Jamaicas,” he said while addressing the public session of the People’s National Party’s 88th Annual Conference at Independence Park in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland.

He questioned whether increased Government spending on health was translating into better conditions for patients, saying, “They love to tell you that the budget has grown, but I ask them, show me the money! Walk into any hospital and show me the money that you have put into health, because we are seeing the same crowded emergency rooms, the same broken down theatres and elevators, the same broken down machines. The care went down when the funding went up,” he alleged.

“So don’t ask them what they spent, ask them what they built, and show me the money. Show me the [intensive care units] without the ventilators and show me the money. Show me the ambulances in the garages and show me the money. Show me the $28 million, 10 years later, no [Cornwall] Regional Hospital, still not functional, and show me the money,” he said.

World.title: Dry run
World.content:
According to the latest update from the National Water Commission, 99 of its 450 water supply systems are being affected by drought conditions.

WATER suppliers are struggling to keep pace with a surge in demand amid drought conditions, with one Manchester-based operator describing the current situation as the busiest he’s had in his 15 years of business.

Rohan Smith, owner of Rohan’s Water Truck in Mandeville, said the demand has become so intense that customers are calling at least once every day to refill.
