Polish President Karol Nawrocki “does not like” the fact that the Trump administration has invited Vladimir Putin to this year’s G20 summit in the United States, says his chief foreign policy aide. However, Nawrocki, who is a close ally of Donald Trump, still plans to attend the event – which Poland has been invited to as a guest rather than a full G20 member – in order to represent Polish interests and push for full membership of the group. 🔴 "Nie podoba nam się to". Nawrocki ma problem po decyzji Trumpa Prezydent Karol Nawrocki weźmie udział w grudniowym szczycie G20 w Miami, na który zaproszono również Władimira Putina. Szef Biura Polityki Międzynarodowej Kancelarii Prezydenta Marcin Przydacz przyznał na antenie… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 26, 2026 The G20, a major intergovernmental forum, holds an annual summit whose location rotates among members. This year’s event will take place in December at a golf resort in Miami owned by Trump. On Wednesday this week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Trump has invited Putin to attend the summit, saying that “we think it’s an opportunity for him to engage…with other world leaders” and “we hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept”. “If you only meet with people that you agree with, then these are very nice meetings but nothing happens,” added Rubio. “In order to solve problems, you have to meet with people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with.” Marco Rubio on Russia: We’ve invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with Trump, but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he will accept. pic.twitter.com/e0GSz7Y8gm — Clash Report (@clashreport) September 23, 2026 Last December, Rubio also announced Poland’s invitation to the summit as a guest, saying that it would be “assuming its rightful place in the G20”. In May this year, the US also “expressed its strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member”. Poland will be represented by Nawrocki, who is a vocal critic of Putin and Russia, and is himself on a Russian wanted list for his work leading efforts to demolish Soviet-era monuments in Poland. In an interview on Sunday with news website Wirtualna Polska, the head of Nawrocki’s international policy office, Marcin Przydacz, was asked if the US was right to invite Putin. “We don’t like it,” he replied. “But we were invited to the G20 summit as guests, and it’s not our role to tell the participants who should be part of it,” he added, noting that Russia is a founding member of the G20. However, “if it were up to us, Russia should be isolated in all international forums.” Nevertheless, “President [Nawrocki] is going to Miami and doesn’t intend to change his plans at this stage”, confirmed Przydacz. “Poland will be at the G20 summit because it’s in our interest…This isn’t the only format in which we sit with countries we disagree with.” However, he also added that, “if the Russian leader actually intends to come, and is not just invited, we will discuss this with our European and Euro-Atlantic allies”. Putin has not attended a G20 summit in person since 2019, initially due to the COVID-19 pandemic and later amid the fallout from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant against him. The US is not a member of the ICC, so the arrest warrant does not apply on its territory. Przydacz told Wirtualna Polska that Putin “should be held accountable for his crimes”. Asked if Nawrocki would shake hands with the Russian president at the G20, Przydacz said that he “doesn’t think any interactions will occur”. The United States has expressed "strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member" following talks in Warsaw, after which it also emphasised "strong and growing" Polish-American relations https://t.co/qTpCACnMfu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 2, 2026 He also emphasised that Poland’s invitation to the summit was a “major success, demonstrating our growing role”. He said that Nawrocki would use the event to push its ambition to become a full member of the group. He added that it would also seek to “bring a Central European perspective” to the event, representing its entire region, which has so far been excluded from the G20. Earlier this week, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski said that, in his opinion, the US should make Putin’s invitation to the G20 conditional upon Russia implementing a ceasefire in Ukraine, reported news website Interia. However, he noted that, when a G20 meeting of finance ministers took place in the US earlier this year, Poland had attended alongside Russia. President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support to its eastern neighbour. Poland has also been one of the primary targets of Russia’s hybrid actions against European countries, including airspace violations, acts of sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation. World.title: Poland extends tax rights to same-sex couples with foreign marriages
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad and have had their wedding certificates transcribed into the Polish registry the same tax rights as other married couples. The decision follows a ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) requiring Poland – whose domestic law does not allow same-sex couples to form any type of legal union – to recognise same-sex marriages contracted in other EU member states. Podpisałem dziś interpretację ogólną, która zapewnia, że osoby, które uzyskały transkrypcję aktu małżeństwa będą miały w polskich urzędach skarbowych takie same prawa i obowiązki podatkowe jak wszyscy małżonkowie. — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) September 24, 2026 “Today, I signed a general interpretation ensuring that persons who have obtained a transcription of their marriage certificate will have the same tax rights and obligations in Polish tax offices as all other married couples,” announced finance minister Andrzej Domański in a social media post. A general interpretation is an official position taken by the finance ministry aiming to clarify the application of tax law in a specific area. Among the benefits that couples with a transcribed foreign marriage certificate can now receive include preferential treatment under inheritance and gift tax rules and the ability to file joint personal income tax returns. Couples may also pay tax on behalf of a spouse and refuse to testify as a witness in proceedings involving their spouse. “This is about basic equality, justice and fairness,” Domański told broadcaster TVN. “We want these rights to be enforceable in an effective way.” The finance minister said that the decision would have a “negligible” impact on the state budget. He also noted that such couples would be subject to the obligations that apply to other married couples in Poland, which include liability for their spouse’s tax obligations. Osoby, które uzyskały tak zwaną transkrypcję aktu małżeństwa, będą miały przed polskimi urzędami skarbowymi dokładnie takie same prawa i obowiązki jak pozostali małżonkowie – powiedział minister finansów Andrzej Domański w rozmowie z Grzegorzem Kajdanowiczem w @faktypofaktach w… pic.twitter.com/uVwDaD3ZDk — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 24, 2026 The finance minister’s decision has drawn criticism from right-wing politicians, who argue that recognition of same-sex marriage violates the constitution, which states that “marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland”. Paweł Szefernaker, chief of staff to President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, said Domański’s actions were “inconsistent with the constitution” and had been carried out “without legislation, without debate, without honestly telling Poles what is really happening”. “Everyone has the right to a private life,” he added. “However, the state has a duty to protect the legal order and provide tax support for marriage.” Patryk Jaki, a deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition party, said that the finance minister’s actions “clearly violate Polish law and will have legal implications in the future” for Domański, who is “writing additional points in the indictment against himself”. Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) group, said the tax interpretation “will be revoked on the very first day” if his party comes to power. To jest niezgodna z Konstytucją próba faktycznego zrównania małżeństwa ze związkami jednopłciowymi. Bez zmiany Konstytucji, bez ustawy, bez debaty, bez uczciwego powiedzenia Polakom, co naprawdę się dzieje. Każdy ma prawo do prywatnego życia według własnych wyborów. Ale państwo… https://t.co/0CQ9Lnfl02 — Paweł Szefernaker 🇵🇱 (@szefernaker) September 24, 2026 The changes follow a ruling issued by the CJEU in November 2025 ordering Poland to recognise same-sex marriages contracted in other EU states. The court found that failing to do so infringes the freedom to move and reside within the EU as well as the right to respect for private and family life. In light of that ruling, in March this year, Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA) ordered Warsaw’s registry office to recognise a marriage conducted by two Polish men in Germany by transcribing it into the Polish civil registry. In May, the Polish government issued a regulation allowing such transcriptions of foreign same-sex marriages to take place nationwide. It went into force in August. However, even before then, some cities had begun transcribing marriage certificates, beginning with Warsaw and Wrocław in May. At the end of August, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski reported that 84 same-sex couples had already transcribed their foreign marriages under the government’s new regulation. Poland has begun paying benefits to same-sex couples who married abroad then entered their marriage into the Polish registry. The EU court ordered Poland to recognise such marriages, even though domestic law does not allow for any form of same-sex union https://t.co/svnRjyBO8Q — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 22, 2026 While foreign same-sex marriages can now be entered into Poland’s civil registry, questions have remained as to what that will mean in practice for such couples, especially as domestic law does not recognise same-sex relationships. In another development, labour minister Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk announced last week that the Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) has begun paying care allowances to qualifying same-sex couples who married abroad and have had their wedding certificates transcribed into the Polish registry. World.title: Prosecutors drop case in which Wałęsa was accused of lying about being communist collaborator
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prosecutors have ended a decade-long case in which former president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa was accused of falsely claiming not to have authored documents relating to his alleged cooperation with the communist authorities. Wałęsa, who led the Solidarity movement that helped bring down the communist regime in the 1980s, has always denied longstanding claims that, in the 1970s, he acted as an informant to the communist security services. The case has become highly politicised, with right-wing figures – especially from the Law and Justice (PiS) party that ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023 – critical of Wałęsa. By contrast, the former president, who turns 83 next week, enjoys good relations with the current ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Waldemar Żurek, Tusk’s justice minister and prosecutor general, welcomed the decision to drop the case against Wałęsa, saying that, under PiS, “a politicised state apparatus hounded the legend of Solidarity, deliberately ignoring facts and basic logic”. Now, “truth has triumphed over an attempt to rewrite history”. Prokuratura ostatecznie umorzyła śledztwo przeciwko Lechowi Wałęsie. Przez lata upolityczniony aparat państwa ścigał legendę „Solidarności”, celowo ignorując fakty i elementarną logikę. Zignorowano bezsporny fakt historyczny – SB masowo fałszowała dokumenty i podpisy Wałęsy w… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 24, 2026 The case in question stems from statements made by Wałęsa in 2016 during an investigation by the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that also has prosecutorial powers. Those proceedings, in which the former Polish president testified as a witness, were launched after documents apparently carrying his signature were found in the home archives of former communist interior minister Czesław Kiszczak. The files indicated that Wałęsa, working under the code name TW Bolek, signed a commitment to collaborate with the communist Security Service (SB). They also included payslips and informant’s notes. The former president had told the media at the time when the documents were discovered that they had been forged. When speaking to IPN investigators, he also denied having drafted or signed all but one of the documents. However, prosecutors subsequently claimed that – after comparing the documents from Kiszczak’s file with others they said had been written and signed by Wałęsa, as well as consulting forensic handwriting experts – Wałęsa’s testimony was false in the case of over 50 of the documents. In 2021, the former president was charged with giving false testimony. Then, in 2023, he was indicted, meaning the case was sent to court. However, in 2024, after Tusk’s government had taken power from PiS, prosecutors asked that the case be returned to them by the court, which agreed to the request. Now, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw has announced that it is discontinuing the case entirely, after finding that there are no grounds for Wałęsa to be prosecuted. Lech Wałęsa will face trial accused of falsely testifying not to have signed documents of cooperation with the communist authorities. If convicted, he can be jailed for up to 3 years. He calls the claims against him "terrible insults and monstrous lies" https://t.co/X0eb4e5ahm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2023 In a statement explaining the decision, prosecutors claimed that there had been significant “methodological errors” made previously in attributing handwritten texts to Wałęsa and in handwriting comparisons between them. “There was no evidence to assume with 100% certainty that the comparative material actually came from Lech Wałęsa,” they wrote. In fact, “the evidence collected clearly indicated that Lech Wałęsa did not write long manuscripts during his life, and especially not in the 1970s”. “Some witnesses explicitly stated that, at that time, he was a secondary illiterate,” meaning someone who has lost their ability to read and write, said the prosecutors. “He was not able to write and could barely read.” This, along with other concerns over how the case was previously conducted, “led to the conclusion that there was no certain basis to assume that Lech Wałęsa was the author of the documents disclosed in the ‘Kiszczak files’, and therefore there was no evidence that he lied during the interrogation”. Hit! Ekipa Tuska ogłosiła Wałęsę analfabetą by wybronić go przed Bolkiem! To się nie dzieje! To niemożliwe! pic.twitter.com/PQnOn5XDb0 — Sławomir Cenckiewicz (@Cenckiewicz) September 24, 2026 Prosecutors also said that “the testimony of numerous witnesses proves that the files of TW Bolek, discovered in the possession of General Kiszczak’s widow, were most likely fabricated. Finally, they argued that, even if Wałęsa had given false testimony, he was protected by the constitutional right against self-incrimination while being interviewed as a witness. “The prosecution found that Lech Wałęsa could have feared that if he admitted to having prepared or signed the documents from the ‘Kiszczak files’…all his testimonies in which he denied being secret collaborator “Bolek” in previous proceedings…would be deemed false and would lead to his being held criminally liable.” Lech Wałęsa, Angela Merkel and Volodymyr Zelensky have been named the first distinguished members of the European Order of Merit. The award was created by the European Parliament to "honour those who did not simply believe in Europe, but helped build it" https://t.co/inosiiRQkW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 11, 2026 In response to the announcement, Wałęsa shared on his Facebook page the post by Żurek praising the prosecutors’ decision. Wałęsa then added a comment claiming that Jarosław and Lech Kaczyński, the founders of PiS, had ordered a right-wing historian, Sławomir Cenckiewicz, to fake the Kiszczak files. Cenckiewicz has written extensively about Wałęsa, including about his alleged collaboration with the communist security services. He also recently served as national security advisor to current Polish President Karol Nawrocki, who was elected last year with the support of PiS. In a series of social media posts on Thursday, Cenkiewicz said that he had “never read a bigger lie” than the prosecutors’ statement justifying dropping the case. He also ridiculed the idea that Wałęsa could have led the Solidarity movement in the 1980s and served as president in the 1990s if he was a “secondary illiterate”. Większego kłamstwa przebranego w wymiar sprawiedliwości RP nigdy nie czytałem! To większe kłamstwo niż skandaliczny wyrok Kapińskiego i spółki z 2000 r.! Reżim Tuska uznał, że Wałęsa nie był Bolkiem, a Instytut Sehna niczego kategorycznie nie ustalił! I powtórzyli brednie… — Sławomir Cenckiewicz (@Cenckiewicz) September 24, 2026 The accusations of communist collaboration have tarnished Wałęsa’s reputation among some Poles. In 2017, shortly after the Kiszczak files were uncovered, a poll by IBRiS for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 28% believed Wałęsa was not a national hero. However, 62% said that he was. Earlier this year, Wałęsa was named as one of the first three distinguished members of the European Order of Merit, a new initiative launched by the European Parliament, alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and former German Chancellor Angela Merkel. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Polish government has launched an information campaign on how to respond in the event of an air strike. It has also announced that 85,000 shelters are to be marked with clear signs across Poland and an evacuation plan is being developed. The moves come amid growing concerns over Russia strikes in Ukraine near the Polish border. The prime minister and foreign minister have warned that Russia could be planning “something big” this year, without specifying what that might involve. 🟡 KOMUNIKAT | MSWiA publikuje instrukcję reagowania podczas zagrożenia atakiem z powietrza. 📄 Ministerstwo Spraw Wewnętrznych i Administracji udostępnia nową instrukcję postępowania na wypadek ataku z powietrza. To rozwinięcie treści zawartych w „Poradniku Bezpieczeństwa”,… pic.twitter.com/aw3h07mdeF — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 25, 2026 On Friday, Poland’s interior ministry published information on how to respond to the threat of an air attack, expanding on a safety handbook sent to all 17 million households in the country earlier this year. The new guidelines explain where to seek cover during an air raid, how to prepare homes and what to do if an attack occurs while people are at home, at work, outdoors or in a car. They advise people to seek a shelter point, take a prepared evacuation backpack and any necessary medication, and use only stairs. If reaching a shelter would require spending a long time outdoors, people are advised to remain inside and move to a central room without windows. Separately, the ministry has prepared guidelines for schools after some were criticised last week for evacuating children outside school buildings during alarms in the eastern province of Lublin. W całej Polsce mają pojawić się obowiązkowe oznaczenia Punktów Schronienia. Specjalna aplikacja pokaże ich lokalizacje, a nowe oznakowanie ma ułatwić mieszkańcom znalezienie bezpiecznego miejsca w sytuacji zagrożenia. Materiał 🎥 Michał Niewodowski pic.twitter.com/HVoo3ypETT — 19.30 TVP (@1930_tvp) September 21, 2026 To make shelter points easier to identify, the interior ministry has prepared a draft regulation requiring local authorities and managers of designated sites to mark them clearly by the end of the year with a blue triangle on an orange background, as well as a green sign saying “Punkt schronienia” (“Shelter point”). The locations can also be found using a mobile application launched last year. According to the ministry’s own data, Poland currently has about 85,000 shelter points, which could host 23.7 million people, or 64% of the country’s population. A national plan is also being developed to coordinate potential evacuation as a result of war, a threat of war or a natural disaster. The plan is intended to establish evacuation routes and reception areas in advance, including how many people may need to be moved and where they could be accommodated. “When a threat arises, we warn the Polish people and defend our security. It is only natural that we prepare for worst-case scenarios, while deeply believing that they will never come to pass,” interior minister Marcin Kierwiński told the Rzeczpospolita newspaper. “Evacuation plans are being prepared…These plans rely heavily on the strength of the entire crisis response system. The more we strengthen that system, the more precise the plans will be,” Kierwiński added. Poland has launched a mobile application and website that allows people to find their nearest shelter in times of war or other emergencies https://t.co/YE3rsltCj5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 22, 2025 The evacuation plans have become the subject of false claims circulating on social media. These posts allege that the government is preparing to forcibly displace Poles and ultimately eliminate the Polish nation, with some linking the alleged plan to an agreement between Berlin and Kyiv, reports the Onet news service. They claim that evacuees would never be allowed to return, allegations the government quickly moved to debunk. 📢 STOP FAKE NEWS! W sieci krążą fałszywe informacje, jakoby przygotowywany Krajowy Plan Ewakuacji miał oznaczać masowe wysiedlenie mieszkańców Polski ‼️To nieprawda‼️ 🔎 FAKT: Krajowy Plan Ewakuacji określa procedury na wypadek wojny, zagrożenia wojną lub klęski żywiołowej.… pic.twitter.com/YNEqXF3StJ — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 18, 2026 The measures are part of a broader effort to strengthen Poland’s civil protection system. Last week, Kierwiński said Poland plans to triple the current number of warning sirens in Lublin province to more than 1,000 by the end of 2026. This follows a series of Russian attacks in western Ukraine, including a drone strike on a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw about 2 km from the Polish border. The recent escalation comes after several incidents in recent years involving violations of Polish airspace, including the entry of around 20 Russian drones on one night last year, as well as the explosion of a Russian missile in a field in eastern Poland earlier this year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned last week that Russia’s further plans could include attacks designed to test NATO’s response. Those warnings were echoed yesterday by Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, who said that multiple sources suggested that “Russia is planning something big this year.” “I think Putin needs a pretext for mobilisation, so they might carry out a false-flag attack to tell the Russians, ‘We are under attack, and that is why we must mobilise,’” he added. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has expressed his horror at an “evil” knife attack carried out today by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland, which left one priest dead and others seriously injured. The incident has caused shock in Poland, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledging that the perpetrator, who is in police custody, will face the “full severity of Polish law”. W Opactwie Sióstr Benedyktynek w Jarosławiu obywatel Ukrainy dopuścił się straszliwej zbrodni. Jesteśmy wstrząśnięci tym złem. Według dotychczasowych informacji zginął ksiądz katolicki, a kilka innych osób zostało rannych. Składamy najgłębsze kondolencje rodzinie i bliskim… — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 24, 2026 The attack took place on Thursday morning on the grounds of a Benedictine abbey in the town of Jarosław in southeast Poland. Local police reported that a 31-year-old Ukrainian man had stabbed four male victims and one female. Three were members of the clergy and two laypeople. Authorities later confirmed that one of the men, a priest, had died of his injuries in hospital and that two others were in serious condition. The cathedral in the nearby city of Rzeszów named the deceased as Stanisław Zbojnowicz. The superior of the Benedictine Sisters Monastery, Barbara Dendor, told news website Interia that Zbojnowicz had been in a confessional when the attack began. He had rushed out to attempt to close the gates and protect other people, but was stabbed by the assailant before he could do so. In its initial social media post announcing Zbojnowicz’s death, the cathedral also said that a second priest, Marek Pieńkowski, had died. However, a few minutes later it deleted that claim, blaming the “enormous information chaos surrounding today’s tragic event”. One person was killed and four were injured in a knife attack at a Catholic convent in Poland this morning, with clergy among the victims. Police have detained a 31-year-old Ukrainian man on suspicion of carrying out the attack. The motive remains unknown https://t.co/93nbqpwnIA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 On Thursday afternoon, prosecutors revealed that the suspect, who has not been named, had entered Poland from Germany in the early hours of Thursday and “was heading to the border crossing [with Ukraine] in Korczowa”, which is around 30km (18.6 miles) from Jarosław. However, he ultimately did not cross the border and, for unknown reasons, ended up in Jarosław, where he entered the grounds of the abbey and began his attack, using a knife taken from the kitchen. Prosecutors said that doctors would assess the suspect’s condition before he was interrogated. Blood samples were also taken to be tested for the presence of narcotics and alcohol. The motive for the attack remains unknown. Dendor told news website Wirtualna Polska that the perpetrator was unknown to them. “He looked like a madman, in shorts and a T-shirt, even though it was cold today,” she said. Wirtualna Polska reports, based on the accounts of unnamed witnesses, that the Ukrainian man had earlier in the day knocked on the gates of the abbey and asked for financial assistance. However, he was turned away due to the suspicion that he was drunk or under the influence of drugs and was asked to come back later. That is standard practice for places that offer aid, reports the news service. The man “flew into a rage when he didn’t get help and allegedly threatened priests”, said one of the unnamed sources. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk expressed his sympathy for the loved ones of the victims of the attack and pledged that the perpetrator “will be punished with the full severity of Polish law”. President Karol Nawrocki likewise expressed his condolences and called on the authorities to “quickly and thoroughly clarify all the circumstances of this tragedy”. Later on Thursday afternoon, Zelensky also extended his condolences in a social media post published in Polish. “We are shocked by this evil,” he wrote. “The perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility in accordance with the applicable law.” Morderca z Jarosławia jest w rękach Polskiej Policji. Trwają czynności. Sprawca to obywatel Ukrainy. Będzie ukarany z całą surowością polskiego prawa. Łączę się w bólu z bliskimi ofiar tego brutalnego ataku. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 24, 2026 Earlier, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw had “condemned the brutal attack” in Jarosław. However, it also appealed for people “not to allow pain to turn into hatred or further violence”, saying that “accountability for the crime must be based solely on the law”. Polish-Ukrainian relations have been tense in recent months, amid rising anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland and anger at Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during World War Two. There has been a rise in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland this year. Marcin Piotrowski, a board member of the Folkowisko Foundation, which provides aid to Ukrainian refugees, told newspaper Rzeczpospolita today that the tragedy in Jarosław was already being exploited on social media. World.title: Polish constitutional court officials charged with preventing entry of new judges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further, after prosecutors charged two senior TK officials over their role in preventing new judges from taking up their positions on the court. Those judges were chosen by the government’s majority in parliament but rejected by President Karol Nawrocki and the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, both of whom are aligned with the right-wing opposition. Following news of the charges, Święczkowski announced that he has initiated proceedings of his own against three other new judges who were admitted to the court this year after being chosen by the ruling coalition. That could result in them being expelled from their positions. Zarzuty w śledztwie dotyczącym niedopuszczenia sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego do orzekania: ⬇️https://t.co/MPiKCEqGBs — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) September 23, 2026 After coming to power in December 2023, the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk refused to recognise the TK, which was stacked with judges appointed by the former Law and Justice administration. It argued that, because some of those judges were unlawfully appointed, the TK itself was illegitimate. Earlier this year, Tusk’s majority in parliament finally began the process of appointing new judges to the TK to fill the growing number of vacancies. Normally, 15 judges sit on the tribunal, but many seats were empty after incumbents’ nine-year terms had expired and the government had previously refused to fill them. However, under Polish law, new TK judges must take an oath “before the president” in order to take up their position. Nawrocki, who was elected last year with the support of PiS, has refused to swear in four of the six judges chosen by parliament in March. Nawrocki argues that there were legal doubts surrounding their election. The government rejects this, as do the judges themselves, who organised their own swearing-in ceremony before a notary and then submitted the documents to the presidential chancellery. Afterwards, the four judges attempted to take up their positions at the TK. However, Święczkowski, who served in the PiS government before becoming a TK judge, refused to admit them, arguing that they had not taken the necessary oath before the president. The judges took their case to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which in May issued an interim order requiring that they be allowed to take up their positions. But Święczkowski has refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the competence to make such a decision. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 While Święczkowski himself is protected from prosecution by legal immunity, two senior TK officials have now been charged over their role in refusing entry to the four judges. One of the two suspects, who can be named only as Zofia H. under Polish privacy law, is the director of the TK’s chancellery; the other, Piotr P., is the commander of the TK’s security service. They have been charged with abuse of power by a public official, which is punishable by up to three years in prison, and “maliciously and persistently” violating the employment rights of the judges, an offence that carries a sentence of up to two years. Prosecutors say that the officials’ actions were “to the detriment of the private interests of judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and the public interest in the proper functioning of the judiciary in Poland”. Both of the accused have been questioned and pleaded not guilty. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further after the tribunal ruled that the president is not obliged to swear in new TK judges appointed by parliament. President Nawrocki last month refused to swear in four new judges https://t.co/ycnweW9pSR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 13, 2026 The decision to bring charges was welcomed by Waldemar Żurek, who serves as justice minister in Tusk’s government as well as prosecutor general. “In a building that should stand guard over the constitution, unlawful blockades were organised, humiliating inspections were conducted, and malicious bullying was directed at legally elected judges,” he wrote on social media. “A state official has no right to place themselves above the law, and the gates of the tribunal are not the gates of a private fortress,” he continued. “Anyone who carries out unlawful political orders and destroys the foundations of the rule of law must reckon with criminal liability.” W budynku, który powinien stać na straży Konstytucji, urządzono bezprawne blokady, upokarzające kontrole i złośliwy mobbing wobec legalnie wybranych sędziów. Urzędnik państwowy nie ma prawa stawiać się ponad prawem, a bramy Trybunału nie są bramami prywatnej twierdzy.… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 23, 2026 The TK itself, however, condemned prosecutors’ actions, calling them “unlawful” and a “tool of personal pressure and a form of intimidation”. “The director of the chancellery and all other employees of the TK have performed and continue to perform their duties and official orders in accordance with the applicable law,” wrote the tribunal on its official X account. It argued that it would, in fact, have been a criminal abuse of power to have “allowed persons who have not taken the oath before the President to assume the office of a TK judge”. W dniu dzisiejszym @PK_GOV_PL przedstawiła Pani Dyrektor Kancelarii Trybunału Konstytucyjnego absurdalne zarzuty z art. 231 § 1 i 218 § 3 Kodeksu karnego, które od początku do końca są oparte na wymyślonych podstawach prawnych. Działanie to stanowi kolejną próbę wywarcia wpływu… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) September 23, 2026 On Thursday, the day after the charges were announced, the TK issued a further statement saying that Święczkowski had initiated proceedings against three new TK judges who were chosen by parliament this year and sworn in by Nawrocki (two in March, the other in June). The TK said that it was assessing complaints that two of those judges filed against tribunal employees, as well as their refusal to participate in sessions of the TK’s general assembly. Those three judges have shown solidarity with their four excluded colleagues by refusing to participate. “These proceedings may conclude with the most severe ruling of the disciplinary court in the form of removal from office of the aforementioned TK judges,” wrote the TK. Prezes @TK_GOV_PL Bogdan Święczkowski, działając na wniosek jednego z sędziów, wszczął dzisiaj postępowanie mogące się zakończyć zarzutami dyscyplinarnymi wobec trojga sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego: Magdaleny Bentkowskiej, Dariusza Szostka oraz Sławomira Patyry.… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) September 24, 2026 An eighth new TK judge chosen this year, Maciej Berek, who was elected by parliament earlier this month, has also not yet been sworn in by Nawrocki. Berek’s appointment has been particularly controversial, given that he served in the government until being nominated to the TK. Tusk described Berek as his “right-hand man”. Even some MPs from Tusk’s ruling coalition voted against Berek’s appointment, arguing that it contradicted the government’s own efforts to “depoliticise” the judiciary, including by banning recently serving politicians from sitting on the TK. The presidential chancellery has so far refused to swear in Berek based on a technicality, arguing that there is no evidence he has previously served for at least ten years as a legal counsel, which is a requirement to sit on the TK. Berek says that he has presented such evidence. A fire last night at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company, was caused deliberately, says digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which relies heavily on Starlink connections. Although the fire is still being investigated, “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian”, says Gawkowski. 🔴 Gawkowski o pożarze stacji Starlink. "Element wojny hybrydowej" Wicepremier Krzysztof Gawkowski ocenił pożar stacji Starlink na Mazowszu jako celową próbę zakłócenia łączności. – Wiele wskazuje na to, że pożar stacji Starlinków na Mazowszu to kolejny element wojny hybrydowej… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 24, 2026 Firefighters were called out at around 9 p.m. on Wednesday to the facility, which is located in the village of Wola Krobowska, just south of the capital Warsaw. Due to suspicions that the fire had been caused deliberately, police and officers from the Internal Security Agency (ABW) were also later dispatched to the scene. “We’re dealing with an arson attack that was intended to impact critical telecommunications infrastructure that influences internet operation,” Gawkowski, who also serves as deputy prime minister, told broadcaster TVN on Thursday morning. In a separate interview with TVP, the minister said that the facility is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel and “provides internet transmission through Poland, and also to Ukraine”. He noted that other internet providers use Exatel’s facility, including Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which is the owner of Starlink. Starlink terminals have been vital in Ukraine during Russia’s war against the country. Gawkowski told TVN that “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian” and “is another element of the hybrid warfare we are facing”. Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe, including a series of arson attacks. “The Russians want to paralyse critical infrastructure, cut off water, gas and electricity, paralyse the internet,” said the minister. “All these processes have one goal: to incite panic and stir up emotions.” However, in his remarks to TVP, Gawkowski acknowledged that, for now, “it is impossible to say” for sure whether Russia was behind the attack. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 The spokesman for Poland’s security services, Jacek Dobrzyński, likewise told TVN that “at this stage it is still too early to talk about the causes or motives of this fire”. However, he confirmed that “everything points to arson”. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek also told broadcaster RMF that “this could be an act of sabotage, and we are taking that into account, so nothing can be ruled out here, especially since these are sensitive elements that ensure satellite communications”. Polish news service Defence24 notes that ground stations are used by Starlink to connect its satellite constellation with terrestrial communications infrastructure. The facility in Poland, alongside one in Lithuania, serves the entire Central and Eastern Europe region, including Ukraine. Tu nieco więcej o roli stacji naziemnych w systemie Starlink. https://t.co/EYys481dSi — Mariusz Marszałkowski (@MJMarszalkowski) September 24, 2026 Earlier this month, a fire broke out at a drone plant in Poland belonging to WB Electronics, which supplies the armed forces of Ukraine and Poland, among others. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that there was “no doubt” the fire was caused deliberately, and that Russia was likely behind it. The Polish government has in recent months warned that Russia is planning to escalate its hybrid actions against Poland and other countries in the region, including through acts of sabotage, disinformation, and potential airspace and border violations. In July, a Russian missile entered Polish airspace before landing in a field in eastern Poland. On Wednesday this week, the same day as the fire in Wola Krobowska broke out, a Russian helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace. World.title: Czech Women Win Billie Jean King Cup Again After Eight Years
World.content:
Czech Republic eased past Ukraine to win the Billie Jean King Cup for the 12th time.

This year’s Wimbledon finalists Linda Noskova and Karolina Muchova breezed past their opponents to secure a 2-0 victory and deny the Ukrainians a first title in the competition.



Muchova, the runner-up at Wimbledon, comfortably beat Anhelina Kalinina 6-2 6-3 in the opening singles match before Noskova’s 6-3 ⁠7-6 (7-5) win over world number seven Elina Svitolina ‌secured the title.

It is the Czechs’ first win at the event since 2018, making them the second-most successful nation in its history after the United States, who have 18 titles.

In her first year as Czechia captain, Barbora Strycova has made history.

Former Grand Slam doubles champion Strycova is just the fourth woman to win the Billie Jean King Cup as both a player and a captain. Strycova joins a Hall of Fame cast of Margaret Court, Chrissie Evert and Billie Jean King in achieving that feat.

CZECHIA'S NEW ALL-STARS ARE WORLD CHAMPIONS 🇨🇿🏆#BJKCup pic.twitter.com/W8B2WucxI0 — Billie Jean King Cup (@BJKCup) September 27, 2026

She’s also the first player in event history to win the Billie Jean King Cup juniors title as a player and the Billie Jean King Cup title as a player and a captain. Strycova won the Billie Jean King Cup juniors title alongside Petra Cetkovska and Lucie Safarova in 2001.

The Czechs also knocked out Great Britain in the quarter-finals in Shenzhen, China, which led GB captain Anne Keothavong to describe them as “the strongest team here”.

World.title: Bolt and Lucid Plan 25,000 Autonomous Vehicles Across Europe
World.content:
Bolt and U.S. electric vehicle maker Lucid Group have announced a partnership to develop autonomous mobility services in Europe, with plans to deploy more than 25,000 fully autonomous vehicles across European cities over the coming years.

The vehicles will be based on Lucid’s upcoming Midsize platform and use NVIDIA Hyperion, a reference architecture and development platform for autonomous vehicles.



The companies plan to develop the vehicles for SAE Level 4 autonomous driving, which allows vehicles to operate without human control within defined conditions.

Bolt says the project is part of its wider ambition to have 100,000 autonomous vehicles operating on its platform by 2035.

The companies will work together from the early stages of vehicle development. Bolt will contribute traffic and mobility data, operational experience and knowledge of European markets, while Lucid will provide its software-defined vehicle platform and automotive technology.

Bolt will also define requirements covering the vehicle, software, safety and passenger experience. Its autonomous driving division will oversee the partnership and develop the infrastructure needed to operate the fleet.

This will include vehicle dispatch, charging, maintenance, remote assistance and customer support. Bolt also plans to own and operate the autonomous vehicles itself.

Rollout will depend on local regulations

The companies have not yet announced which European cities will receive the service first.

Bolt and Lucid said launches will take place city by city and depend on local regulations, official approvals and operational readiness. The companies also plan to work with autonomous driving technology providers, European regulators and policymakers before introducing the service.

For the foreseeable future, autonomous vehicles on the Bolt platform will operate alongside vehicles driven by human drivers.

Lucid’s side of the project will be led by Lucid Technologies, a newly established division bringing together artificial intelligence, advanced driver-assistance systems, autonomous driving and other digital technologies.

Bolt currently operates in more than 850 cities across 50 countries and says its platform serves more than 200 million customers. Its services include ride-hailing, car-sharing, electric scooters and food and grocery delivery.

Lucid Group, listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker LCID, develops electric vehicles and related technologies. The company operates manufacturing facilities in Arizona and Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Prague Airport Works to Speed Up Border Checks for Non-EU Travellers
World.content:
Prague Airport and the Czech Ministry of the Interior are preparing additional measures to reduce waiting times for passengers arriving from non-Schengen countries following the introduction of the EU Entry/Exit System (EES).

The new system has made border checks more complex, particularly for travellers from outside the EU. Prague Airport says it has already introduced several measures aimed at keeping passenger flows moving during busy periods.



Airport staff, known as the Red Team, are assisting passengers in the terminal, directing them through the new procedures and providing information where needed. The airport has also adjusted passenger flow corridors based on data collected since the system was introduced.

One of the main issues identified so far is the self-service registration process. According to the airport, a significant number of passengers do not complete their registration at the kiosks, which can lead to additional delays at passport control.

Prague Airport is therefore examining the entire journey from the registration kiosks to passport control and looking at ways to make the process easier, particularly for families and older passengers.

“Data has shown us that the most common delays occur when people interrupt the registration process at the terminals,” said Radomír Lašák, Chairman of the Board of Prague Airport. “Together with the Police of the Czech Republic, we are not merely putting together temporary stopgaps but are redesigning the entire process so that it remains resilient even during peak periods.”

Further measures are also being prepared at the European level, including the possibility of allowing passengers to complete parts of the EES registration before departure. Airlines could also provide passengers with information about the process during flights.

The Czech Ministry of the Interior and the Immigration Police are working with Prague Airport on the next steps and have committed additional resources to help manage the new system.

Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the authorities’ priority was to maintain security standards while limiting the impact of the new procedures on passengers.

The airport said it will continue monitoring passenger flows and adjusting its procedures based on actual operations, particularly during peak travel periods.

World.title: Czech Statehood Day 2026: What Is Open and What to Do in Prague
World.content:
September 28 is a public holiday in the Czech Republic, marking Czech Statehood Day and the feast of St. Wenceslas. This year, the holiday falls on a Monday, giving many people a three-day weekend.

For anyone planning to spend the day in Prague, however, there are two practical questions: which shops will be open, and what can you do around the city?



Where you can shop on September 28

Under Czech legislation regulating retail opening hours, shops with a sales area of more than 200 square meters must close on September 28.

The restriction applies throughout the day and covers large supermarkets, hypermarkets and home improvement stores.

Smaller shops with sales areas of up to 200 square meters are exempt and can open at their owners’ discretion. Petrol stations and pharmacies can also operate.

Other exceptions include shops located at airports, railway stations and bus terminals, as well as retail outlets inside healthcare facilities.

Why September 28 is Czech Statehood Day

The holiday commemorates Prince Wenceslas, a member of the Přemyslid dynasty who became one of the central figures in Czech history.

Wenceslas was killed by his brother Boleslav I on September 28, 935, in Stará Boleslav. His death later became the foundation of a cult that developed around him from the late 10th century onward.

His remains were transferred to Prague in 938 on Boleslav’s orders and buried in the Rotunda of St. Vitus. The reasons behind the transfer are not known with certainty, but the move helped strengthen Wenceslas’s status as a religious figure while also reinforcing Prague’s position as the center of the emerging Czech state.

Over the following centuries, Wenceslas became the patron saint of the Czech lands and an important symbol of Czech statehood.

The connection between Wenceslas and Czech political tradition was further strengthened under Charles IV, who commissioned the Crown of Saint Wenceslas. The crown became one of the principal symbols of the Czech monarchy and remains part of the Czech Crown Jewels.

See the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle

September 28 is also the final day of this year’s exhibition of the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle.

The jewels are being displayed in Vladislav Hall as part of the exhibition Habsburgs 500. Admission is free, and the display also includes a coronation robe dating from 1653 and other historical objects.

The exhibition closes at the end of the day on September 28.

Government buildings open to visitors

Several normally restricted buildings will also be accessible to the public.

Straka Academy, the official seat of the Czech government, will open its doors on September 28. Visitors can see the government meeting room, ceremonial areas and the building’s garden.

The program also includes an interactive exhibition called Journey of the Republic. Tours are free and begin at 10 a.m., with the final group scheduled to leave at 5 p.m.

The Ministry of Finance on Letenská Street will also welcome visitors. Tours start at 9:30 a.m. and include the ministry’s historic premises and the former monastery.

Museums and other attractions

The National Technical Museum in Letná will remain open on September 28, giving visitors access to its permanent exhibitions.

The Postal Museum will also be open.

For those looking for a more traditional Prague attraction, September 28 will be the final chance this year to ride the historic Letná Carousel.

Another option is the National Museum, where the Přemyslids exhibition examines the history of the dynasty that ruled the Czech lands during the country’s early medieval period.

The exhibition runs until October 15, 2026, making the public holiday particularly relevant for visitors interested in the history behind Czech Statehood Day.

World.title: Bangkok Gears Up for the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings
World.content:
All eyes are on Thailand as the country prepares to host the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) Annual Meetings, also known as the 2026 Annual Meetings or AM2026 Thailand.

Running from 12-18 October 2026, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, the event will mark Thailand’s second time hosting the meetings, following its first in 1991. This will make Thailand one of only three nations to have hosted the IMF–WBG Annual Meetings twice.



The IMF–WBG Annual Meetings, held for two consecutive years in Washington D.C. and every third year in one of the 191 member countries, serve as a gathering of top economic figures from around the world. By covering a broad range of issues, the meetings aim to strengthen global financial stability, combat poverty, and ensure inclusive economic growth and job creation.

Thailand’s selection to host again in 2026 highlights how the country has advanced over the past three decades in terms of its institutional progress, economic resilience, and sustained engagement with international partners. As host, Thailand brings decades’ worth of experience in economic transformation and regional leadership to the table.

The “Olympics of Finance”

Often dubbed the “Olympics of Finance,” the meetings are set to attract more than 15,000 participants, including finance ministers, central bankers, economists, business leaders, civil society representatives, and journalists from the IMF and World Bank’s 191 member countries, including the Czech Republic.

The Annual Meetings will be held under the theme of “Thailand’s New Horizons: Empowering People, Building Resilience”. Therefore, the meetings will focus on enhancing people’s potential and creating opportunities, with the goal of fostering a financial and economic system that is safe, sustainable, and inclusive.

Under the theme, the government plans to showcase four policy priorities it believes are increasingly relevant in an era marked by geopolitical fragmentation, economic volatility, and demographic change. These are indeed the issues that warrant serious conversation and sincere collaboration among the global community and all stakeholders to address them in the most efficient way:

Digital Transformation: The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems.

The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems. Connected Economy: A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored.

A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored. Climate Finance: The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change.

The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change. Longevity Economy: The final priority seeks to turn the challenges of ageing populations into new sources of economic growth.

Alongside these focus areas, the Bank of Thailand plans to unveil the “Bangkok Blueprint,” an international framework developed jointly with the IMF and the World Bank aimed at combating digital financial fraud and strengthening trust in the digital economy.

Readiness in All Aspects

According to the Fiscal Policy Office, Thailand’s overall readiness has been assessed at “Grade A” following months of coordination between the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Thailand, and the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings Secretariat.

Preparations extend beyond the conference venue. Authorities have developed contingency plans for traffic management, emergency responses, and arrangements for high-level foreign officials. A working group has also been established to address cybersecurity matters.

Beyond Tourism: A Regional Economic Capital

Beyond its long-established reputation as a world-renowned tourist destination, the 2026 Annual Meetings offer Thailand an excellent opportunity to present another dimension of the Kingdom to the international community.

AM2026 reinforces Thailand’s standing as a trusted international partner while highlighting its growing role as a regional economic capital and a hub for finance, investment, policy innovation, and multilateral dialogue in Southeast Asia. Having said that, countries and companies vying for economic and business opportunities cannot overlook Thailand and its potential to become an important impetus for their long-term prosperity and growth.

(Source material and reporting courtesy of Thailand NOW)

World.title: Hotline for Foreigners in Czechia: Tips to Save Time and Frustration
World.content:
Reaching the Client Centre for residence-related questions in Czechia requires patience.

More than 2,000 calls are received every day, so some waiting time is unavoidable.

However, you can significantly reduce your waiting time by calling during less busy hours, which are published through the authority’s official channels.



It is also worth having your identification document number ready before calling. This can speed up the process, particularly if you are calling to book an appointment.

Those who do not want to wait on the phone can use other ways to get in touch. Answers to many common questions are available in the Frequently Asked Questions section of the Information Portal for Foreigners (ipc.gov.cz).

If your matter is not urgent or your question is more complicated, you can also contact the centre by email at [email protected].

The current status of your application can be checked online using the dedicated service on the same portal.

When it comes to appointments, most bookings can be made through your personal account on the Information Portal for Foreigners.

You only need to book by phone in three cases: to provide biometric data, to inspect your case file, or to collect a residence card as an EU citizen.

World.title: Czech President Warns NATO Allies May Need to Shoot Down Russian Aircraft
World.content:
Czech President Petr Pavel has warned that NATO may eventually need to shoot down Russian aircraft or drones that deliberately violate the alliance’s airspace.

Speaking to Fox News Digital in New York during the U.N. General Assembly, Pavel said Russia was testing NATO’s readiness and could interpret continued restraint as a sign of weakness.

“There might be the time when we will have to shoot down some of these planes or unmanned vehicles that are testing our readiness,” Pavel said.



Pavel said the alliance needs to distinguish between accidental airspace violations and deliberate incursions in which an aircraft ignores warnings to leave.

“If it is deliberate and the violator doesn’t respond to our measures, then we will have to act, because otherwise Russia simply would push further on,” he said.

His comments came after a series of incidents involving Russian aircraft and drones near NATO territory.

On Wednesday, a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace after crossing from the Kaliningrad region. According to Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command, the helicopter travelled around 300 metres into Polish territory and remained there for 42 seconds.

On Thursday, Romania also scrambled two F-16 fighter jets after an unidentified aerial target entered its airspace from the direction of Ukraine. The object later crashed near the country’s border with Ukraine, with no casualties reported.

Pavel said Russia’s actions reminded him of incidents during his time at NATO, when Russian aircraft repeatedly tested the responses of allied forces.

“They are, on one hand, provoking. On the other, testing what will our reaction be,” he said.

In a speech to the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, Pavel said Russia’s “aggressive posture poses a direct threat to European security” and warned that the risks were increasing.

The Czech president also questioned whether Russia was genuinely prepared to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine. He said Moscow would need to agree to a ceasefire before entering meaningful negotiations without conditions.

World.title: New Sports Complex Opens in Prague’s Riegrovy Sady
World.content:
A new sports complex has opened in Riegrovy Sady, giving residents of Prague 2 access to a refurbished court, parkour equipment, a climbing wall and an outdoor fitness area.

The facility, next to the TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady building, was officially opened Tuesday afternoon. The renovation and installation of new equipment cost CZK 8.7 million, excluding VAT.



The site is intended for people of different ages and can be used for several sports. The refurbished court is suitable for football and basketball, while the new equipment includes a parkour area, climbing wall and a small fitness zone.

The project forms part of the district’s longer-term plans for Riegrovy Sady. Officials said the upper section of the park has lacked sufficient space for outdoor sports and exercise.

The sports area occupies land that until last year was used by two unauthorized structures, the Ice Magic ice sculpture exhibition and the Containall sports and cultural center.

The district is also considering a much larger project for the site. A multifunctional hall for sports and cultural events could eventually replace the current outdoor facility.

Petr Janů, deputy chairman of TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady, previously said the goal was to create a building designed to remain in place for decades or longer.

The project is still at an early stage. Prague 2 plans to discuss the design with local residents, heritage authorities and Prague’s Institute of Planning and Development. An architectural competition is also expected to be held.

World.title: PM Magyar: Parliament to hand over two corrupt politicians to investigators on Monday
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Sunday evening that Hungary’s newly created National Asset Recovery and Protection Office will begin investigating several high-profile corruption cases on Monday, while parliament is expected to vote on lifting the immunity of two former ministers.

In a Facebook post published on Sunday evening, Magyar said the government’s “Operation Purgatory” would move into a new phase on Monday.

“On Monday, the landing begins as part of Operation Purgatory. The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office will begin investigating several high-profile corruption cases. Parliament will also hand over two corrupt politicians to investigators,” Magyar wrote.

The “two corrupt politicians” reference appears to concern former ministers Balázs Hankó and Miklós Seszták, whose immunity is due to be considered by parliament on Monday. Both face criminal allegations, but neither has been convicted, and both have denied wrongdoing. Parliament is also expected to consider the immunity of Prime Minister Péter Magyar and MP Mária Gurzó in separate cases.

What is the asset recovery office?

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) was established in 2026 as an independent state institution tasked with tracing, protecting and recovering public assets believed to have been unlawfully removed from public ownership.

Under the law establishing the body, it can examine transactions involving public procurement, state subsidies, concessions, EU funds, state-owned companies and other forms of public property. It also has investigative powers and can represent the public prosecution in court in cases falling within its remit.

The office was one of the central elements of Magyar’s “Operation Purgatory”, which he first announced in parliament in June as part of a broader anti-corruption and institutional reform programme.

For more on Monday’s high-profile immunity votes, see our earlier report: Hungarian immunity rights: Prosecutors seek suspension for PM Magyar and two former Fidesz ministers

Several corruption cases already in focus

Magyar did not specify in his Sunday post which cases the NVVH would formally open first. He has, however, repeatedly pointed to several high-profile cases involving public funds, state contracts and institutions linked to the former government.

Prosecutors are seeking to suspend Balázs Hankó’s immunity in connection with an investigation into the National Cultural Fund, while Miklós Seszták faces a separate corruption case linked to Volánbusz.

Monday’s extraordinary parliamentary session will add further political weight to the launch of the new office, with lawmakers expected to vote on several immunity cases involving senior politicians.

At the same time, the NVVH is expected to begin turning the government’s anti-corruption campaign into actual investigations and asset-recovery proceedings. That will make Monday an early test of how far the new authority is prepared to go — and which cases it chooses to prioritise first.

World.title: Hungary moves to cut hospital waiting times with weekend operations and extra pay
World.content:
Hungary is launching a new programme aimed at cutting hospital waiting times by expanding surgery into afternoons and weekends, while offering extra financial incentives to medical teams. The move comes as patients in some hospitals still face waits of several months for planned procedures.

Hospital waiting lists are one of the most visible pressure points in Hungary’s healthcare system.

According to the National Health Insurance Fund’s current waiting-list database, average waiting times for cataract surgery exceed 200 days at several hospitals. At the Markhot Ferenc Hospital in Heves County, the average waiting time over the previous six months stood at 310 days, while patients at the Nagykanizsa hospital waited an average of 246 days. In Zala County, the figure was 188 days.

Against this backdrop, Health Minister Zsolt Hegedűs announced on Sunday that the government is launching a new waiting-list reduction programme previously promised by Prime Minister Péter Magyar.

“There is a strong commitment from the medical profession. Our task now is to bring together the additional funding, professional expertise, the right incentives and the available capacity in a way that allows patients to feel the benefits as soon as possible,” Hegedűs Zsolt wrote.

In his announcement, the minister said the aim is not simply to perform more operations, but to make better use of existing surgical capacity and give healthcare workers a direct financial incentive to take on additional work.

More surgeries after normal hours

The programme will primarily expand operations into the afternoon hours after regular shifts, while hospitals with sufficient staffing and professional capacity will also be able to perform additional surgery at weekends. A new financing incentive will be introduced to support this extra workload.

Hegedűs said a significant share of the additional funding would go directly to the teams that make the extra procedures possible, including doctors, nurses and other hospital staff.

Part of the new funding would be linked to quality indicators, patient-reported outcomes and patient satisfaction. The model is intended to move closer to what Hegedűs described as a “best practice tariff” approach, in which financing rewards both efficiency and measurable clinical outcomes.

Hospitals to be assessed individually

Each hospital will receive its own “problem map” identifying the main bottlenecks limiting surgical capacity. These may include staff shortages, inefficient operating-room management, competition from private healthcare providers and limited personal incentives for additional work.

The ministry also plans to monitor operating-room utilisation, actual surgical time, the time needed to change patients between procedures and the efficiency of the entire process.

Hegedűs argued that operating theatres are among the most expensive parts of hospital infrastructure and that unused capacity represents a significant loss.

If you missed it: Construction projects in Hungary could be halted for six months over environmental violations

Semmelweis and Pécs expanding capacity

Semmelweis University and the University of Pécs are already working on expanding surgical capacity under the programme.

Foreign specialists experienced in ERAS, or Enhanced Recovery After Surgery protocols, are also expected to participate. These protocols are designed to shorten hospital stays where medically appropriate, speed up patient recovery and allow hospitals to admit the next patients sooner.

The programme will also include a review and “clean-up” of waiting lists, with the aim of identifying which patients are still genuinely waiting for surgery and removing outdated or inactive cases.

BMI rule also set to change

Another important change concerns orthopaedic surgery. A protocol introduced in April 2025 automatically placed temporary restrictions on certain patients with a BMI above 35. Hegedűs said this rule is now being reviewed.

Instead of an automatic threshold, future decisions would be based on individual patient risk, professional assessment and the judgment of the treating team.

Patients may also receive more comparable information about hospital performance, quality and outcomes, allowing them to make more informed choices about where to seek treatment.

World.title: Construction projects in Hungary could be halted for six months over environmental violations
World.content:
Hungary has tightened its construction rules, allowing authorities to suspend permitting procedures and block new construction or facility permits for at least six months if a project breaches environmental or nature protection requirements.

Hungary’s parliament has approved amendments to the country’s construction rules that significantly strengthen the consequences of environmental violations at major development projects.

Under the new framework, if authorities establish a breach of environmental or nature protection requirements, the relevant construction permitting procedure must be suspended. In addition, new construction or facility permits may be withheld until the unlawful situation is remedied — and for a minimum period of six months, according to Kormány.hu.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar presented the measure as a response to earlier cases in which major projects continued despite environmental concerns.

“We have seen the consequences in recent years when nothing happened after environmental rules were violated during a priority investment. We are putting an end to that now,” Magyar said in a video announcing the change.

The changes also affect major housing developments linked to the Otthon Start programme, where some priority projects may face temporary permitting restrictions while the government reshapes its wider housing construction policy.

Otthon Start projects also face new restrictions

The amendment specifically covers certain large-scale housing projects connected to the government’s fixed 3% Otthon Start housing loan programme.

Under the scheme, large housing projects can receive priority investment status if they meet specific conditions.

According to the government’s Otthon Start Programme Office, qualifying developments generally need to include at least 250 homes, with at least 70% of the units meeting the programme’s eligibility criteria. Priority status can significantly speed up administrative and permitting procedures.

The latest changes, however, introduce the possibility of temporarily halting permits even for projects that have already received priority status.

The government says this is necessary because some previously planned large-scale Otthon Start developments now need to be coordinated with a broader housing construction programme that is still being prepared. The amendment allows the government to set, by decree, a period during which authorities may not issue new permits for certain already-prioritised Otthon Start developments.

If you missed it: Budapest streets could change dramatically under new pedestrian plan

This is potentially significant for developers because priority status was originally designed to speed up these projects. In practice, the new framework means that a fast-track development could still face a pause if environmental rules are breached or if the project needs to be brought into line with the government’s revised housing policy.

New rules for construction material exports

The parliamentary package also removes an earlier restriction on exports of construction materials.

Since 2021, companies planning to export certain building materials have been required to notify the Hungarian state in advance. The state also had a pre-emption right over the products concerned.

That system will now be abolished. Exporters will no longer have to file the same notification, and the state will lose its right to intervene in those transactions or purchase the materials before they are exported.

The change follows a ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union, which found that the Hungarian mechanism restricted the free movement of goods and therefore conflicted with EU law. The European Commission subsequently launched infringement proceedings after the measure remained in force.

World.title: Cold mornings, warm afternoons: Hungary braces for huge temperature swings next week
World.content:
Hungary is heading into a mostly sunny and dry week, with afternoon temperatures climbing to around 25°C in many areas. The catch: mornings will be sharply colder.

A stretch of settled early autumn weather is expected across Hungary next week, with plenty of sunshine and little to no rain.

According to HungaroMet’s latest forecast, daytime highs will generally remain between 21 and 26°C, keeping conditions pleasantly warm for the end of September and start of October. At the same time, nights and early mornings will feel considerably colder, with minimum temperatures falling as low as 1–2°C in some areas.

The sharp contrast will be one of the defining features of the week.

Weather portal Időkép says daily temperature swings could exceed 20°C in places, particularly where clear skies and light winds allow temperatures to drop quickly overnight before sunshine drives rapid warming during the day.

In practical terms, that means a jacket or cardigan may be essential when leaving home in the morning, while a T-shirt could be enough by the afternoon.

Sunshine dominates the week

Monday is expected to bring largely uninterrupted sunshine across the country, with dry conditions and afternoon temperatures of around 22–26°C.

Tuesday is forecast to remain similarly bright and dry. Morning temperatures could fall to between 1 and 11°C, followed by highs of 22–26°C later in the day.

Wednesday will also be mostly sunny, although some high cloud may reach northern Hungary later in the day. Temperatures are expected to range from around 1–11°C at dawn to 22–25°C in the afternoon.

The dry pattern is then set to continue into Thursday and Friday, with filtered or uninterrupted sunshine and daytime highs mostly between 21 and 25°C.

Despite the warm afternoons, the colder nights mean autumn is becoming increasingly noticeable. Időkép notes that temperatures could fall close to 5°C in many places, while ground frost may still occur in some of the country’s more frost-prone locations.

If you missed it: Budapest streets could change dramatically under new pedestrian plan

Little sign of rain

HungaroMet expects mostly dry conditions throughout the working week, with sunshine dominating and only limited cloud cover at times. Winds should generally remain light or moderate, although stronger gusts may develop locally, particularly around Sopron and parts of eastern Hungary.

The result will be a classic early autumn pattern: cold starts, warm afternoons and large temperature swings throughout the day.

For anyone heading out early, layering will likely be the safest option — because what feels like jacket weather before breakfast may feel almost summery just a few hours later.
