World.title: Marko Mihkelson: Defeatism is not deterrence
World.content:
The snowball of speculation about an imminent Russian attack on Europe is gathering pace. Isolated facts are being mixed with wishful thinking, worst-case scenarios and, at times, little more than the need to grab attention, writes Marko Mihkelson.

We should be careful not to confuse speculation with strategy. The reality is straightforward: a major war is raging in Europe, yet the Allies continue either to ignore it or to treat it as merely a regional conflict over territory. Russia has not changed its strategic objectives. Its aim is to destroy Ukraine's sovereignty and reshape the existing European security architecture - in other words, to weaken and ultimately dismantle NATO.

The uncomfortable truth is that we have done far too little to force the Kremlin to abandon these objectives or to make clear that pursuing them would come at an unbearably high price. Instead, we are creating, almost as a self-fulfilling prophecy, the impression that a Russian attack on NATO is inevitable.

Russia understands that it can confuse and paralyse us through information operations alone. Constant speculation about the Baltic states and Poland risks creating the impression that this is primarily a problem for two or three countries on Russia's doorstep, while the rest of Europe can somehow remain untouched.

We have seen this delusion before with Ukraine: if only the issue in Donbas could somehow be settled, peace would return. The same logic is now being applied to NATO's eastern flank. If Russia gets what it wants there, perhaps everyone else will be safe.

"Above all, we need to stop the submissive avalanche of speculation along the lines of: 'Help, the Russians are coming!'"

But this is not how Russian strategy works. We should not forget Moscow's December 2021 ultimatum, which demanded that NATO roll back its military infrastructure to the 1997 lines. Russia was not merely asking for a settlement over Ukraine. It was demanding a fundamental revision of Europe's security order.

And if Russia sees that even members of the Coalition of the Willing are unwilling to articulate a clear strategic objective — namely, helping Ukraine achieve victory and pushing back Russian aggression — why should the Kremlin believe that we will have the resolve to defend NATO itself?

Russia's campaign against the West would not necessarily begin with a conventional attack. It can start by undermining NATO from within: interfering in elections, amplifying polarising narratives, exploiting political divisions and spreading fear. It can seek to isolate Ukraine by limiting Western support and then test our willingness to stand together.

This is already a war in which Russia is using terror against the West, and we need to recognise that reality if we are serious about bringing it to an end.

The first step is strategic clarity: Russia will not stop simply because we ask it to. It will stop when the costs of continuing its aggression become greater than the benefits it expects to gain.

That means the Coalition of the Willing should, at a minimum, pursue three concrete objectives.

First, we need a substantial increase in military support for Ukraine — for example, a minimum of 0.25% of GDP annually — alongside continued support for Ukraine's financial system to help cover the costs of the war.

Second, we should prepare for a military humanitarian mission to protect Ukrainian cities and critical strategic infrastructure from Russia's massive aerial terror campaign.

Third, we need to apply decisive economic pressure on Russia so that its war machine can no longer operate at its current scale.

If we fail to do this, we should expect more acts of Russian terror across Europe. Defense companies and their executives may become targets. We must also be prepared for false-flag operations in which Russia could attempt to blame Ukraine for an attack causing casualties in a NATO country.

And we must recognise another vulnerability: our own political divisions. Russia is actively seeking to deepen them through interference and information operations. Developments in the France and Germany, as well as in Poland, show how important it is that our political disagreements do not become a strategic gift to the Kremlin.

Above all, we need to stop the submissive avalanche of speculation along the lines of: "Help, the Russians are coming!"

This kind of defeatism does not strengthen deterrence. It weakens it. Instead of endlessly speculating about where Russia might attack next, we should be talking - and acting - to ensure that Russia loses the war of aggression it started. And we should make clear that such aggression will have serious consequences for the dictatorship ruling Russia.

The fear that decisive action might somehow undermine strategic stability is itself becoming a tool of Russian escalation. If every step that could strengthen Ukraine or Europe is rejected because it might provoke Moscow, Russia learns precisely the wrong lesson: that fear works.

That is not deterrence. A new strategic stability in Europe cannot be built on permanent Russian threats, Western hesitation and Ukrainian sacrifice. It can emerge only when the security architecture of Europe is defended and strengthened — and when Russia has been defeated in the war of aggression it launched against it.

Our task is not to predict the next Russian attack. Our task is to make sure Russia understands that aggression will fail.

World.title: Tattoo culture researcher: Women have always been the main source of inspiration
World.content:
Tattoo artist and researcher of Estonian tattoo culture Oskar Poll told ETV that while tattoos during the Soviet era often featured maritime motifs and women, the range of subjects has since expanded considerably.

Oskar Poll has been tattooing for about 10 years. "A solid eight years," he said with a smile. "The first two were a trial period."

His studies are also closely tied to tattooing: he wrote both his bachelor's and master's theses on the history of tattooing in Estonia and is now pursuing the same subject for his doctoral dissertation. Poll earned his bachelor's degree in graphic art from the Estonian Academy of Arts. While there, he began photographing Soviet-era tattoos, a project that later developed into his master's thesis. Poll approached people on the street to find tattoos to photograph.

"Sometimes I felt like a stalker," he said. "I'd spot someone with a tattoo from a distance, follow them, explain what I was doing and ask how, when and where they got it and whether I could take a picture. Eventually, I got to the point where I could tell what kind of tattoo a certain type of person would have."

For his master's thesis, Poll examined, among other things, which tattoos were most popular during the Soviet era and what they meant. According to Poll, maritime imagery was the most common at the time, including anchors, ships, seagulls and similar motifs. Images of women were also popular.

"Women have always been the main source of inspiration in tattooing. In the West, tattooing was very male-dominated for a long time because it was associated with male-dominated subcultures and men would have images of women tattooed on themselves," he explained.

For his doctoral dissertation, Poll has moved on to the transition period. He is studying how Estonia's first professional tattoo artists began working in the country starting in the 1990s.

"I'm focusing on how the first studios and tattoo artists emerged here, where the machines and other equipment came from and where the idea of becoming a tattoo artist came from because for a long time, that kind of job simply didn't exist," Poll said.

The history of tattooing in Estonia has not previously been studied in this way. According to Poll, that is both interesting and daunting. "Everything you say and do is what people will later either accept as the truth or argue with you about."

Comparing Soviet-era tattoos with those of today, Poll said the main difference is the sheer range of choices available.

"Back then, there were certain set images: you'd see skulls, roses, cats, military symbols and anchors. Now the range of places to draw motifs from is so broad, especially thanks to the internet. And the tools used are certainly different as well. Today we have machines. During the Soviet era, there were homemade machines in prisons at one point, but before that, it was a needle and ordinary ink," he said.

Tattoos have also become popular among women. "During the Soviet era and before that, it was more of an exception," Poll said.

World.title: Mikk Kasesalk: Estonian culture has no other refuge anywhere in the world
World.content:
Estonia's competitiveness must largely rely on capable, educated people, but that idea is under pressure as the education system's capacity fails to keep pace with demand, writes Mikk Kasesalk.

Societies are held together not only by laws and institutions, but also by shared beliefs. When those beliefs are strong, we take many of the common obligations stemming from them for granted. When they weaken, we increasingly have to ask why we should take on those obligations at all and bear the costs associated with them.

I would highlight three convictions that have played a key role in Estonia's development:

We must defend our country. Everyone is responsible and individual effort matters. Culture is a cornerstone of the Estonian state.

The annual drafting of the state budget provides the clearest indication of how important these convictions are to the government of the day and how it weighs them against one another.

We must defend our country

The story of a small nation that, against all odds, built a state of its own, lost it and then regained it through song is one of the deepest layers of our shared beliefs. That story has shaped Estonia's self-image and also strongly influences our thinking on security and foreign policy.

There is currently a very broad political consensus in Estonia on the need to rapidly increase defense spending. NATO and relations with allies are at the heart of our security policy, while the security threat posed by Russia gives defense spending an exceptionally strong position in state budget discussions.

The broader the political consensus on the necessity of a particular expenditure, the more important it is to maintain critical oversight of how the money is used. The need for defense spending does not mean that every defense expenditure is automatically justified. Even before the recent scandals in the defense sector, experts warned that money may have been allocated to defense faster than it could be put to effective use.

Every euro spent without justification undermines trust in government decisions and strengthens the hand of those who argue that public money is being spent carelessly. When it comes to national defense, there is no question whether the state is willing to pay for it — its importance is clearly reflected in the state budget. But the greater the spending, the greater the accountability must be for ensuring that it is justified.

Everyone is responsible and individual effort matters

After the restoration of independence, Estonia was built on the belief that a free market and individual effort lead to success. Estonia's competitiveness must largely rely on capable, educated people because we have neither vast natural resources nor historically accumulated wealth on which to build our success. That idea is now coming under pressure because the education system's capacity is not growing in line with demand. This is particularly evident in higher education where funding stumbles from one crisis to the next.

The promise of a society built on effort is credible only if people have a reasonable opportunity to develop their abilities and advance through their own efforts. The education system is one of the institutions that creates that opportunity. If capable people who are willing to work hard are denied educational opportunities for reasons beyond their control, the moral promise that "work hard and you will succeed" becomes less credible.

This spring, negotiations on administrative agreements between the education and research minister and the Council of Rectors raised the question of what will happen to young people graduating from high school in the coming years. Their numbers are higher than in previous years and there are not enough places for them in higher education. The problem did not emerge overnight. A few years ago, the same parties sought to resolve the long-term funding crisis in higher education, but the Ministry of Education and Research ultimately failed to fully pay the amount promised to universities under the agreement reached at the time.

During negotiations on the administrative agreements signed in May, it was agreed that universities would gradually add up to 1,000 study places a year over the next four years, while the education and research minister pledged to find €146 million to fund them and included that commitment in the state's next budget strategy.

If the additional funding is not found, increasing admissions will mean either dividing existing funding among more students or abandoning plans to create the additional study places. In either case, pressure on the capacity and quality of Estonian-language higher education will increase as demand grows.

This is where the principles of individual effort and state responsibility come together. The state cannot promise people that effort matters while failing to create the opportunities through which that effort can bear fruit. If we consider individual effort to be a foundation of Estonia's success, the importance of the education that makes it possible must also be reflected in the state's budget choices.

Culture is a cornerstone of the Estonian state

Estonian culture has no refuge anywhere else in the world, no place where it will survive if we ourselves do not value it. It is therefore difficult to understand why culture has been one of the areas expected to make additional savings year after year. Why is culture repeatedly among the first areas to come under pressure for cuts whenever the state's finances deteriorate?

Lennart Meri is credited with saying: "Culture is as important to society as vitamins are to the human body." The effects of a deficiency may not be immediately visible. The consequence of prolonged underfunding of culture may not be the immediate closure of an institution or the cancellation of an event. The shortfall may also manifest itself in existing activities being kept going at the cost of lower pay and heavier workloads for those working in the field.

Culture should not be seen as an expense that can be afforded only when there is money left over. Its value does not lie solely in what can be measured in ticket revenue, visitor numbers or economic impact. Culture also creates new meanings and connections through which society makes sense of itself.

That value cannot be totaled up in a spreadsheet. But the meanings that are never created and the bridges between people that are never built make the Estonia we collectively experience increasingly duller, poorer and easier to abandon. If culture is a cornerstone of the Estonian state, its place in the state budget must reflect that as well.

Inevitability or political will

How much can the Estonian state weaken the institutions through which the Estonian language and culture are passed on to the next generation before it begins to undermine the very rationale for its own existence?

The scale of the sums involved helps illustrate the choices we are actually talking about. Estonia's 2027 state budget amounts to about €20 billion. Defense spending will reach approximately €2.4 billion in 2026 and will account for at least 5 percent of GDP in the following years as well.

Covering the agreed increase in higher education funding will require €146 million over four years. There is no comparable overall figure for the needs of the cultural sector, but the entire budget of the Ministry of Culture's area of government is around €350 million a year. Purely to illustrate the scale, even if we were to use one-tenth of that amount as a point of comparison, we would be talking about roughly €35 million.

These figures do not mean that defense spending, higher education and culture are directly interchangeable items in the budget. They do show, however, that the sums involved are on very different scales. Scarce resources place limits on the choices available, but they do not predetermine how we choose among the options we have.

The budget is where abstract values become concrete choices. Every line in the budget is the result of someone's decision and many of those decisions could be made differently.

This brings us back to the three convictions mentioned at the outset. National defense protects the possibility of the Estonian state's continued existence. Education gives people the opportunity to develop their abilities and advance through their own efforts. Culture creates and carries forward the meanings through which society makes sense of itself. None of these can replace the others.

World.title: Iraq starts receiving gasoline from Syria
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq has officially started importing gasoline through Syria, creating a crucial overland energy corridor between the two nations.

This transit route serves as a critical alternative for Baghdad to secure vital fuel supplies amid difficulties facing maritime shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The initial consignment consisted of roughly 32,800 metric tons of high-octane gasoline brought by sea from the United States. The shipment arrived at Syria’s Baniyas port aboard the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Avanti.

The fuel was moved to storage tanks at the Baniyas refinery before being loaded into tanker trucks. At least 77 tanker trucks have already left the port, headed toward Iraq’s Baiji refinery, according to Reuters.

A transit contract between the state-owned Syrian Petroleum Company (SPC) and Qatar’s UCC Holding, which provided the gasoline and is in charge of logistics, governs the operation.

Iraq’s State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) has finalized the agreement to ensure the continuity of these supplies.

The route was only used in one direction, transporting Iraqi fuel oil by road to the Syrian port of Baniyas before being exported out by sea, reaching the US market for the first time in July.

According to officials, while the present transportation arrangement only covers gasoline, the corridor might potentially grow to include other petroleum products, crude oil, and other items.

World.title: Vitol becomes second-largest buyer of Iraq’s oil after UAE’s ADNOC
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Vitol has strengthened its presence in the Iraqi oil market by purchasing at least 25 million barrels of crude in September 2026, a move reflecting how major oil traders are capitalizing on supply disruptions in the Gulf region.

The Swiss-based Dutch multinational energy and commodity trading company is leveraging its shipping and logistics capabilities to provide export outlets for Iraqi crude amid the challenges facing tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz due to the conflict between the United States and Iran.

These purchases come as Baghdad seeks to maintain oil flows to global markets following a decline in exports during the early months of the war, when securing the transport of shipments from Iraq’s southern ports proved difficult.

The deal highlights the shifting dynamics of the Middle East oil trade, where the ability to secure tankers and arrange transportation has become a critical factor in accessing crude oil, alongside Iraq’s use of price discounts to attract buyers willing to take on shipping risks.

Vitol has purchased between 25 and 30 million barrels of Iraqi crude scheduled for loading this September.

An official in the Iraqi energy sector indicated that the company’s share amounted to approximately 25 million barrels, according to Reuters.

Vitol has become the second-largest buyer of Iraqi oil this month, trailing the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), which purchased approximately 40 million barrels, compared to about 32 million barrels in August.

The moves came amid a drop in Iraq’s oil exports during the early months of the conflict, owing to the country’s ports’ position in the northern Arabian Gulf and the lack of its own shipping fleet, which hindered petroleum delivery to global markets.

According to data from Kpler, a leading data platform that tracks commodity flows and maritime shipping, Iraqi oil exports from southern ports averaged approximately 2.35 million barrels per day in August.

In August, Iran granted a number of Iraqi oil tankers permission to transit the Strait of Hormuz, following repeated requests from Baghdad for arrangements to ensure continued oil exports.

Iraqi oil shipments face challenges due to navigational risks in the Strait of Hormuz. Vessels transiting the waterway are exposed to the threat of Iranian attacks, prompting buyers to demand price discounts to offset higher transportation and insurance costs.

World.title: Iraq studies proposals to store oil in Oman, Egypt, Singapore
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is studying proposals to store crude oil in storage facilities in countries including Egypt, Oman, and Singapore.

The spokesperson for the Iraqi Oil Ministry, Salim al-Rikabi, told Attaqa News that the government is studying proposals to participate in refinery and storage projects outside Iraq to select the best options.

To move forward with storing crude oil in Egypt, Iraq needs to complete the Basra-Haditha pipeline project, which would then extend out toward the Jordanian port of Aqaba and finally to the city of Arish in the northeastern Sinai Peninsula, according to al-Rikabi.

In September 2025, Iraq’s State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) has signed two agreements with OQ, formerly known as Oman Oil Company, and its subsidiary, Oman Tank Terminal Company (OTTCO).

The first agreement establishes a strategic partnership to develop an integrated project to store Iraqi crude oil in the Special Economic Zone at Duqm (SEZD), the largest special economic zone in the Middle East and North Africa.

The second agreement outlines OQ’s responsibility to market Iraqi crude oil in global markets. The deal aims to leverage the administrative and commercial strengths of both parties to enhance the trading value of Iraqi crude oil internationally.

The proposals are part of the Iraqi government’s effort to bypass the Strait of Hormuz—the main route for the country’s oil exports—where maritime shipping has been facing difficulties since the start of the military conflict involving the United States, Israel, and Iran.

Since the outbreak of the war on February 28 and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Iraq’s seaborne oil exports collapsed to unprecedented levels.

Iraq’s oil exports fell to approximately 550,000 barrels per day in March, 132,000 barrels per day in April, and 98,000 barrels per day in May, before gradually rising to 2.16 million barrels per day in August.

World.title: International coalition halts financial aid to Peshmerga
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The US-led international coalition has officially halted financial aid to Iraqi Kurdistan’s Peshmerga forces following the expiration of a four-year agreement.

The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) and the United States Department of Defense inked an agreement that extended from September 21, 2022, until September 21, 2026.

On Thursday, the troops received their final allowance for August and September 2026.

According to the Secretary-General of the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs, Bakhtiar Sadiq, the financial aid under the initial agreement was planned to steadily reduce by 25 percent each year until reaching a complete halt.

This cash halt aligns with the overall conclusion of the international coalition’s military operations in Iraq, with a full stoppage of combat and training responsibilities expected by September 30, 2026.

Additionally, the proposed US Counter-ISIS Train and Equip Fund (CTEF) plan for 2027 includes no support for the Peshmerga.

The international coalition has tied its financial assistance to necessary reforms and the unification of the Peshmerga forces, particularly the integration of politically separated units. Earlier in September, the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) publicly announced that the unification process was complete.

To address the newly established funding imbalance, the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs has formally requested the federal government in Baghdad to adjust Peshmerga salaries to align them permanently with federal Iraqi military and security forces.

World.title: Iraq seeks US exemption to resume Iranian flights
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi government revealed on Saturday that it is holding discussions with the US administration to obtain an exemption for certain Iraqi airports from the ban on Iranian airline flights imposed under US sanctions, citing the disruption caused to traveling patients, students, and pilgrims.

According to the Iraqi Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), the Iraqi government is engaged in direct talks with the US side to exempt specific Iraqi airports from these measures.

The exception would allow for the resumption of flights for humanitarian grounds, which include medical care, education, religious pilgrimages, and civilian interests.

Iranian airlines primarily handle the transport of Iranians traveling to Iraq in large numbers to visit the shrines of Shiite Imams, as well as Iraqis flying to Iran for religious pilgrimages, studies, or medical treatment.

Iraq joined several other nations in suspending Iranian flights to and from its territory after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that all Iranian airlines will cease operations as of September 23.

Under the new measures, any country or firm that provides services to Iranian aircraft is completely removed from the global US dollar system. The services include fueling airplanes, offering ground handling and landing services, and selling passenger tickets.

World.title: Iraq unveils plan for data centers in Baghdad, Basra, and Mosul
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Communications unveiled an ambitious strategic blueprint on Saturday, September 26, 2026, to construct a distributed network of enterprise data centers across Baghdad, Basra, and Mosul, aiming to upgrade national digital infrastructure and localize hosting for global technology conglomerates.

In an exclusive statement granted to the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the Director General of the General Company for Communications and Informatics, Ali Yassin, confirmed that establishing tier-standard data centers across multiple provinces stands among the ministry’s top executive priorities to accelerate digital transformation.

Yassin revealed that the capital city of Baghdad will host three dedicated data centers situated across prime connectivity hubs, specifically at the Al-Sinak telecommunications complex, the Al-Intisar facility, and the Al-Mamoun Telecommunications Tower compound adjacent to the ministry’s headquarters.

The geographical distribution within the capital ensures redundant network routing, continuous uptime, and high-speed fiber interconnection to support both federal e-governance platforms and commercial cloud services.

Beyond Baghdad, the national strategy targets key regional logistics and transit corridors, including a specialized facility planned in Basra Governorate in close proximity to the international submarine cable landing station, directly capitalizing on Iraq’s high-capacity maritime fiber-optic gateways.

Additionally, the ministry is preparing to establish another facility in Mosul to anchor cloud architecture across the northern provinces.

Yassin emphasized that these specialized data centers are purpose-built to attract major multinational technology companies, creating localized environments capable of hosting global content, accelerating low-latency data delivery, and reinforcing Iraq’s sovereign digital ecosystem.

World.title: Iraq reaches 100,000 LPG converted cars as Parliament urges factory model access
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Gas Filling and Services Company, an operating affiliate of the Iraqi Ministry of Oil, announced on Saturday, September 26, 2026, that the cumulative number of vehicles converted to run on liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) has reached approximately 100,000 across Iraq.

Speaking to the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the company’s media director, Mahdi Al-Nouri, confirmed that retrofitted vehicle figures currently range between 98,000 and 100,000 cars, noting an escalating pace of adoption among motorists seeking economical alternatives to conventional liquid fuels.

Al-Nouri stated that installation and technical maintenance services are carried out across a nationwide network of 26 specialized workshops operating under the state-owned gas company.

The growing consumer uptake reflects heightened public interest in cleaner, subsidized autogas, prompting the Ministry of Oil to scale up workshop throughput and expand fueling station capacity to keep up with escalating demand.

Despite this milestone, converted vehicles represent a modest fraction—less than 1.5 percent—of Iraq’s national automobile fleet, which currently totals approximately 7 million registered cars. The autogas initiative has simultaneously sparked parliamentary scrutiny regarding regulatory bottlenecks.

Lawmaker Amer Abdul-Jabbar raised the issue on the floor of the Council of Representatives, criticizing the Ministry of Oil for restricting autogas dispensing exclusively to locally converted vehicles while denying fuel to imported cars equipped with factory-installed LPG systems.

Abdul-Jabbar called on the federal government to reform existing fuel distribution policies, authorize gas sales for all compatible vehicles, and incentivize the commercial importation of factory-built LPG cars to accelerate emissions reduction and alleviate domestic gasoline consumption.

World.title: Iraq launches first smart pneumatic waste collection system with Spanish backing
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s National Investment Commission (NIC), in coordination with the Ministry of Environment and the Spanish Embassy in Baghdad, officially launched the country’s first smart automated pneumatic waste collection system (URD) on Saturday, September 26, 2026, marking a pivotal milestone in the modernization of municipal sanitation and sustainable urban management.

The initiative introduces advanced underground vacuum collection networks designed to eliminate conventional curbside dumpsters and heavy collection vehicular traffic across newly planned smart cities and licensed residential investment developments.

Speaking at the launch conference attended by an Iraqi News Agency (INA) correspondent, NIC Deputy Chairman Salar Mohammed Amin affirmed that the adoption of the URD pneumatic network represents a comprehensive national initiative requiring deep cross-institutional synergy between public ministries, municipal directorates, and private developers.

He revealed that the commission has already secured all statutory and regulatory approvals to mandate the underground system within master plans for new satellite cities and residential complexes, establishing a national technical committee alongside the Ministry of Environment to oversee phased execution and enforce strict environmental compliance benchmarks.

Amin emphasized that sustainable investment must transcend structural brick-and-mortar construction to create integrated, livable urban ecosystems that elevate daily public health and quality of life.

He noted that operational success relies on an interconnected institutional network encompassing the Ministry of Construction, Housing, Municipalities and Public Works, the Municipality of Baghdad, local governorate authorities, the Ministry of Electricity, and telecommunications operators, working collectively to provide dedicated power grids, subterranean civil infrastructure, and smart sensor integration necessary for automated municipal services.

Spanish Ambassador to Iraq Alicia Rico Pérez del Pulgar underscored that the rollout of the pneumatic vacuum infrastructure represents a substantial qualitative leap toward modernizing waste management practices through cleaner, more energy-efficient technologies.

Highlighting Madrid’s dedication to technical knowledge transfer and bilateral capacity building, the ambassador framed the project as a catalyst for expanded Spanish-Iraqi commercial and environmental partnerships in green infrastructure, renewable energy, and smart city urban planning, calling upon public institutions and private enterprises from both nations to leverage the project into enduring bilateral economic cooperation.

World.title: LPU protests: Over 2,000 police deployed after stone-pelting, vehicles set ablaze
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Punjab Police deployed more than 2,000 personnel at Lovely Professional University (LPU) after student protests over an alleged rape case turned violent on Sunday, with senior officers saying the situation had been brought under control.

ADGP M F Farooqui told news agency ANI, that the force would remain deployed on campus through the night to maintain security.

âWe will ensure security on the campus throughout the night... A force of over 2,000 personnel is currently deployed here. Law and order has been fully maintained and restored... The process is ongoing, and we are working to keep the situation under control,â Farooqui told ANI.

He appealed to families not to panic, saying, âTo the families whose daughters are staying in the hostel here: please do not worry; everyone is safe...

The atmosphere here is completely calm, and the university students are also cooperating with us in restoring peace...â

Fresh violence erupted on Sunday evening after the protesting students pelted stones at police personnel and attacked their vehicles, leaving several cops injured, officials said.

The protests began after claims circulated on social media about the alleged rape of a university student on the LPU campus.





Students later blocked National Highway 44 outside the university from around 8 am, according to officials.

Police said the situation escalated when protesters allegedly pelted stones at personnel and attacked police vehicles. Officers used a lathi charge as they attempted to clear the highway, after which protesters moved towards the campus.

Two police vehicles were set on fire, while several police personnel were injured.

Jalandhar Police Commissioner Satinder Singh said reports of disturbances inside hostels were rumours and that checks had found no such incidents.

âFirst of all, reports of disturbances in the hostels were merely rumours. All hostels have been checked, and there are no issues. Traffic has resumed, and the situation is normal,â Singh said.

He added, âOther matters will be resolved through discussions with the students...

Overall, the atmosphere is fine, and any minor issues will be addressed... Please inform the families that all students are safe and there is no cause for concern.â

DIG (Jalandhar Range) Naveen Singla also said, âThe situation has been brought under control. Traffic movement on NH-44 will be restored soon.â

Meanwhile, LPU postponed its mid-term examinations until further notice and suspended regular classes for 10 days from September 28. The university urged students to remain calm, follow official instructions and stay connected for further updates.

Police said the deployment would continue overnight as authorities work to maintain order on campus and assess the situation.

World.title: Boeing flags 737 MAX glitch that may turn off auto pilot
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Boeing has identified a software issue that could potentially lead to auto pilot disengaging during certain go-arounds (aborting landing to take off again and make a second attempt) on the B737 MAX when pilots change their planned altitude and path.

India has about 100 of these aircraft between Air India Express and Akasa.

Aviation insiders say this is not a safety scare and Boeing has issued an advisory to pilots regarding what to do in the rare event of a B737 MAX going around and then the altitude window being changed from what is in the system for that particular sector.

A Boeing spokesperson said: "Last month, we informed all 737 operators about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario.

We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases. Our engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue."

A spokesperson for Akasa said: "We are closely coordinating with Boeing and can confirm there is no impact to safety... Our aircraft continue to operate safely in accordance with established procedures and applicable regulatory requirements."

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines





AI Express has over 50 of these planes.

US Federal Aviation Admi-nistration has said in a statem-ent that it will "convene a corrective action review board and take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern".

What was to be Boeing's answer to rival Airbus's best-selling A320 new engine option which boasts lower fuel burns, the B737 MAX came under intense scrutiny soon after it entered commercial passenger service in May 2017. Two back-to-back MAX crashes within five months - Lion Air in Oct 2018 and Ethiopian Airlines in March 2019 - that left 346 people dead led to the aircraft being grounded globally in March 2019. After Boeing made some crucial changes, the aircraft was allowed to fly again in Dec 2020.

World.title: Karnataka flags drug landing cost-MRP gap at hospitals of up to 52.6 times; seeks Centre's intervention
World.content:
Concerns have been raised over critical-care medicines, oncology medicine, high-value injectables, implants and surgical supplies, besides diagnostic-linked consumables and disposable devices.

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration commissioner K Srinivas has sought urgent regulatory intervention over the pricing of medicines, medical devices and consumables supplied to hospitals at discounted institutional prices but billed to in-patients at the printed maximum retail price (MRP) or close to it.In some cases the difference between the landing cost and MRP is as high as 52 times. In a letter to the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) and the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Srinivas has flagged critical-care medicines, oncology medicine, high-value injectables, implants and surgical supplies, besides diagnostic-linked consumables and disposable devices. The letter says the practice âmay be especially harmfulâ in these categories.Tens of examples have been enclosed with the letter, showing substantial differences between the reported landing cost and MRP of several products.Some with massive margins are: Gufipol, manufactured by Criticare, has a landing cost of Rs 86 and an MRP of Rs 4,528, a difference of 5,165.1%, or 52.6 times the landing cost. Guficycline-50 injection, manufactured by GUFI, has a landing cost of Rs 160 and an MRP of Rs 7,110, a 4,343.7% difference or 44.4 times the landing cost.Terlitis has a landing cost of Rs 118 against an MRP of Rs 4,416, a 3,642.4% difference or 37.4 times.Among the cancer drugs listed, Taxocare 120 mg from Intas has a landing cost of Rs 1,000 and an MRP of Rs 21,617.6, a 2,061.8% difference or 21.6 times. Romy 250 mcg injection, also from Intas, has a landing cost of Rs 1,650 and an MRP of Rs 4,109, a 149% difference or 2.5 times.The commissioner said a recurring pattern had been reported in hospital procurement and billing: a manufacturer or importer supplies an item to a hospital at a very low institutional price, while the pack carries a substantially higher retail MRP. The hospital then supplies it to an in-patient and charges the MRP or a nominal discount on it despite the lower acquisition price.âThe patient, who is generally unable to obtain an immediate substitute during admission, bears the entire benefit of the manufacturer-hospital discount being retained within the supply chain,â the letter says.Srinivas described the issue as an âinformation-asymmetry and captive-patient problemâ, saying patients generally do not know the institutional acquisition cost and do not have an effective choice at the point of use.The letter argues that MRP-only regulation is insufficient. âMRP operates as a ceiling on retail sale to a consumer, but it does not by itself ensure that the MRP is a fair patient-facing price in an institutional setting,â it says.It proposes mandatory disclosure of institutional transaction prices, a patient-facing price ceiling linked to acquisition cost, anti-evasion provisions, MRP rationalisation and an enforceable reporting and penalty framework.Under the proposed system, the patient-facing price would be the lowest of the applicable statutory ceiling or notified retail price, the printed MRP, and the net institutional acquisition cost plus a prescribed maximum service margin and applicable taxes.The letter also proposes disclosure on hospital bills of the product details, MRP, net institutional acquisition cost, permitted service margin, taxes and final amount charged. It seeks quarterly electronic reporting, risk-based audits, a grievance channel and refunds with interest where overcharging is established.Srinivas has also sought an expert working group and amendments to the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, and asked that the matter be treated as âurgentâ with a reasoned action taken report communicated.

World.title: IndiGo A321 suffers tail strike during go around at Bangalore; plane lands safely in second attempt
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In yet another instance of an

Airbus A321 tail strike, an aircraft (VT-NHP) operating a Guwahati-Bengaluru flight on Sunday suffered the same while going around at its destination.

The flight (6E 6542) aborted landing on the first approach at the destination.

During ascent, it suffered a tail strike. The aircraft landed safely on the second attempt. The DGCA is probing this latest tail strike.

IndiGo spokesperson said 6E 6542 âexperienced an âabnormal runway contactâ while landing during gusty weather at Kempegowda International Airport, Bengaluru. All customers and crew are safe and have disembarked safely.

In line with standard operating procedures, all relevant authorities were informed, and the aircraft is undergoing maintenance checks. It will resume operations after securing necessary clearances.

As always, the safety of our customers and crew is our top priority.â

The DGCA has raised this issue with IndiGo, and the airline has told it that the focus on pilot training for this particular area has been enhanced.





About a year back, they used to happen mostly during landings. Now they are seen more during go-arounds. Airbus itself says, âThere is also a higher risk of tail strike when a go-around is required near the ground.â

UKâs Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau says the ârate of tail strike incidents per aircraft landing for the A321 is four times greater than that for the A320, probably as a result of the smaller margin from the normal flare attitude.

Damage to the structural integrity of the fuselage should not pose a significant flight risk to the aircraft provided the tail strike is detected during or after landing.â

An Airbus publication on safety says: âPerforming a go-around near the ground is a very dynamic phase with a risk of tail strike. If a go-around is initiated, the (required) manoeuvre must be completed. Between Jan 2022 and Sept 2024, 49 tail strike events were reported to Airbus, with five (10%) during takeoff, 23 (47%) during landing and 21 (43%) during a go-around near the ground.â

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Tail strikes are a global phenomenon. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA) Safety Report, tail strikes were the most frequent type of incident in 2024 and in 2025, although fatality risk remains low. IATA data shows tail strikes were the most frequent non-fatal incidents globally at nine, followed by landing gear issues at seven and runway excursion at six.

âThe ATR 72 and Boeing 737NG (-800/-900ER) were most frequently involved, accounting for 46% of events. Most tail strikes occurred during landing (69% when including rejected landings). Asia Pacific recorded the highest number of events, with the US, India, and Brazil among the most affected countries,â says the IATA Annual Safety Report - 2025.

World.title: 'Will never bow our head': Iran embassy invokes Baahubali to echo Pezeshkian's defiant UN speech
World.content:
In a dramatic blend of cinema and diplomacy, the Iranian Embassy in Hyderabad has drawn a parallel between Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's defiant address at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) and the iconic battle scenes from the Telugu blockbuster Baahubali.

The embassy shared a video featuring the film's protagonist taking on the enemy army, accompanied by a message asserting Iran's determination to stand firm against external pressure.

The video features scenes from Baahubali: The Beginning, in which Amarendra Baahubali, played by Prabhas, leads his forces against the Kalakeya army.

"Dr. Pezeshkian, President of Islamic Republic of Iran at UNGA: 'Will never bow our head or bend the knee' Like Baahubali standing against the Kalakeyas, we also shed our own blood in sacrifice for the homeland," the embassy wrote alongside the video.

The comparison draws on one of the film's most memorable sequences, in which Baahubali refuses to retreat despite facing a formidable enemy.

The post follows Pezeshkian's address at the 81st UNGA in New York on September 23, where he rejected the prospect of Iran surrendering to US pressure. Responding to US President Donald Trump's remarks a day earlier, Pezeshkian said that sanctions, pressure and threats would only strengthen the Iranian people's resolve.





"We will never bow our head or bend at the knee," he declared, while also expressing Iran's willingness to pursue dialogue and diplomacy without accepting coercion.

Pezeshkian's speech came amid escalating tensions between Iran and the United States.

He accused Washington and Israel of attacking Iranian territory and defended his country's military response, while maintaining that Tehran remained open to negotiations. He also criticised sanctions and raised concerns about civilian casualties and the conflict in West Asia. These remarks formed the backdrop to the embassy's subsequent social media post.

World.title: Trump expects new Iran talks despite rejecting deal offer
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday (September 27, 2026) that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, despite his rejection of a truce proposal put forward by Tehran.

Iranian officials brought with them to the UN General Assembly in New York a plan for a seven-day truce followed by the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz shipping channel.

Mr. Trump dismissed the plan and has mused on resuming full-scale air strikes on Iranian targets, but he told the news platform Axios that he expects negotiations to resume.

“They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make,” Mr. Trump told Axios. “It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago.”

“They overplayed their hand,” Mr. Trump said, in the interview published Sunday.

Citing sources familiar with the matter, Axios reported that indirect talks between Washington and Tehran could take place as early as Monday (September 28, 2026).

On Sunday (September 27. 2026), Iran was still standing by its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the Gulf front of the West Asia war locked in a stalemate, while fighting rages in Yemen.

‘We will not back down’

Hormuz is a key chokepoint for the world’s energy supplies and is now central to the conflict between Washington and Tehran, which was started nearly seven months ago when the U.S. and Israel launched a wave of strikes against Iran.

Iran’s plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in West Asia, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and a return to the conditions in an earlier ceasefire deal that fell apart.

That agreement, which collapsed during fighting over Hormuz, called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the U.S. naval blockade.

“Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them,” Mr. Araghchi said on Sunday (September 27, 2026), state broadcaster IRIB reported.

“We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights.”

Washington’s ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, accused Tehran of demanding too much in exchange for a return to the negotiating table.

“This was, I think, a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable. To ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions and access to billions in assets, just to talk,” he told NBC News in an interview broadcast Sunday.

“I think it’s kind of common sense that the president doesn’t have a lot of confidence this time after we just tried a few months ago.”

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards meanwhile said that they seized an American submersible drone on Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz.

It said the underwater vehicle was being used “for espionage purposes”, adding that it was “now in the hands of the force’s specialists for data recovery”.

‘Tool for pressure’

Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at ending the war, reopening the strait and launching talks on Iran’s nuclear programme.

But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.

Iran requires ships to obtain authorization before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.

Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.

Mr. Araghchi said at the UN that Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan, adding: “The choice now rests with the United States.”

Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: “We will not cease punishing the U.S. until Iran’s seven conditions are met.”

Mr. Mohebi had told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran’s demands.

World.title: 3 people killed, 4 injured in shooting at Detroit strip club, police say
World.content:
Three people were killed and four more were injured when an argument led to gunfire at an after-hours strip club Sunday (September 27, 2026) morning in Detroit, officials said.

Police responding to the 7:21 am shooting on a largely residential street found three men who had been fatally shot, Detroit Police Chief Todd Bettison told reporters at a news conference.

Four more people — two men and two women — were taken in private cars to area hospitals. None are thought to have life-threatening injuries.

All the victims are thought to be in their 20s and 30s, Mr. Bettison said.

“A fight occurred, an altercation occurred, and as a result individuals decided to settle it with gun violence,” he said.

“This address is not new to the Detroit Police Department,” he said, noting police had seven calls to the location this year. He said the department had leads but wouldn't discuss them any further.

“This was an after-hours location,” he said of the shooting scene. “Imagine a strip club. … I'll leave it at that.”

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield urged anyone with information to contact authorities.

“We know that we need more people to speak up to bring justice to the situation,” she said at the news conference. “It's heartbreaking and our community should not suffer from this type of violence.”

Earlier Sunday (September 27, 2026), a shooting broke out at a birthday party at a park in Macon, Georgia, leaving 12 teens with gunshot wounds, Bibb County Sheriff David Davis said during a news conference. Two of the injured were in critical condition, while the others were stable. There were no immediate arrests, but Davis said investigators had several persons of interest.

World.title: Nandigram and Rejinagar bypoll: Ballot without the battle
World.content:
In West Bengal, the Bharatiya Janata Party has the support of 207 MLAs in the 294-member Assembly. Two constituencies are up for bypolls, a situation created because the elected representatives won from other constituencies in the State elections earlier this year.

Editorial | Freezing democracy: On the Election Commission of India and West Bengal

The main parties in the fray are the BJP, the Trinamool Congress, the Congress, and the Left. This is the first election in which former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee’s Trinamool will fight on the symbol of a footballer rather than its flowers-and-grass insignia.

Nandigram: a fight for prestige

The Nandigram Assembly seat, with 17 panchayats, has about 2.5 lakh people, of whom about 27% of the electorate is Muslim. This is Suvendu Adhikari’s home district.

Mr. Adhikari has stated several times that the constituency is a prestige fight for him.

Also Read: YouTuber behind Kolkata restaurant beef row, influencers, RJ and actors funded by BJP during Bengal polls

The constituency

During the Vietnam War that peaked in the 1960s, West Bengal’s Left Front, powerful in the State then, protested on behalf of the country, with the slogan: “Amar naam, tomar naam, Vietnam, Vietnam [My name, your name, Vietnam, Vietnam].” In 2007, during the movement against forcible land acquisition for a chemical hub, which saw 14 people die, the Left Front government was still in power.

But this time, the same slogan went against it: it became “Amar naam, tomar naam, Nandigram, Nandigram [My name your name, Nandigram, Nandigram].”

Nandigram, a predominantly rural Assembly constituency in coastal Purba Medinipur district of West Bengal, has been synonymous with political change. The fight against forcible land acquisition brought the downfall of the Left Front government in 2011.

In 2021, when Mr. Adhikari defeated former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee by a margin of 1,956 votes in Nandigram, the constituency brought to the fore a new leader.

In 2026, he contested and won the seat by a margin of about 9,665 votes. Since he was elected from two constituencies, Nandigram and Bhabanipur, he decided to represent Bhabanipur, where he defeated Ms. Banerjee again.

Key candidates

The BJP has fielded Hasirani Rath, the mother of Mr. Adhikari’s slain personal assistant.

Ms. Hasirani has an emotional appeal because she lost her son in the post-poll violence in West Bengal this year. Her son, Chandranath Rath, was shot dead at point-blank range on May 6, just two days after the BJP came to power in the State for the first time, ending the 15-year-old Mamata Banerjee rule.

“This place has been nurtured by Suvendu Adhikari. Of course he is the only one who will win here,” Ms. Hashirani says, after she offered puja at 13 local temples in the constituency as part of her poll campaign in the last week of September.

“Most people in Nandigram have spontaneously accepted me as the daughter of Nandigram and the mother of their homes,” Ms. Hasirani says.

She insists that Adhikari will remain the leader of the people of Nandigram, and it is not victory that she is concerned about. “We want the margin of the victory to be 1.5 lakh votes,” she adds.

The Chief Minister had urged the people of Nandigram to ensure the highest-ever margin of victory in the constituency.

Former CM Banerjee initially announced her support for Sanchita Pradhan Dey, who withdrew from the contest. Then she supported the Congress nominee from Nandigram, Milan Pradhan. Within hours, he was arrested in a 19-year-old case. He was a leader and activist who was part of Nandigram’s land movement in 2007. Mr. Pradhan has been sent to judicial custody till October 3. His bail plea at the Calcutta High Court was denied on September 22.

“He has always been here at public events; why was he not arrested before? Why arrest him now when he became the Congress candidate?” Arpita, his wife, said in a video message shared by State Congress leaders.

The Left Front has fielded Communist Party of India’s Shanti Gopal Giri for the bypoll.

Key issues and campaign

In the Nandigram bypoll, the Congress is running its campaign on its candidate being arrested by the West Bengal police. “We are all Milan Pradhan. He cannot be here because he was wrongfully arrested. We are all standing here as the candidate,” a campaign member of the Congress said while asking people to vote in the party’s favour.

“Even Mamata didi has asked everyone to support our candidate,” the Congress workers tell people of Nandigram as they go from house to house. The arrest of Pradhan has brought the Congress leadership in West Bengal together and evoked a strong response from the party’s high command. Leader of Opposition in Parliament, Rahul Gandhi, called it “political revenge, the murder of democracy”.

“The BJP has no faith in fair elections — that’s why it wants to cling to power, sometimes through vote theft, sometimes through stealing governments, and sometimes through stealing parties,” Mr. Gandhi said on X.

Meanwhile, the BJP is driving its by-poll campaign on the emotional appeal of a mother who has lost her child. Mr. Adhikari accompanied Hasirani when she filed her nomination papers.

Addressing a gathering after the nomination, the Chief Minister exuded confidence by saying that the BJP will win by “such a big margin in Nandigram that no one has ever imagined”. He said that Chandranath Rath’s biggest sin was that he was his aide.

He promised to fulfil all the promises made to the people of Nandigram.

What the electorate says

Purnima, 50, from Gopalchak area in Nandigram is emotional about the mother’s loss. “A mother lost her child in these politics. We are bound to vote for her,” she says.

Amina Bibi, 65, from the Mohammadpur area says that people of Nandigram have always spoken truth to power and she does not shy away from speaking the truth now.

“I fought shoulder to shoulder with Suvendu during the Nandigram protests. But since he became CM, he has not dared to come back here because he knows he has not done anything for us,” she says. A man in his mid-50 from Mohammadpur in Nandigram who did not want to be named, says, “This is not a democracy where there is no fair election and people are not allowed to participate. In a democracy every candidate should get a fair chance to campaign and contest. That is missing here.”

Rejinagar: wall graffiti speaks

Rejinagar constituency has over 2.56 Lakh voters and about 69% of the electorate in the constituency are Muslim voters. The Bhagirathi river, a distributary of Ganga passes through the constituency, which spans over two blocks: Beldanga I and II, comprising nearly 14 panchayats. A predominately rural constituency, the region has little employment opportunities and youth migrate for work.

The constituency

Rejinagar is located less than 15 kilometres from Plassey, where a war between the East India Company and Nawab Siraj-u-Daullah of Murshidabad almost 270 years changed the history of the subcontinent forever.

The constituency, located in West Bengal’s Murshidabad district, was a highlight of the 2026 Assembly polls. Aam Janata Unnyan Party (AJUP) leader Humayun Kabir’s had attempted to construct a mosque styled on the lines of the Babri masjid in Ayodhya.

Mr. Kabir’s campaign in the 2026 Assembly polls on the issue of construction of the mosque, split the Muslim votes, polarised Hindus, and eventually was one of the reasons that led to fall of the 15-year-old Trinamool Congress government. Kabir, who was expelled from the Trinamool Congress, set up AJUP and won elections from Naoda and Rejinagar in the district. He vacated Rejinagar where his margin of victory was over 58,000 votes.

The project of construction of the Babri-style mosque next to a national highway has been stalled and the site that had hundreds of people thronging before the Assembly polls, is desolate.

The constituency had witnessed violent protests during the anti-CAA [Citizenship Amendment Act] protests in 2019. In 2024 there was an explosion during a Ram Navami procession, which left about 20 people injured.

Key candidates

The by-polls at Rejinagar have been necessitated after Humayun Kabir resigned from his Rejinagar seat on June 4. The AJUP chairperson has fielded his son Golam Nabi Azad. Neither is campaigning in a big way, saying there is intimidation by the administration, controlled by the ruling party.

The Banerjee-backed faction of the Trinamool Congress has fielded Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, a former MLA, as their candidate. Chowdhury had represented the seat for three terms, first being elected from the Congress in 2011, and later as a Trinamool Congress nominee. Chowdhury too had said he would withdraw from the contest, but later decided to reconsider, after intervention from Banerjee.

Congress fielded Abdullahil Kafi, Leader of the Opposition from the Murshidabad Zila Parishad. The Ritabrata Banerjee-led TMC faction (Democratic TMC) fielded Safiuzzaman S.K.

CPI (M) has fielded Saeed Asad Ali. The BJP is hoping for a split of minority votes and that a polarisation of Hindu votes will make way for its victory, the BJP is banking on a polarisation of Hindu votes and have fielded Sakharav Sarkar.

Key issues and campaign

The leaders of the AJUP and Banerjee-backed Trinamool Congress have alleged intimidation by the police and said that they are not being allowed to contest. Mr. Kabir has decided to stay away from the campaigning, accusing the local police of slapping fake cases against his workers and arresting them.

According to Mr. Kabir, “Fifteen of my workers have been arrested by the police, while many have fled to other places fearing the police’s constant threats. This is terrifying. Police are picking up everyone they see with me. They have become the BJP’s agents. I can’t risk my workers’ lives,” he says. The MLA was also called for questioning to Berhampore Police Station on September 21 and 23, in relation to a viral audio clip that pointed to subject matter pertaining to communal tension.

Mr. Kabir adds that his son is still visiting some areas, “But we stopped major campaigning. I will communicate with people and campaign for my son through Facebook only,” he says.

On September 19, West Bengal police arrested Saiful Islam, an independent candidate from Rejinagar, who has close associations with the AJUP leadership. While the graffiti of the Opposition candidates has come up all across the constituency, the only candidate who is actively campaigning is the BJP’s Sarkar.

While the party offices of the candidates in Opposition wear a desolate look, the party office of the BJP at Rejinagar is bustling with activity. “TMC has not done anything for this area in the last 15 years. Humayun Kabir’s corruption has also been exposed. He duped people of crores in the name of his Babri Masjid replica project. The public is not foolish. They want a change,” Sarkar says. The BJP candidate says that he is fighting this election on a development pitch and getting good response from people across communities.

While Mr. Sakharav is campaigning across the constituency, the graffiti of Opposition candidates — the hammer and sickle of CPI(M), hand of Congress, football player of Ms. Banerjee’s All India Trinamool Congress, and whistle of AJUP — are on the walls of Rejinagar.

What the electorate says

Mohsin Sheikh, who resides near Beldanga Police Station in Rejinagar, says, “The election looks very different this time. There is not much show of parties and their candidates, unlike previous elections. A strange silence has captured the area.”

There are voters who lament the lack of development in the region, health facilities, and transport. “The nearest hospital in our area is 5-6 km away. Those who stay in the part of the constituency which is connected to the national highway may still get proper transport to reach there in emergency cases. But what about the people from the other side of the river?” says Nafisa Bibi, who runs a teashop at Saktipur village, which is around 12 km from the ferry-ghat.

Hamid, a street vendor, stops at the boundary of the under-construction mosque. “It was a good initiative. When it’s completed, everybody will come to pray here from even the neighbouring districts. Our business will grow,” he says, as he prepares his jhaalmuri mix.
