World.title: Mike Baird resigns as Cricket Australia boss amid BBL sale fallout, Boon to fill role
World.content:
Breaking SportCricketAustralian cricket Mike Baird resigns as Cricket Australia boss amid BBL sale fallout, Boon to fill role Daniel Brettig September 28, 2026 — 9:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mike Baird has resigned as chair of Cricket Australia after his home state NSW withdrew support for the former premier to carry on as a director over his decision to push ahead with plans to sell Big Bash League clubs. Decorated former Test batsman David Boon will take over as interim leader of CA at the governing body’s AGM next month, holding the role while a search is conducted for another longer-term chair. Mike Baird has resigned as Cricket Australia chair. George Chan Though Baird had served on the Cricket NSW board before becoming CA chair in 2023, he found himself totally at odds with Australia’s largest state over the issues of BBL privatisation and the game’s financial model. Baird was informed last week that Cricket NSW, chaired by John Knox, had withdrawn support for him to carry on as their nominee for another three-year term. The state also rejected a proposal for Baird to move into an independent director’s spot – vacated recently by Sarah Adam-Gedge – for an interim period while a new chair was found.



Former CA chair Wally Edwards spoke out last week at Cricket Western Australia’s AGM, expressing his opposition to the sale of BBL clubs and calling for the CA board to be spilled by the states. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket ‘Dire consequences’: BBL sell-off slammed amid fears for grassroots cricket Baird told this masthead that he hoped his decision to quit would reduce the temperature of discussions between CA and the states, and called for the game’s decision-makers to unite behind Boon. “My term had come to an end in discussion with NSW and I was happy to help the transition to a new chair, but ultimately I leave with absolute gratitude and thanks,” Baird said. “It’s been a real privilege, and I have appreciated working with every single state and stakeholder. It’s been a real life highlight. “It’s time to unite, and I hope all of cricket will unite behind David. He’s respected by every person in cricket, whether a fan, a volunteer, a player, media, broadcasting, even internationally, David is someone respected from top to bottom.



David Boon will step up as interim chair of Cricket Australia. Getty Images “My hope is there’s a chance for a reset. There’s been a decision made [on the BBL] and CA will continue to crack on with that. But the game is much stronger when we’re united, and there’s a chance to unite now.” Despite its contribution to his resignation, Baird insisted that CA had pulled the right rein by allowing states to go to market to sell BBL clubs without securing unanimous agreement. Cricket Victoria is pushing to sell-off 100 per cent of the Melbourne Renegades by the end of this year, while other states are considering their options under a “self-determination” model suggested by South Australia. Baird said he knew that he was risking his own position by announcing the sale process at the SCG earlier this month. “We had started discussions [about my tenure],” Baird said. “I was open to continuing to serve, but I think the process needed to be run, the discussions needed to be run and done, and from my point of view it was only decided in the past week.”



Baird was chair during a period of significant success on the field, and he listed the 2023 men’s ODI World Cup victory in Ahmedabad and the women’s T20 Cup win at Lord’s this year as high points. But he has also joined former chairs David Peever (2018) and Earl Eddings (2021) as CA chairs who fell afoul of NSW and Knox, who evolved from curious explorers of private investment in the BBL to dogged opposers over the past year. Cricket NSW chair John Knox. Louie Douvis Fellow NSW directors Ed Cowan and David Gallop were also involved in discussions with Baird that ultimately led to his exit. Given this cycle of dysfunction, which has coincided with heavy debate over the financial sustainability of Australian cricket, Baird agreed that it was time for further changes to the way the game was governed.



“The states are looking at governance and I think it’s needed,” he said. “There is a need to look at what’s the best form of governance in the world, looking at other sports, what can we adopt and learn,” he said. NSW Premier Chris Minns with Cricket Australia chairman Mike Baird (right) and Australian cricketers Nathan Lyon and Josh Hazlewood in 2024. Edwina Pickles “But ultimately, it comes back to a simple principle. Robust debate, constructive engagement. That won’t mean everyone agrees all the time, but there’s alignment around majority or key decisions that are made. My real hope is now is the time to unite. “Whatever the structure, if people start with the principle that we’re stronger together, that’s the way forward.” Baird’s exit will also force a significant reshuffle at the International Cricket Council, where he has served as chair of the financial and commercial affairs committee and worked closely with the global body’s chair Jay Shah.



The ICC board is due to meet in Bali in November, and Baird said that CA may ultimately need to consider choosing a dedicated director to focus primarily on the ICC table, allowing the chair more time for domestic issues. Editor's pick Exclusive

Big Bash Renegades put up for sale as players launch fresh dispute action with Cricket Australia “There’s some merit in thinking about that, it depends who ultimately ends up in the chair, the time and availability,” he said. “But I can see that working. The demands are significant, the time is significant, and that is one model that could work.” Boon is the first former Test cricketer to be CA chair since Edwards, and the most accomplished player to do so since Sir Donald Bradman finished his second term as chair in 1972. “It is an enormous honour to take the role of Interim CA Chair during what is a hugely exciting and also challenging time for cricket,” Boon said.



“I look forward to leading the CA board as we continue to make decisions that ensure the long-term health and prosperity of the game here and advancing Australia’s interests globally.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: MTV VMAs 2026: Full list of winners and nominees
World.content:
The blue carpet has officially been unrolled for the wildest awards show in entertainment, but the best is yet to come from the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs).

The VMAs earned their chaotic reputation long before the artist formerly known as Kanye West interrupted Taylor Swift’s acceptance speech in 2009, and that’s in large part thanks to Madonna. And on Sunday night at Los Angeles’ Peacock Theatre (Monday morning AEST), the queen of pop is gracing the stage and performing at the VMAs for the first time in 23 years.

Madonna received 13 nominations and Taylor Swift has nine nods. AP

A quick refresher for the uninitiated: Madonna’s first performance at the VMAs was in 1984, an edgy rendition of Like A Virgin some critics dubbed obscene. She upped the edgy ante in 2003, when she performed the opening medley with Britney Spears and Christina Aguilera … and locked lips with them.

It’s not just the Madonna show – though she is nominated 13 times, the most of any artist this year. Fellow VMAs heavy hitter Swift is receiving the inaugural VMA Artist Director Honours, marking her 31st VMA win overall and breaking her tie with Beyoncé to become the most-awarded artist in the award show’s history (Swift is nominated in nine categories, going up against Madonna in seven of them).

World.content:
South Korea’s presidential office demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of disclosing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea and then falsely denying that the two sides had agreed to keep the move confidential.

“The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement,” said Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations. He said the government was reviewing additional measures over the issue if necessary.

Seong said Ukraine had requested the secrecy, arguing that public disclosure could trigger domestic criticism that Kyiv had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners.

South Korea agreed to keep the transfer confidential given security, diplomatic and humanitarian concerns, including the safety of the prisoners and their families, he said.

According to the statement, Ukraine later disclosed the transfer in President Volodymyr Zelensky’s address to the UN General Assembly without sufficient prior consultation – and then subsequently denied the existence of any confidentiality agreement.

Seong said the denial had seriously damaged trust between the two governments and could harm bilateral relations. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Reuters

David Boon will step up as interim chair of Cricket Australia. Getty Images “My hope is there’s a chance for a reset. There’s been a decision made [on the BBL] and CA will continue to crack on with that. But the game is much stronger when we’re united, and there’s a chance to unite now.” Despite its contribution to his resignation, Baird insisted that CA had pulled the right rein by allowing states to go to market to sell BBL clubs without securing unanimous agreement. Cricket Victoria is pushing to sell-off 100 per cent of the Melbourne Renegades by the end of this year, while other states are considering their options under a “self-determination” model suggested by South Australia. Baird said he knew that he was risking his own position by announcing the sale process at the SCG earlier this month. “We had started discussions [about my tenure],” Baird said. “I was open to continuing to serve, but I think the process needed to be run, the discussions needed to be run and done, and from my point of view it was only decided in the past week.”



Baird was chair during a period of significant success on the field, and he listed the 2023 men’s ODI World Cup victory in Ahmedabad and the women’s T20 Cup win at Lord’s this year as high points. But he has also joined former chairs David Peever (2018) and Earl Eddings (2021) as CA chairs who fell afoul of NSW and Knox, who evolved from curious explorers of private investment in the BBL to dogged opposers over the past year. Cricket NSW chair John Knox. Louie Douvis Fellow NSW directors Ed Cowan and David Gallop were also involved in discussions with Baird that ultimately led to his exit. Given this cycle of dysfunction, which has coincided with heavy debate over the financial sustainability of Australian cricket, Baird agreed that it was time for further changes to the way the game was governed.



“The states are looking at governance and I think it’s needed,” he said. “There is a need to look at what’s the best form of governance in the world, looking at other sports, what can we adopt and learn,” he said. NSW Premier Chris Minns with Cricket Australia chairman Mike Baird (right) and Australian cricketers Nathan Lyon and Josh Hazlewood in 2024. Edwina Pickles “But ultimately, it comes back to a simple principle. Robust debate, constructive engagement. That won’t mean everyone agrees all the time, but there’s alignment around majority or key decisions that are made. My real hope is now is the time to unite. “Whatever the structure, if people start with the principle that we’re stronger together, that’s the way forward.” Baird’s exit will also force a significant reshuffle at the International Cricket Council, where he has served as chair of the financial and commercial affairs committee and worked closely with the global body’s chair Jay Shah.



The ICC board is due to meet in Bali in November, and Baird said that CA may ultimately need to consider choosing a dedicated director to focus primarily on the ICC table, allowing the chair more time for domestic issues. Editor's pick Exclusive

Big Bash Renegades put up for sale as players launch fresh dispute action with Cricket Australia “There’s some merit in thinking about that, it depends who ultimately ends up in the chair, the time and availability,” he said. “But I can see that working. The demands are significant, the time is significant, and that is one model that could work.” Boon is the first former Test cricketer to be CA chair since Edwards, and the most accomplished player to do so since Sir Donald Bradman finished his second term as chair in 1972. “It is an enormous honour to take the role of Interim CA Chair during what is a hugely exciting and also challenging time for cricket,” Boon said.



“I look forward to leading the CA board as we continue to make decisions that ensure the long-term health and prosperity of the game here and advancing Australia’s interests globally.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: MTV VMAs 2026: Full list of winners and nominees
World.content:
The blue carpet has officially been unrolled for the wildest awards show in entertainment, but the best is yet to come from the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs).

The VMAs earned their chaotic reputation long before the artist formerly known as Kanye West interrupted Taylor Swift’s acceptance speech in 2009, and that’s in large part thanks to Madonna. And on Sunday night at Los Angeles’ Peacock Theatre (Monday morning AEST), the queen of pop is gracing the stage and performing at the VMAs for the first time in 23 years.

Madonna received 13 nominations and Taylor Swift has nine nods. AP

A quick refresher for the uninitiated: Madonna’s first performance at the VMAs was in 1984, an edgy rendition of Like A Virgin some critics dubbed obscene. She upped the edgy ante in 2003, when she performed the opening medley with Britney Spears and Christina Aguilera … and locked lips with them.

It’s not just the Madonna show – though she is nominated 13 times, the most of any artist this year. Fellow VMAs heavy hitter Swift is receiving the inaugural VMA Artist Director Honours, marking her 31st VMA win overall and breaking her tie with Beyoncé to become the most-awarded artist in the award show’s history (Swift is nominated in nine categories, going up against Madonna in seven of them).

World.content:
South Korea’s presidential office demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of disclosing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea and then falsely denying that the two sides had agreed to keep the move confidential.

“The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement,” said Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations. He said the government was reviewing additional measures over the issue if necessary.

Seong said Ukraine had requested the secrecy, arguing that public disclosure could trigger domestic criticism that Kyiv had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners.

South Korea agreed to keep the transfer confidential given security, diplomatic and humanitarian concerns, including the safety of the prisoners and their families, he said.

According to the statement, Ukraine later disclosed the transfer in President Volodymyr Zelensky’s address to the UN General Assembly without sufficient prior consultation – and then subsequently denied the existence of any confidentiality agreement.

Seong said the denial had seriously damaged trust between the two governments and could harm bilateral relations. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Reuters

World.title: US congratulates Naoero on ICC withdrawal decision
World.content:
The United States has congratulated Naoero on its decision to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC).

At the United Nations General Assembly last week, Naoero's President David Adeang announced his country's intention to revoke its membership in the ICC, calling it an irrelevant institution.

"A multilateral agency with which we see of increasing irrelevance to the Naoero, namely the International Criminal Court, is one which calls for Nauru to end its participation and to revoke its membership," Adeang said.

"Before I depart New York, Naoero will be depositing our instruments of withdrawal with the Rome Statute repository."

This followed US President Donald Trump using his speech at the UN to attack the ICC, while his administration is reported to be considering issuing sanctions against the Hague-based court as an institution.

The US Assistant Secretary of State Michael George DeSombre has now met with the small Pacific country's Deputy Foreign Minster Russ Kun to offer congratulations.

A Facebook post about the meeting from the US Embassy in Suva said: "Naoero joins a growing number of nations standing up for their sovereignty against the ICC's illegitimate overreach."

Tensions between the Trump administration and the ICC have increased after the court issued arrest warrants in late 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and others in his cabinet over alleged crimes related to the Gaza war.

World.title: 'The most significant industrial revolution of our time': Labour's Reuben Davidson on NZ's AI future
World.content:
In the lead-up to November's election, Midday Report is speaking with the technology spokesperson for a range of parties about their biggest hopes and fears with artificial intelligence and the role of government in regulating the technology. On Monday, Guyon Epsiner sat down with Labour's Economic Development, Science Technology spokesperson Reuben Davidson.

In Reuben Davidson's eyes the world is looking at potentially the most significant industrial revolution of a generation with Artificial Intelligence (AI).

In an interview with Midday Report, he said there was "enormous opportunity" with AI and the government had a responsibility to get involved and help navigate what that looked like for Aotearoa.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405380791112

It was hard to know what the impacts of AI would be in a decade, Davidson said, but the speed of which it was morphing and the speed of the uptake globally was "unprecedented".

"Questions need to start being asked... given that few people know what it will look like in 10 years we need to take a more active role to steer and decide what we want it to look like the next 10 years. We need to have a really clear framework for New Zealand and a really clear plan on how we want to navigate our way through this."

Davidson believed the AI strategy put forward by the current government wasn't "fit for purpose" and didn't give New Zealanders a level of security they needed or deserved.

For Labour, Davidson said the key points would be creating an office of AI.

"We see that need to be elevated right to the Cabinet table with a single minister responsible that means we can look after copyright frameworks... the impact of AI on education... and have really clear rules for data centres..."

He said there was also a need for an independent online safety regulator.

"The government need to have a really strong action plan to engage with this it's not acceptable anymore for the government to step back and say we're gonna wait and see what happens.

"We need to actively shape and be involved in how it evolves to serve us."

Davidson said there was no question AI would be disruptive to the workforce and the way it had worked up until now.

"I think the urgency now is for the government to map to see the kinds of roles being impacted and acknowledge 12 to 18 months ago we weren't thinking it would be those roles."

AI would create new roles, he said, and new jobs as new technologies always had, but what needed to be thought about was how to manage it and ensure human skill was still being utilised.

Davidson himself said he did use AI but only in a very "conscious" way.

"I'm very aware when I'm doing online searches, very aware of the role AI is playing in sorting and selecting the information it is returning to me.

"I'm very careful on checking the forms of information and the sources..."

He said he normally used an AI product created in Christchurch called Contented AI. He used it to present his thoughts and ideas as words, but said he would go through and edit to make sure it accurately reflected what he was thinking and wanting to get forward.

"It's assisted my productivity... but I'm still actively involved in all of those processes as opposed to relying on AI to do my thinking for me."

Davidson said his biggest fear with AI was that the government didn't take it seriously and see the very real opportunities for New Zealand and didn't protect New Zealanders from the very real risks.

World.title: Meth withdrawal symptoms getting 'scarier' in the Northern Marianas, recovery agency says
World.content:
A drug recovery programme in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) says it is seeing more severe withdrawal symptoms among some methamphetamine users than it did five or six years ago, including hallucinations and psychotic episodes.

Substance Abuse Addiction and Rehabilitation (SAAR) Program manager Charlotte Flores said the change comes as health authorities report a sharp rise in methamphetamine-related illnesses and deaths in the territory.

"I was just really shocked to see the increase in numbers. It's really alarming. But we could also say at the HOPE Recovery Center that we've also seen an increase ourselves," Flores said.

Flores said the Marpi-based HOPE Recovery Center is now seeing withdrawal symptoms that are different from those it encountered several years ago.

"What we've been seeing are different withdrawal symptoms, different from like five, six years ago. And the withdrawal symptoms now are a lot scarier because hallucinating is part of it, just having some psychotic episodes," she said.

She said that five or six years ago, participants going through withdrawal would typically sleep and eat a lot while recuperating. Those symptoms are still seen, but are now accompanied in some cases by more concerning symptoms.

The Commonwealth Healthcare Corporation CHCC said methamphetamine-related cases rose from 71 in 2022 to 78 in 2023 and 122 in 2024, before more than doubling to 252 in 2025.

Another 179 cases had been identified through 31 August this year.

Between 2022 and 2026, CHCC also recorded 612 emergency department visits involving patients with identified methamphetamine use, 509 instances requiring urine drug screening and 57 psychiatric interventions.

Flores said people trying to stop using meth can experience exhaustion, depression and strong cravings, while the brain can take months rather than days to heal.

Participants at HOPE undergo about four to five months of residential treatment, including relapse prevention, early recovery and life skills programmes, anger management, drug education and recovery support.

CHCC public health medical director Dr Andrzej Szefler said the increase represented a growing public health concern affecting individuals, families and the wider community.

"Behind every statistic is a person whose life has been affected," Dr Szefler said.

World.title: No regulations on too-hot homes likely until 2031
World.content:
Audio player for " No fix for overheated homes until 2031 " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/community/1619940%2Fno-regulations-on-too-hot-homes-likely-until-2031

No fix for overheated homes until 2031 Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Advocates for people living in overheating new builds are dismayed that officials will not consider comprehensive changes to fix the issue until 2031.

Residents of the glut of townhouses and apartments built in the last few years have repeatedly raised concerns about dangerous heat in their homes during summer, because of common design flaws.

The Building Research Association (BRANZ) and Green Building Council are among organisations advocating for changes to the Building Code, which currently does not include any controls on overheating or maximum internal temperatures.

However, Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment officials have confirmed they are working on the issue, but it would not be part of a regular code review in 2028, and instead would be considered during the subsequent review in 2031.

"We're really shocked to hear that we're facing a significant delay in dealing with this," Green Building Council chief executive Andrew Eagles said.

"That's hugely alarming when you talk to these families and they're in sweltering conditions."

Green Building Council chief executive Andrew Eagles is among those advocating for urgent regulation changes. Supplied / NZGBC

Jared Laidlaw and his family moved into their two-storey Auckland townhouse at the end of 2021 and discovered almost immediately that the upstairs overheated.

The house was west-facing, with a floor-to-ceiling window in the master bedroom, minimal ventilation, no eaves and no external window shading.

"You just have five or six hours straight of sun smashing that side of the house," he said.

Audio player for " Andrew Eagles discusses concern over overheated homes " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/community/1619940%2Fno-regulations-on-too-hot-homes-likely-until-2031

Andrew Eagles discusses concern over overheated homes Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Temperatures upstairs typically got to 35°C during the day and were still in the high 20s late in the evening, he said.

Some parts of the house were not just uncomfortable but dangerous - like the aluminium front door, which reached 60° or 70° degrees on a summer day and radiated heat back into the house.

"You can't touch the door - it burns your hand."

When his young sons were born, he and his wife were hyper-vigilant about monitoring the temperature.

"We used to have thermometers and stuff because ... it's not safe for babies."

In the time they had lived in the house, they had tried ceiling fans and a noisy portable air-conditioning unit, and finally paid $2500 for ducted air-conditioning.

He and his next-door neighbour ordered a roll of foil-covered bubble wrap from Temu, which they used to make huge shades that could be attached by Velcro to the internal window frames.

"That has made the biggest difference, aside from the AC," he said.

"This will stay up weeks or months at a time ... We can't enjoy the view because it's 35°C in here during the day."

The features that contributed to overheating at Laidlaw's house were typical of many new-build townhouses and apartments, Andrew Eagles said.

"You've often got windows going floor to ceiling ... you've got no eaves and no shading allowance," he said.

"You're then getting the full effect of the sun during the day and smaller rooms, so the combination of all of that is you just get this massive heat build-up."

File photo Sharon Brettkelly

His organisation and BRANZ both supported an interim fix to a schedule in the Building Code that would require modelling at the design stage to check if a dwelling would overheat.

The software capable of doing that modelling was already used by hundreds of firms around the country, he said.

"I [would] need to put into a calculator the size of the home, the orientation, the size of the windows, and then it comes back and says, oh look - you are going to overheat this proportion of that time."

The design would then have to be tweaked until it was under the modelling limits, Eagles said.

"The steps people are likely going to take is reduce the amount of glazing - that will save them money - or put some shading on or put some eaves on or slightly change the orientation, those sorts of things."

BRANZ senior building physicist Stephen McNeil said without regulation, people in Laidlaw's predicament would suffer even more as average temperatures increased.

"It's also those extremes ... and we have other concerns with the increasing humidity in the air as well."

BRANZ senior building physicist Stephen McNeil. Supplied/Rob Suisted

In a written response, MBIE manager for building performance and engineering Dave Gittings said officials were working through how overheating requirements could be integrated into the Building Code, but overheating was a complex issue without a single fix.

"We need to make sure any changes work together as a package and don't create unintended consequences elsewhere in the building system. That includes considering an approach where designers would need to demonstrate through modelling that their designs will not exceed a maximum indoor temperature."

The 2031 review was appropriate timing because of the considerable technical and policy work involved, he said.

"Overheating is influenced by a broad range of interconnected factors, including solar gain, shading, the heat absorption of building materials, ventilation, airtightness and building orientation. It takes time to consider any consequences, develop options for change and thoroughly consult on any changes to ensure we've considered every angle before implementing them."

The ministry would provide informal guidance to designers and homeowners in the meantime.

Officials were currently looking at how building designs may need to demonstrate they do not exceed maximum indoor temperatures.

Introducing a requirement such as the one proposed by the Green Building Council would involve "more than simply setting a temperature limit", Gittings said.

There would also need to be appropriate capability among those doing the modelling, which would require industry acceptance with any changes, along with clear expectations for building consent authorities about the evidence they should receive, what they needed to check and when specialist review may be required.

But Stephen McNeil said changes could be staged.

"Rather than one big hit where you deliver this perfect regulatory thing that solves every problem, you've got to take the industry on a journey and give them time to build into it," he said.

"Simple measures now will save us a lot of pain down the track because we could capture the riskiest buildings quite early in the piece."

Andrew Eagles said in this case, "perfect is the enemy of good".

"We should just get the bloody hell on with it.

"We've already got people writing to us horrified that they're spending tens of thousands of dollars and that their kids are in rooms that are far, far too hot."

Jared Laidlaw agreed five years was too long to wait.

"I'd anticipate a lot of houses in between now and then are going to be townhouses, so you're going to only exacerbate the situation," he said.

World.title: ACT's David Seymour slams 'unethical' promises to break up supermarket duopoly
World.content:
ACT leader David Seymour has hit out at promises to break up the supermarket duopoly, calling them "unethical" and a betrayal of "free enterprise".

Seymour was in Auckland on Monday speaking at engineering consultancy firm Aurecon in Newmarket.

During his speech, Seymour slammed his opponents and coalition partners saying it was hard to "overstate how bad these ideas are".

"Foodstuffs and Woolworths have spent 104 and 97 years respectively building logistics, procurement and distribution networks that run through this country like arteries.

"That's economies of scale. That's how the shelves stay full and prices stay lower than they'd otherwise be."

Each political party has promised some kind of supermarket reform: the Greens want to set up a publicly owned competitor, National and New Zealand First want to break them up, Labour would separate their wholesale and retail arms and Te Pāti Māori would spend $3.1 billion on tax breaks and seed funding for Māori-owned competitors.

Seymour said he was "so disappointed" to see the National Party "shamelessly join the pile-on".

"These policies aren't just bad economics. They're unethical. They undermine the rule of law and property rights in this country, and they betray the basic idea of free enterprise.

"It tells every Kiwi entrepreneur, and every foreign investor watching, don't bother building here. Grow a successful business in New Zealand, and if a politician spots votes in tearing it apart, they will."

Seymour disagreed food prices were going up because of the supermarket duopoly.

"Butchers, bakers, greengrocers, chemists - including large chains - hardware stores and liquor stores compete with supermarkets from every angle. It is wrong to say New Zealanders have only two options, we actually have many."

He pointed to over-spending during the pandemic, the war in Iran and New Zealand's geography which he said was "bigger than you think".

"We are thinly spread, dotted with small rural towns, split down the middle by a mountain range and across the middle by the Cook Strait.

"Geographically, we're about as remote as a country can be - next stop, Antarctica. Building and running supply chains here is expensive and complicated by default."

Seymour said ACT would set up a "one-stop consenting shop" for new market entrants to make it easier for them to get set up and pointed his work bringing product labels more in line with other countries.

World.title: 'We will not forget': Vanuatu comes together to honour 45 lives lost at sea in recent weeks
World.content:
The people and leaders of Vanuatu came together for a national day of mourning and remembrance on Sunday to pay their respects to the more than 40 people who lost their lives in major boating tragedies in recent weeks.

The MV Matui sank in the waters between Espiritu Santo (Santo) and Ambae on 11 September. Fourteen people survived the disaster, while two people were confirmed dead by local authorities and 39 remain missing at sea.

Tui's Shipping is the company which owns the MV Matui ferry. Supplied / Tui's Shipping / Facebook

In another boating incident, six men lost their lives while travelling between Erromango and Tanna on 7 August.

The day of mourning and remembrance - the first-ever such event - was held at Feiawa Park in Port Vila on Sunday afternoon. It was led by Vanuatu's Prime Minister Jotham Napat, government ministers, traditional leaders, and families of those who had lost their loved ones to the tragic maritime incidents.

Napat thanked everyone of you who turned up in support of the event.

"You came in black and white, you brought your flowers, you stood with us - to remember the 45 lives we lost at sea. To the families, thank you for allowing us to mourn with you," he said in a statement.

People have gathered at Fewia Park on Sunday, joined by the country’s leaders, for a remembrance service honouring the 45 lives lost at sea in the MV Matui tragedy and the Erromango boat incident. 27 September 2026 VBTC News

The Torba and Penama provinces also held simultaneous remembrance events as well.

"Though separated by sea, today we were one nation, one family, one heart. Your presence shows that Vanuatu cares. That we will not forget. And that we stand together to build safer seas."

Meanwhile, the Vanuatu Daily Post reported that 13 Pentecost chiefs, backed by chiefs and communities in Torba, Malampa, Shefa and Tafea provinces, have called for urgent and permanent reforms to Vanuatu's maritime safety system.

The newspaper reported that, in a petition dated 15 September, the chiefs said the sea was the country's highway, livelihood and heritage and must not become a graveyard.

World.title: Australian middle order collapses again as South Africa claims ODI
World.content:
Australia's world champions have been found wanting again, falling well short in a chase for the second time in four days as South Africa prevailed by 32 runs in Johannesburg to seal the three-match ODI series triumph.

As a reconnaissance mission for their World Cup defence in southern Africa in a year's time, the loss overnight felt like another alarming capitulation after a fine start to their pursuit of a big Proteas total was wasted, just as on Thursday in the first-match collapse at Durban.

Chasing South Africa's formidable 9-365, which featured superb hundreds from captain Temba Bavuma and the ever-reliable David Miller, Australia's stand-in skipper Mitch Marsh and Travis Head, who had teed off with a brisk 90 together in Durban, this time clattered 130 off 17 overs at the Wanderers.

But the same old failings of cheap dismissals and inability to build partnerships came back to haunt the visitors, with not even a rousing late show of defiance from Xavier Bartlett, with a thumping 50 off 28 balls, able to get them to within a sniff of the target as they succumbed to 333 all out with one ball remaining.

Temba Bavuma was electric again for South Africa, bringing up another ton. (Getty Images: Sydney Seshibedi/Gallo Images)

After losing a second-straight match in which they had won the toss and sent the Proteas in, Australia, who again kept captain Pat Cummins on ice with the Test series around the corner, were left with further big concerns over their middle order stuttering in the face of quality spin.

"Really disappointing — we came here to ensure the series went to the last game but, fair play to South Africa, ultimately we've been outplayed again," Marsh said.

"In both games, the way we've set up the innings has been really good but we just haven't been able to execute in those middle phases.

"We've got to keep improving, we don't want to be whitewashed."

A third match will be played in Potchefstroom on Wednesday.

Cummins was unquestionably missed and a side injury that ensured Australia's outstanding quick Nathan Ellis could bowl only four overs meant their attack was always under pressure, even if Jack Edwards offered genuine all-round promise with his 5-67 and a solid knock of 25 in support of Bartlett.

Josh Hazlewood took three wickets while going at seven an over, but more alarming was Adam Zampa's continuing struggle, as he went for 0-77 off his 10 overs, in stark contrast to South Africa's excellent spin trio of Keshav Maharaj (2-54), Bjorn Fortuin (2-70) and Aiden Markram (1-55).

They helped put the brakes on Australia's chase after Marsh and Head had cracked 84 apiece, the captain's knock featuring five sixes and 10 fours off 53 balls and Head's start coming off 103 balls, with one six and 12 fours.

Apart from the openers, though, Australia was soon struggling, Cooper Connolly chipping one tamely off Lizaad Williams (3-54) to short midwicket to depart for 10 and wicketkeeper Alex Carey trapped lbw by Maharaj, who then did the same to dismiss Matt Renshaw for 32.

Cameron Green had a struggle, limping to 17 off 34 balls, before Bartlett showed him the way belatedly with his five mighty sixes, only for his innings, and Australia's last hope, to be ended by a cracking leg-before yorker from Williams.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Birrell claims long-awaited WTA title, but loses top Aussie ranking
World.content:
Kim Birrell has been left reflecting on an emotional and thrilling breakthrough day for Australian women's tennis in south-east Asia as she scooped the first WTA title of her career, while also losing her national number one ranking.

Birrell rocketed into the world's top-50 for the first time with her long-awaited maiden triumph at the Korea Open WTA 250 event.

She admitted her landmark day was not easy as she had to get there by beating her Australian pal Maya Joint in the final.

While the popular 28-year-old Queenslander was celebrating her victory with sympathetic words for her young tearful compatriot, Talia Gibson was annexing her Australian number one ranking elsewhere on the Asian swing.

Gibson, another player enjoying a breakthrough 2026 campaign, had reached the Singapore Open final on the same day.

Even though she lost to Canadian Leylah Fernandez, missing out on her maiden title, her big points haul at the bigger WTA 500 event meant she would leapfrog Birrell in the rankings.

Birrell capped her breakthrough year, which had featured a sensational win over Jessica Pegula in the French Open, with a 6–4, 6–2 victory over Joint in the Seoul final.

It was the first all-Australian WTA championship match since Sam Stosur beat Daria Gavrilova at Strasbourg in 2017, with Queenslander Birrell ending up finally lifting a trophy after losing her two previous finals in Osaka in 2024 and Chennai last year.

"It was quite difficult for us today because we are very good friends," Birrell said before speaking directly to Joint.

"You've had a tough year, I know. I hope you know how proud I am of you and how amazing you are."

Joint has had an up-and-down year, with a back injury and a long losing sequence finally ended when she earned her triumph over the returning Serena Williams at Wimbledon that made worldwide headlines.

"It's tough against a friend and I'm really proud of you," Joint said, congratulating her compatriot.

Europe downs Team World at Laver Cup

A day after Alex de Minaur beat Alexander Zverev to keep Team World's hopes alive in the Laver Cup, a doubles loss featuring the Australian and American Taylor Fritz ended Andre Agassi's team's bid for victory.

Agassi had planned to lean on de Minaur again after the doubles to take on Carlos Alcaraz, but the loss to Italy's Flavio Cobolli and Czech Jakub Mensik meant Europe took an unassailable lead in the competition.

"We were very close," de Minaur said.

"Yesterday, we won two supers [10-point tiebreakers] and lost one with Taylor playing an epic match.

"We were up against it from the get-go; we were the underdogs and put in a hell of a fight. A couple points here and there could have changed the whole tie."

World.title: Cleary requires surgery on both feet after horrific NRL injury
World.content:
Nathan Cleary will require surgery on both feet, with his father Ivan revealing the superstar halfback had been playing on a broken right foot before suffering a compound fracture of his left ankle.

In the gruesome aftermath to the Panthers' 22–14 preliminary final loss to Newcastle, it was revealed Dylan Edwards played through a ruptured PCL, Isaah Yeo a ruptured pec, and Blaize Talagi came off with an Achilles rupture.

The injuries ultimately cursed the Panthers, who led the Knights 14–6 at half-time, and will likely have long-term ramifications for Australia in the end-of-season World Cup.

Penrith had hoped to get Cleary through Sunday's game unscathed after keeping him and his injured right foot on the bench for the opening 25 minutes.

But 10 minutes later the superstar halfback was exiting the field on the back of a medicab sucking on a green whistle, after a hip-drop tackle from Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland.

Crossland was sent off, with Cleary's ankle also dislocated and his mother, Bec, among those in the stands in tears.

"He watched the game in the ambulance, but it made him feel worse probably," coach and father Ivan Cleary said.

"I went and saw him at half-time and saw the whole crew and my family were in there. That was a bit hard, it was a bit emotional. But the show goes on."

Dynasties and destinies swing on Cleary's horror ankle injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

Cleary also confirmed his son had been battling a broken bone in his right foot. Penrith had previously been coy about the nature of a "stress-related bone issue".

The Penrith halfback had been in doubt for Sunday's match in the lead-up, after he limped through the end of their week-one win over the Sydney Roosters.

"He'll have to get the other foot done as well because that was broken as well," Ivan Cleary said.

"That's why I was even more emotional with what happened to him because I knew what he went through to get himself right to play today."

Beyond their halfback, Edwards was hurt when making a break in the opening half and Talagi limped off with 13 minutes to play.

Yeo, meanwhile, returned from a ruptured pec to play in the finals. He will now require surgery, with the Kangaroos captain in doubt for the World Cup.

World.title: Matty Johns breaks down in tears after Knights end NRL grand final drought
World.content:
Former Knights star Matty Johns has broken down in tears as he heaped praise on the Newcastle team and its fans after a gripping and gritty NRL preliminary final win over Penrith.

The Knights played more than half the game with 12 men on the field after Phoenix Crossland was sent off for a hip drop that graphically broke Nathan Cleary's leg.

Penrith scored shortly after to take a 14-6 lead into half-time, but Justin Holbrook's Knights defended resolutely against a scrappy Panthers side and managed to score three second-half tries to progress to the grand final against the Roosters.

Knights stun Panthers to reach GF The Newcastle Knights reach their first NRL grand final since 2001, defeating the Penrith Panthers 22-14 after Nathan Cleary suffered a catastrophic leg injury in the first half.

The women's team won back-to-back NRLW premierships in 2022 and 2023, but Newcastle has not played in a men's grand final since Andrew Johns led the Knights to victory over the Eels in the 2001 grand final.

A quarter of a century and five wooden spoons later, the team will return to the final day of the season next week after a similarly remarkable upset win over the most dominant team in NRL history.

So it is hardly surprising that Hunter native and former Knights star Matty Johns was incredibly emotional straight after full-time.

"To be honest, I don't know what to say," he said on Fox Sports.

"It was unbelievable. Incredible effort in that second half. I just feel so happy for all the fans."

Players past and present, as well as coach Justin Holbrook, hailed the fans who travelled to the game. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

It became increasingly hard to find the words as tears started to flow and emotion took over.

"They've had to put up with a lot of shit for a lot of years to get back to where they are now," Johns said.

Even getting to the game on Sunday was tough as an issue with a freight train caused delays and cancellations on the Central Coast and Newcastle train line, forcing fans to find alternate routes and replacement services to get down to Sydney, which led to traffic jams on the M1 motorway on a sodden afternoon.

"But it just didn't stop them in the wet," Johns said of the crowd at Homebush, which was hugely in favour of the visiting Novocastrians.

The Stadium Australia crowd was heavily favouring the away team. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"When you run onto a field like that and you look up and you see all those Newcastle fans, you don't leave the field defeated.

"If not for the fans they don't win today."

Holbrook sprinted around the field to pay tribute to the fans who turned up, and who have continued to turn up even when the team was struggling, including last year when they finished last for the fifth time in 21 seasons.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

"We want to make our community proud, our Hunter region, and for the boys to deliver that performance, it was so good to see them all hang around," he said.

"We went down to 12 [when Crossland was sent off] and then 30,000 make you feel like you've got 14 out there."

Captain Kalyn Ponga agreed the supporters helped the team get over the line.

"They're a big reason why we won today," he said.

"They're loud, they're passionate, they're vocal and we're gonna need them next week."

World.title: Freo finds joy in AFLW win, Pies finally off the mark
World.content:
Fremantle's women have lifted their club as they surged into the AFLW top eight, while Collingwood broke through for its first win of the season.

The fast-starting Dockers outscored Adelaide 28-0 in the first quarter and led by as much as 45 on their way to a comfortable 9.6 (60) to 5.5 (35) victory over Adelaide at Unley Oval.

Adelaide (3-4) kicked three straight goals either side of three-quarter time, but never got the deficit below 25, as Fremantle (4-3) defended its advantage, unlike its male counterparts in Saturday's AFL grand final.

It was the Dockers' first win in their past seven AFLW encounters with Adelaide, who had a 9-1 record in the fixture before Sunday.

In the other early game on Sunday, Collingwood (1-6) outlasted GWS 4.10 (34) to 3.7 (25) in a low-scoring arm wrestle at Victoria Park.

The Giants (1-6) led by margins of one, four and seven at the end of the first three quarters respectively, but Collingwood dominated the final term.

They finished with 18 more inside 50s and 16 more contested possessions.

In Sydney, the Lions fell short of a stirring comeback of their own in a 5.7 (37) to 3.5 (23) defeat to the Swans.

The victory held Sydney's position in the top four and saw Brisbane's record fall to a disappointing 2-5.

The Lions were second best for most of the afternoon but managed to stay in touch through three quarters, and were only a point behind at the final term.

But after Cynthia Hamilton goaled inside the first minute of the last quarter, the Swans didn't look back, running out comfortable 12-point winners.

In the final game of round seven, Gold Coast took St Kilda another step closer to the wooden spoon by running out 10.9 (69) to 6.3 (39) winners.

The Saints led by 15 points at half-time but were gunned down by the home side after the break, conceding eight goals to one as the Suns moved to sixth place on the AFLW ladder.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Dynasties and destinies swing on Cleary's horror injury
World.content:
Mark the 35th minute of Sunday's NRL preliminary final as the hinge on which a storied dynasty and a potential premiership destiny swung.

Penrith and Newcastle had fought a first-half that made both look like worthy foes for the Roosters in next week's grand final.

The Knights faithful turned Stadium Australia into a little piece of the Hunter, proving yet again they would follow their team into hell itself if Sid Fogg's would charter a bus there.

Francis Manuleleua's long-range try, the latest scorching adventure of the screaming Knights, gave the beast inside the 55,000-strong crowd a smell of blood and it turned the Panthers into strangers in their own country.

The Penrith half of the crowd rose for Blaize Talagi's score off a clever Jack Cogger kick, but never has Nathan Cleary, benched before kick-off, copped such treatment on his home turf as he did before he entered the game in the 20th minute.

Just 10 minutes later came the tackle that ended his season as he suffered a graphic fracture to his ankle, also ending Phoenix Crossland's afternoon after he was sent off, and putting this game on the raggedy edge.

In the end, it was the Knights who pushed the Panthers over the side to write their names in history, with a 22-14 win that sends Newcastle to their first grand final in 25 years.

Cleary suffered a compound fracture after a tackle from Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The two sides provided a fascinating contrast from the start as they left the field following the warm-up.

Penrith, the ultimate professionals and avatars of pure ruthlessness, had eyes of steel, a picture of focus.

Newcastle, by contrast, waved to friends and family, faces beaming that they were here together on the verge of a dream.

Rage and joy proved to be equally potent fuels, with rare courage on both sides amid the furious desperation you only see when the stakes are highest.

The Knights finished with 12 on the field after Crossland's dismissal but, somehow, rarely looked shorthanded.

Newcastle through to grand final after Cleary's horrific leg break The Newcastle Knights are through to their first NRL Grand Final since 2001, defeating the Penrith Panthers 22-14 after Nathan Cleary suffered a catastrophic leg injury in the first half.

There is a temptation to call that a miracle, but Newcastle didn't need divine intervention to flat-out-play the Panthers in a second half.

They bent occasionally but never broke as Penrith fought hard, denied only by a series of last-gasp efforts from the Knights.

Kalyn Ponga pulled off a tackle on Moses Leota that any footy hit man would have been proud of, while Manuleleua and another young bull, prop Cody Hopwood, tempted fate and won in taking down a rampaging Brian To'o when the Panthers winger got a clear shot at the line.

Mat Croker dived on loose balls like they were live grenades while Dane Gagai played like his Newcastle life depended on it, and given he has earned one last day as a Knight, it kind of did.

They were able to take advantage of the Panthers not quite being their razor-sharp selves, as best typified by Smith's first try off a quick tap that caught Penrith on the hop.

The Panthers missed Cleary, their edges blunted, but Casey McLean came agonisingly close to scoring.

It is a mark of the steel in the Panthers that they weren't out of it until Sandon Smith's late intercept try, even with injuries mounting.

Aside from Cleary — already carrying a broken foot into the game — Blaize Talagi did his Achilles, Dylan Edwards hurt his PCL and Isaah Yeo defied belief to play through a torn pec.

They regrouped well in the moments after Cleary's injury, scoring through Lindsay Smith while the game was still in something of a punch-drunk stupor.

But they did not trouble the scorers again as Newcastle ran in three tries in the second half, all of which began from their own side of halfway.

Newcastle have a chance to create a special piece of history. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

That ability to strike fast and from anywhere on the field is the Knights' greatest gift — it has happened too many times to call this a charmed run or a triumph of abstract, random brilliance.

It has taken them through a high-octane South Sydney, to the heart of Auckland and back and now, a man down and all, through the greatest dynasty many will ever know.

That dynasty is not at its end, but preliminary final losses in each of the past two years show how thin the margins have become.

Penrith is still one of the heavyweights, but the world is changing and Newcastle, with their speed and hunger and endless belief, are the first of the new powers to rise.

Those Knights will be underdogs again next Sunday against the Roosters, with all their glory and splendour, and they must overcome the weight of history.

Of the 117 premiers in the history of Australian rugby league, 115 have finished in the top four. For Newcastle to prevail, it is beyond once in a lifetime and closer to once in the lifetime of the sport.

But after what the Knights have been through and what they have done to get here, the odds seem to matter little.

At this point it feels like there is nothing Newcastle cannot do, no challenge they cannot rise to and no foe they could fear.

World.title: Wallabies reduced to 11 men in chaotic upset win over world champ Boks
World.content:
The Wallabies have desperately held on to defeat the world champion Springboks 42–38 in Perth after being reduced to 11 players during the final five minutes.

In one of the most chaotic finishes in Test rugby history, the Wallabies were shown four yellow cards late in the match after comfortably leading 42–17.

Captain Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Hunter Paisami were each sent to the sin-bin by referee Andrea Piardi.

Wilson was shown a yellow card for a high shot on Malcolm Marx in the 69th minute, before the Springboks were awarded a penalty try due to an infringement from Lonergan.

As Lonergan received his marching orders, the Wallabies' lead was cut to 42–24.

They subsequently lost Suaalii for the remainder of the match after he committed an offside play.

The Springboks capitalised on their numerical advantage to score a converted try through Morné van den Berg.

Wallabies captain Harry Wilson (left) attempts to speak with referee Andrea Piardi. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

The Wallabies appeared to seal victory in the 76th minute when Tom Wright intercepted a pass from Springboks captain André Esterhuizen.

Wright raced away to cross the goal line, but the try was denied as Paisami was ruled to have made contact with Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu's head in an earlier tackle.

Paisami was given his yellow card, leaving the Wallabies with 11 players.

The Springboks got within striking distance of the Wallabies on the scoreboard after Ox Nché scored a converted try in the 78th minute.

The Wallabies' lead had been slashed to four points, but they managed to hold on and record a famous victory in front of a boisterous crowd of 54,678.

Adding to the bizarre scenes during the final 10 minutes, Piardi was forced to speak with his fellow match officials via a mobile phone following a malfunction with their communications system.

"It was a crazy last 10 minutes," Wilson told the Nine Network after the match.

"But that first 70 minutes … the way we played, we implemented our game plan. We did exactly what we wanted.

"We stepped up in the physical battle and I'm so proud of the boys."

The Wallabies survived an extraordinary finish in Perth. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Wilson was right to highlight the Wallabies' dominance until the flurry of late yellow cards.

They led 24–17 at half-time and extended their advantage in the second term with tries to Wilson and Max Jorgensen.

Lonergan helped build scoreboard pressure with two conversions and as many penalty goals.

Len Ikitau, playing in his preferred outside centre position, impressed in the first half with two tries.

His move back to the number 13 jersey meant Suaalii played on the wing, with the former NRL star handling the role superbly.

The Springboks arrived in Australia following their recent victory in the four-Test series against the All Blacks.

The physical and emotional impact of their win in the series, billed as Rugby's Greatest Rugby Rivalry, will be open to debate.

They made 13 changes to the starting line-up that defeated the All Blacks 43–28 in Baltimore earlier this month.

The triumph saw the Wallabies awarded the Mandela Challenge Plate for the first time since 2022, which was also the last occasion they beat the Springboks on Australian soil.

They face the All Blacks in the first of two Bledisloe Cup Tests in Auckland on October 10.

The return clash will be played in Sydney on October 17.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Wallaroos 'got some work to do' despite snapping losing streak
World.content:
Snapping a six-match losing streak was not enough to leave the Wallaroos satisfied with their 30-10 win over Scotland in Edinburgh this morning.

The Wallaroos were outplayed in the first half, with Scotland entering the break with a 10-5 lead in the WXV Global Series Test.

But following a blunt half-time address from their coaching staff and with the wind behind them in the second term, the Wallaroos regrouped to score 25 unanswered points and secure their first victory since March.

Desiree Miller provided the only points for the Wallaroos in the first half with a try.

Samantha Wood, Brianna Hoy and player-of-the-match Faitala Moleka crossed the stripe in the second half.

The three second-half tries were scored during seven minutes, with Hoy and Moleka's efforts coming while Scotland was reduced to 14 players following Evie Gallagher's yellow card.

Wood added two conversions and as many penalty goals to finish with a 15-point haul.

"Credit to Scotland, they found opportunities, and you could see where they exploited those areas," Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona said after the match.

"Overall, we know we have a lot of things to improve on, but we'll take the positives out of that."

Palu Sekona said the Wallaroos were taught some harsh lessons in the previous week's 29-26 loss to France in Aix-en-Provence.

The Wallaroos had led 19-0 during the match, while France had only 11 players on the field at one stage due to red and yellow cards.

"We learned from last week's game," Palu Sekona said.

"We have to be relentless. When you get opportunities like that [Gallagher's yellow card], you've got to capitalise."

The Wallaroos celebrate Desiree Miller's (right) first-half try. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance Tim Walsh is essentially the Wallaroos' caretaker head coach until Sione Fukofuka assumes the role next year.

Walsh was unimpressed with the Wallaroos' display in the opening half, admitting he did not hide his feelings when he spoke to the players at the break.

"It wasn't a pleasant message," Walsh said.

"I thought if we didn't have two or three individuals that really took the game to Scotland, I reckon it would have been a draw, or we would have lost.

"So I wasn't happy with our performance. Glad we got the win and came home with it, but the advantage was the wind and a few key players who I thought had tremendous games."

The Wallaroos are heading back to Australia, with two WXV Global Series Tests against Scotland coming up next month.

They play each other in Sydney on October 17, ahead of the Wallabies' Bledisloe Cup clash against the All Blacks.

The final Test will be staged in Canberra on October 23.

As far as Walsh is concerned, the Wallaroos will not be taking the easy route on the training paddock over the next three weeks.

"We've got some work to do," he said.

Tech.title: Out of the Park Baseball lets me enjoy baseball even when the Mets suck
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

If you were to ask me what game or game series I’ve sunk the most time into, the answer would be easy: Out of the Park Baseball (OOTP). I have spent roughly 2,300 hours, according to Steam, playing various editions of the game. OOTP isn’t like MLB The Show or Super Mega Baseball. It’s not graphically impressive. It’s not a blast of simple arcade fun. It is basically a spreadsheet pretending to be a video game. It’s fantasy baseball, but without having to wait six months to see how disappointing that sleeper draft pick will be, because you can plow through an entire season in as little as a few hours.

You can play individual games and dig into play-by-play managing in OOTP if you want. But that becomes tedious. And frankly, it’s not where the game is the most fun. Instead, I think the game is at its best when you sit in the GM’s chair and maybe make some helpful “suggestions” about how to structure the lineup or bullpen.

The UI is complicated and dense. 90 percent of the time, you’re just looking at rows of stats and scouting reports. And the level of detail is deep. OOTP includes not just current MLB players, but historical MLB players, all minor league teams, Korea’s KBO League, and even the entire World Baseball Classic.

There’s something thrilling about digging through all this info and trying to find that diamond in the rough during a draft. Someone who might become the new franchise player for your favorite team in this alternate universe. Deciding whether to bet on that prospect developing into a superstar, or to trade them for an undeniable big-league All-Star is stressful. And you even have to worry about fans abandoning you if you fail to re-sign your favorite player.

On my Mets, Brandon Nimmo isn’t just a good player, he’s a damned superstar. Kodai Senga has won three Cy Young Awards. I signed Juan Soto, but also traded a raft of mid-tier prospects for Ronald Acuña Jr., made the playoffs four years in a row, and eventually won a World Series. (Look, as a Mets fan, I need this fantasy world, don’t harsh my vibe.)

Perhaps the best part of OOTP Baseball, though, is that it kinda lets you play however you want. It’s deeply customizable. You can manually play every game if you want. Or you can speed-simulate entire seasons in a couple of hours. Want an easier experience where players don’t get hurt? Turn down or off injuries. Don’t want to worry about budgets? Play in commissioner mode and tell the team owner where to stick it. And because it mostly just sits there, statically waiting for you, it’s easy to just leave it running in the background and dip in and out when you’ve got a few spare minutes.

OOTP Baseball is a cozy sim for a very particular brand of sports nerd. If you love fantasy baseball and wish you could play it year-round (and don’t want to deal with friends arguing about whether their bid for Alonso came in on time), or maybe you dig the idea of a cozy game like Tiny Bookshop, but wish they had a more Sabermetric bent, OOTP Baseball might be for you.

The current version, OOTP Baseball 27, is available now on Steam or directly from the developer.

Tech.title: Engram is a sampler that turns broken AI hallucinations into music
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Music startup Thoughtful Things has just launched the Kickstarter campaign for its first instrument, Engram. It’s a sampler and groovebox that uses AI to mangle incoming audio and even hallucinate completely new sounds. This isn’t Suno in a box, though. This isn’t a “push-button, get-song” device, aimed at creating something that sounds ready for top-40 radio. It’s about creating experimental, uncanny sounds and pushing AI audio models beyond their limits.

Engram isn’t connected to the internet. Instead, it runs a “tiny AI” locally. According to the Kickstarter listing, the model is designed in-house and custom-trained. The company says:

“We’ve trained our audio models on open datasets that only contain audio licensed for commercial use (CC-BY or similar). We have not trained and will never train our models on non-commercial, pirated, or otherwise stolen data.”

The company also plans to open up Engram’s firmware so that others can tweak it or load their own custom models. In the campaign video, founder Evan King uses his voice to ask for “piano,” and Engram spits out something glitchy and vaguely piano-like. He says to think of Engram as a “field recorder for latent space.” It’s about exploring the world of AI hallucinations and experimental sound design. It even draws inspiration from circuit bending, allowing you to tweak and even break its tiny AI models.

Thoughtful Things is launching with a limited run of Engrams for the Kickstarter campaign, starting at $675. The company hasn’t said what the retail price will be, though it’s likely to be between $850 and $900, as the $675 pledge is listed as a 30 percent discount.

Tech.title: OpenAI agents tried to ‘bruteforce’ a UN website
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to Howard-Jones, the agents were likely tasked with retrieving publicly available data related to the Productive Capacities Index (PCI) through the UNCTADstat API. However, the agents did not appear to have direct API access and were limited in their ability to pull data from UNCTADstat because of restrictions on their HTTP tools.

The agents eventually worked out a way to bypass their limitations and start pulling data from the site, but still encountered some errors. At this point, the AI went from creative to deceptive. Believing that the errors were due to its requests being caught by a nonexistent filter, it started to mask its behavior. It eventually realized it could hijack Google’s XSS game (a cross-site scripting learning tool) to accomplish its goals. The agents resorted to increasingly aggressive tactics to get access to UN data.

OpenAI and the UN did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

I asked Brad to share his homescreen and the apps and things he cares about. Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:

Images: Brad Bourque / The Verge

The phone: Pixel 9 Pro XL

The wallpaper: My homescreen wallpaper is just an included Pixel wallpaper of plants in mellow green tones. My lockscreen is a fan-made Tekken Tag Tournament poster featuring Armor King and Modelo. It doesn’t have to make sense if the vibes are right.

The apps:

Right up top you’ll find two of my favorite mobile games. The first is Idle Obelisk Miner , an idle game I recently started playing that I’ve found compelling and generous given the genre’s normal conditions. I’ve been playing for just over a month and a half and I’m only at 3.16 percent completion, so I know I have a long road ahead of me.

The other is Nubby’s Number Factory , an oddball roguelike that I’ve sunk dozens of hours into on Steam. The game has a funky style and charm that reminds me of old Adobe Flash browser games, but with modern sensibilities and huge replayability.

Other than that, there isn’t much exciting to discuss. I like to keep calendar and weather widgets prominently featured on my first screen, mostly because I’m bad at remembering what I have coming up on any given day and Portland is known for surprise rainstorms.

The main screen is mostly the boring stuff that I use every day, with apps like mail, texting, and YouTube given priority positions for easy access. My dark secret is that, if you swipe one page to the right, it’s all a disorganized mess of apps with no sorting or folders. If I’m looking for a specific app, I’ll swipe up and search for it.

I also asked Brad to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:

Ever since the final major Destiny 2 update, I’ve been chiseling away at some of the expansions I missed and finishing up old collections. With the recent announcement that old vaulted content would be coming back, I’m planning on continuing to sink time into one of my favorite games ever.

The other game I’ve been playing quite a lot of over the past few months is Old School RuneScape . We’re at the end of Game Changer ’s latest season. It’s Dropout TV’s groundbreaking game show where the rules change every time, so I’m watching that religiously on Monday evenings. The most recent season has been one of the strongest yet, and constantly has me laughing and occasionally crying over its sweet and incredibly creative episodes.

For music, I’ve been on a really chill kick lately, with Janelle Monáe’s The Age of Pleasure and Tom Misch’s Full Circle headlining a lot of my morning writing and deal-hunting sessions. I’ve been listening to a lot of vinyl recently, which I’ve found gives a nice rhythm and ritual to my day that just turning on Spotify and hitting shuffle doesn’t.

Tech.title: The smart home graveyard is getting crowded
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the fragile state of your connected devices, follow Jennifer Pattison Tuohy. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

A decade ago, a group of former Apple engineers built a beautiful smart oven. With a built-in scale, restaurant-grade heating elements, a camera, and the intelligence to recognize a chicken breast and cook it perfectly, the June Oven set the standard for smart cooking appliances. At $1,495, it was absurdly expensive, but it quickly grew a small, devoted following that expanded when the company introduced a more modestly priced model.

This past Tuesday, June went dark. Weber, which bought the company in January 2021 and stopped making the ovens in 2022, shut off the app and cloud services, leaving its users with a sleek-looking toaster oven. There will be no app control, no software updates, and no new AI food recognition to crisp that strudel perfectly. You can still use it as an oven, but there will be no support or parts, and if you have to factory reset it for some reason, that could be the nail in the coffin. Weber told me it considered open-sourcing the technology for someone else to keep it alive, but decided against it, citing the fact June’s IP is part of its Weber Connect platform.

How it’s going

The silver lining, if you want to see it, is that most of these gadgets degrade rather than die outright. June and Brava will still work as ovens. Nest Thermostats can still control your heating and cooling, just like the $30 plastic wall wart they replaced, and a Neato will still vacuum your floors. But the remote access, voice control, updates, and other smart features you bought the devices for are gone. Some — like Nest Secure — are now pure e-waste.

There’s always the possibility of a rescue, but it’s rare. Some enterprising user may figure out a way to connect a headless corpse to Home Assistant, the open-source platform that has become the default refuge for the smart home undead. When smart lighting platform Insteon shut down in 2022, its users bought the company and resurrected it. Bose reversed course and open-sourced its SoundTouch API, and Pebble’s founder brought the iconic smartwatch back to life after the Rebble alliance kept it on life support. June’s co-founder Matt Van Horn said on X that he tried to keep the servers online but to no avail.

The smart home has reached a tipping point. Many of its early pioneers are aging out — a decade plus is a long time for a startup. Most have been bought by bigger companies, likely attracted by the shiny thing but then quickly dismayed by the bottom line. Back then, a cloud server was cheaper to build than a local hub, but servers continue to cost money, and once a company decides to shut down a product, reasons to keep paying fade rapidly. This appears to be what’s happening to Level Lock, another former-Apple-engineer startup that produced a beautiful replacement for a common household item. Assa Abloy bought the smart lock company and abruptly fired most of the team. It’s still alive, but how long it will continue is a big question.

What happens next

Three things need to happen to prevent the smart home from burning more users: we need consumer protections; manufacturers need to step up and build in safeguards; we need to know how to protect ourselves.

Consumer Reports is pushing for legislation around connected IoT devices, including making manufacturers push a local API to a device before killing its cloud. This would allow it to keep talking to a platform like Home Assistant instead of becoming a paperweight. This is essentially what Bose did with SoundTouch, and other companies should follow that lead (I’m not holding my breath on legislation).

When building a connected device, manufacturers need to make it function without the cloud. Include physical buttons so it doesn’t rely on an app, and use local protocols alongside any cloud connectivity. This is a key issue the smart home standard Matter was designed to address: Matter devices can retain many functions in a Matter platform, regardless of what happens to the manufacturer’s business. Other local protocols like Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread, and Bluetooth similarly help futureproof products.

My advice if you’re buying a smart home device remains the same. Make sure it offers local control, has physical buttons (or a direct remote control), and can operate “offline.” Don’t dismiss cloud-connected features; they can add real value, but remember that any feature reliant on a server could one day die. A gadget that only talks to the cloud is already halfway in the grave.
